ACAD.summary:
Acadia National Park protects about 50,000 acres of the mid-coast of Maine — portions of Mount Desert Island, part of Isle au Haut, the tip of the Schoodic Peninsula and all or part of 16 smaller islands — and the tallest mountains on the U.S. eastern seaboard, Cadillac Mountain at their apex. [1] Glacial ice shaped it: from Cadillac’s domed summit to the U-shaped valley of Bubble Pond, the ice scoured away older rock to reveal the granite beneath and left boulders strewn across the land. Spruce-fir forest dominated the park until 1947, when fire burned 10,000 acres. [2]

The 2011 park brochure says some artifacts from the island’s clam-shell heaps have been carbon-dated to 5,000 years; the 2016 foundation document says the park’s cultural resources span 5,000 years, and also that the landscape has drawn people for more than 10,000 years, beginning with the Wabanaki. Samuel Champlain named the island Isle des Monts Deserts in 1604; after 150 years of French–British war, English colonists settled permanently in 1761. In 1901 Harvard president Charles W. Eliot formed the Hancock County Trustees of Public Reservations, which acquired 5,000 acres of donated land; President Wilson proclaimed Sieur de Monts National Monument on July 8, 1916. Congress made it Lafayette National Park on February 26, 1919 — the first national park east of the Mississippi — and it became Acadia in 1929. [2] [1]

The foundation document calls Acadia the first national park created from private lands gifted to the public. It receives an average of 2.5 million visits a year, and the document names climate change a key issue: a significant number of the park’s roads, trails, buildings and utilities sit directly beside shorelines, threatened by sea-level rise and the frequency and intensity of storms. [1]

climate.html: A 2014 Park Service resource brief compared recent decades with the record since 1901 and found six temperature measures at Acadia in the “extreme warm” range and three precipitation measures “extreme wet,” none extreme cold or dry: recent conditions, it concluded, are already moving beyond the historical range. [5] The park’s climate page puts numbers to it: annual average temperature up 3.4°F over the last century; the surrounding Gulf of Maine up about 3°F and among the fastest-warming parts of the global ocean; sea level up eight inches since 1950, with shorelines — Wabanaki heritage sites among them — eroding. A June 2021 storm dropped more than five inches of rain in under three hours and caused over $1.5 million in damage to carriage roads, trails, streams and paved roads. If sea-level rise continues unabated, the park says, Thunder Hole will very likely be covered. [6]

sources.title: Monahan & Fisichelli, Recent Climate Change Exposure of Acadia National Park (NPS Resource Brief, July 31, 2014)
NPS, Acadia National Park: Climate Change (nps.gov)

indigenous.html:
The park’s 2007 ethnographic overview, by Harald Prins and Bunny McBride, names five Wabanaki nations — Abenaki, Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy and Penobscot; the park’s website names four, without the Abenaki. [3] [4] Wabanaki guiding Champlain to the island in 1604 called it Pemetic, “range of mountains,” and the sakom (chief) Asticou’s invitation led to the 1613 Saint Sauveur mission at Somes Sound, destroyed by an English privateer from Virginia. Within a few decades, the authors write, diseases, firewater and firearms left up to 90 percent of the Wabanaki dead — what they call an American Indian holocaust. From the mid-1800s island Wabanaki encampments sold crafts to summer visitors; in 1970 a short-lived Wabanaki educational center, T.R.I.B.E., was founded within the park. [3]

The park says that for most of the last century the federal government barred Wabanaki people from harvesting sweetgrass inside Acadia; since 2015 the Park Service has worked toward renewed gathering by federally recognized tribes. [4]

sources.title: Prins & McBride, Asticou's Island Domain: Wabanaki Peoples at Mount Desert Island 1500–2000, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment, Vol. 1 (NPS, 2007), Executive Summary
NPS, Acadia National Park: Wabanaki (nps.gov, Wayback Machine snapshot of January 18, 2025; page last updated December 3, 2024), 'Sweetgrass Gathering'

labor_ccc.html: Acadia’s administrators were among the first to apply for a Civilian Conservation Corps company. In May 1933 enrollees arrived at McFarland Hill — today’s park headquarters — and camps followed south of Great Pond in June and at Ellsworth in July. From 1933 to 1942 the three camps took on nearly 450 projects in forestry, watershed development, beautification, trail construction and facility development. Apart from two out-of-state contingents, the companies were Maine men; McFarland was the only camp in Maine, besides district headquarters, to run for the whole program. The park’s CCC study (final draft, 2009), drawing partly on interviews with 26 former enrollees, names the Perpendicular Trail, the Beech Cliffs Ladder Trail and much of the Ocean Trail as surviving CCC work, and Seawall and Blackwoods campgrounds, Sieur de Monts Spring and Sand Beach among enduring New Deal sites — stressing that the Corps was only one of several federal agencies involved. [7]

sources.title: Moreira, Dean, Dudley & Champney, The Civilian Conservation Corps at Acadia National Park (final draft, May 12, 2009)

AMIS.name: Amistad National Recreation Area
AMIS.summary: Amistad National Recreation Area was authorized by Congress in 1965 and established in 1990 along the U.S.–Mexico border near Del Rio, Texas. The recreation area surrounds Amistad Reservoir, a 64,860-acre international lake formed by the Amistad Dam on the Rio Grande, built jointly by the United States and Mexico. The region contains some of the oldest and best-preserved rock art in North America, with over 200 known pictograph sites created by hunter-gatherer peoples over a span of roughly 4,000 years. The Fate Bell Shelter and Panther Cave are among the most significant archaeological sites in the Lower Pecos Canyonlands.

ANDE.name: Andersonville NHS
ANDE.summary: Andersonville National Historic Site in southwestern Georgia preserves the site of Camp Sumter, the largest Confederate military prison during the Civil War. Operational from February 1864 to April 1865, the stockade held up to 32,000 Union prisoners of war in a space originally designed for 10,000, and nearly 13,000 died from disease, malnutrition, and exposure. The site was designated a national historic site in 1970 and also serves as home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, which honors all American prisoners of war throughout the nation's history. The adjacent Andersonville National Cemetery, established in 1865, remains an active national cemetery.

ANTI.name: Antietam National Battlefield
ANTI.summary: Antietam National Battlefield in Sharpsburg, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Antietam, fought on September 17, 1862 — the bloodiest single day in American military history, with an estimated 23,000 casualties. The Union's strategic victory gave President Abraham Lincoln the political leverage to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later, fundamentally shifting the war's purpose to include the abolition of slavery. Established as a national battlefield site in 1890, the park encompasses approximately 3,230 acres of rolling farmland and includes landmarks such as Burnside Bridge, the Dunker Church, and Bloody Lane.

Purcell, An Administrative History of Arches National Park (Museum of Northern Arizona for NPS, April 30, 2019) — ch. 1 timeline, ch. 7

ARCH.summary:
Water and ice, extreme temperatures and underground salt movement carved the red-rock country of Arches, which holds one of the world’s greatest densities of natural arches: more than 2,000 cataloged openings, from three-foot holes to Landscape Arch, 306 feet base to base. The salt bed beneath the park, thousands of feet thick in places, was laid down some 300 million years ago when a sea flooded the region and evaporated; most arches form in the salmon-colored Entrada Sandstone above it. The landscape is still changing. In 1991 a slab 60 feet long fell from the underside of Landscape Arch, and the park’s own brochure concedes that its geologic story is “probably” right, the evidence being largely circumstantial. [1]

Archaic peoples, and later ancestral Puebloan, Fremont and Ute peoples, used this country for thousands of years. Disabled Civil War veteran John Wesley Wolfe and his son Fred ranched here for over 20 years from the late 1800s. [1] After prospector Alex Ringhoffer brought the formations to the attention of a railroad official in 1923, President Herbert Hoover proclaimed Arches National Monument on April 12, 1929, withdrawing 4,520 acres; an estimated 500 people visited that year. The monument grew in 1938 to take in Delicate Arch and in 1969 to 82,953 acres before Congress made it a national park of 73,379 acres on November 12, 1971. [1]

Edward Abbey, a seasonal ranger here in 1956–57, drew on those seasons for Desert Solitaire (1968). Visitation passed 1.5 million in 2016, and the park’s 2019 administrative history describes Arches as approaching the threshold of its visitor carrying capacity. [1]

climate.html: A 2025 NPS science report used satellite images to track the park’s vegetation from 2000 to 2019, which it calls a very dry period. Dry years and multi-year dry spells caused substantial declines in plant cover that largely rebounded by the study’s end, and by then the growing season was starting on average 11.9 days earlier and ending 10.2 days later. The report offers its findings as a guide to what, where and why vegetation may change as the climate does. [1]

sources.title: Landscape Phenology, Vegetation Condition, and Relations with Climate at Arches National Park, 2000–2019 (NPS Science Report NPS/SR—2025/284)

indigenous.html:
In a 2016 ethnographic study by Richard Stoffle and University of Arizona colleagues, representatives of the Pueblo of Zuni (A:shiwi), the Hopi Tribe, the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, the Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation, the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah and the Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians visited five study areas in the park; each, the report says, regards Arches as a very powerful place. In their shared view the park was primarily a place of ceremony for the people who farmed Moab Valley; the arches are portals in space and time, and the hoodoos sentient beings. [1]

Hopi representatives call the region Pavayoykasi, the Place of Rainbows; Zuni representatives describe a clan migration through the park in their origin narrative; Ute representatives identified the park’s Purple Sage area as one of three known Ute gathering areas for that medicine in the Southwest. The report cautions that its summary is not an exact representation of their voices. [1]

sources.title: Stoffle, Pickering, Brooks, Sittler & Van Vlack, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment for Arches National Park (University of Arizona BARA for NPS, June 2016), ch. 1 Executive Summary

labor_ccc.html:
No funds were allocated for development at Arches until 1940, when a Civilian Conservation Corps camp of 200 men, NP-7-U, was built near the mouth of Moab Canyon for the monument’s exclusive use. Its crews began the entrance road up the Moab Fault, blasting the sandstone with large quantities of dynamite, and built most of the custodian’s stone residence, the Rock House (95 percent complete when the camp withdrew, by the custodian’s estimate), at a cost of 3,214 man-days and $5,830.20. [1]

The enrollees came from the Carolinas and other Deep South states and were unaccustomed to Utah’s climate. On December 18, 1940, they struck over what they felt were harsh working conditions in bad weather; the leaders were demoted, the camp telephone line was cut along some 40 poles, and the commanding officer resigned. The camp was withdrawn on May 31, 1942, with less than a mile of the scenic drive finished. [1]

sources.title: Purcell, An Administrative History of Arches National Park (2019), ch. 3, Civilian Conservation Corps

women.html: In 1982 Sherma E. Bierhaus became unit manager of Arches, a post she held until 1986. Purcell’s 2019 administrative history calls her appointment the first time a woman filled the role of superintendent at any national park, a milestone, he notes, at a time when only 22 of 333 other Park Service units were headed by women. When the state worried in 1984 that a new boundary fence would cut 100 head of cattle off from a spring-fed pond 200 feet inside the park, she replied that, given the cliffs used in the fence line, the pond would remain open to them. During her illness for much of 1983, Anna M. Fender served as acting unit manager. [1]

sources.title: Purcell, An Administrative History of Arches National Park (2019), ch. 1 timeline and ch. 3, Custodians, Superintendents, and Unit Managers

ARHO.name: Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial

photos.caption: Arlington House from the air, surrounded by fall foliage
photos.note: On-page caption: "This image was captured from a manned helicopter flight. NPS / Marcey Frutchey"; alt text "Aerial view of Arlington House surrounded by fall foliage." Resized from 5616x3744.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Arlington House archive page — overview (from the 2010 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document Overview, Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial, Virginia (NPS, January 2015)
Snell, Historic Structure Report, Historical Data Section, Vol. I: Arlington House (NPS, 1985), ch. I, Significance of Arlington House

ARHO.summary:
Arlington House stands on a high ridge above the Potomac River, its massive portico facing Washington, D.C. George Washington Parke Custis, Martha Washington’s grandson, was raised by Martha and George Washington; when she died in 1802 he inherited 1,100 acres on the Potomac and the people she had enslaved. Between 1802 and 1818 enslaved workers and free labor built his house, modeled on a Greek temple, as the first memorial to George Washington and a museum for the family’s Washington heirlooms. [1] [2]

In 1831 his only surviving child, Mary Anna Randolph Custis, married Lt. Robert E. Lee in the family parlor. For thirty years the house was the Lees’ home and a working plantation where enslaved people numbered as many as 63 at one time. In April 1861 Lee resigned from the U.S. Army and sided with Virginia; Union troops occupied the heights, the Army built a Freedmen’s Village on the estate in 1863, and in 1864 it declared 200 acres a military cemetery — the beginning of Arlington National Cemetery. By August 1864, the Park Service’s 2015 foundation document says, more than two dozen soldiers had been buried within a few yards of the mansion to keep the Lee family from returning. [1] [2]

A 1925 joint resolution of Congress authorized restoring the mansion as a memorial to Lee; the Park Service took it over in 1933, and it was redesignated Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial in 1972. Only 19 of Custis’s original 1,100 acres lie within the memorial. The 2010 park brochure presents Lee as a figure of post-war reconciliation; the 2015 foundation document also names “Slavery and Freedom” as one of the park’s five interpretive themes and counts the two slave quarters among its fundamental resources. [5] [1] [2]

black.html: The war turned the estate into a refuge. In 1863 the Army founded Freedmen’s Village on roughly 400 acres in the south of the property for people who had escaped or been freed from slavery and come to Washington: it had homes, churches, a school and a hospital, and from 1866 to 1868 residents rented ten-acre parcels of the old estate to farm their way to independence. Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs laid out the 200-acre cemetery so it would not interfere with the village, but wanted soldiers buried nearer the mansion to prevent its future use as a residence. By January 1871 the cemetery’s records counted about 4,100 Black burials — 343 U.S. soldiers and 3,757 former slaves. Once the courts gave the United States clear title, the Army moved to remove civilians from the military reservation: according to the 2024 landscape inventory, the village’s 763 residents were evicted and it was disbanded around 1900 (the 2010 brochure says all were gone by 1890). [3] [4] [1]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Arlington House (NPS, 2009, rev. 2024), Summary pp. 3–4, chronology p. 42, Analysis p. 63
Snell, Historic Structure Report, Historical Data Section, Vol. I (NPS, 1985), ch. III, C.2, Record of Burials table (note to 1871 row)
NPSHistory.com: Arlington House archive page — 2010 NPS brochure (“A Memorial to Lee”)

slavery.html:
George Washington Parke Custis’s will freed the people he held in slavery no later than five years after his death, provided the estate was solvent. He died in 1857; Lee, as executor, managed more than 60 enslaved workers, and in December 1862 he was obliged to carry out the will. The 2010 park brochure quotes Lee calling slavery a moral and political evil while holding that only Providence should decide its fate. Household workers lived in twin quarters built to echo the mansion; Selina Gray, the head housekeeper, lived with her family in one room of the south quarters. [1]

In 1826 Custis gave Maria and Charles Syphax a 17-acre parcel on the estate’s southern edge, where a church for the enslaved community also stood; only in 1865 were they allowed to buy it legally. On March 3, 1930, two of Thornton and Selina Gray’s daughters, Annie Baker (77) and Ada Thompson (73), toured the house with architect L. M. Leisenring and described how its rooms had been used. [3] [4]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Arlington House archive page — 2010 NPS brochure text (“A Home Overrun by War”, “Moment of Decision”, house tour: Winter Kitchen, Slave Quarters)
Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial (NPS, 2009, rev. 2024), chronology p. 41
Snell, Historic Structure Report, Historical Data Section, Vol. I (NPS, 1985), ch. III, B.6.e, Data on Use of Rooms Provided by Former Slaves, 1930

women.html: After her father’s death in 1857 Arlington was legally owned by Mary Anna Custis Lee, though her husband became its master. From her mother’s death in 1853 she managed the household and its enslaved workers despite worsening rheumatoid arthritis; she and her daughters grew roses in the flower garden and sold them to help the American Colonization Society send freed slaves to Liberia. When she left in May 1861 she handed her keys to Selina Gray, who guarded the family’s possessions; by January 1862 Gray found that boxes of Mount Vernon relics had been broken into and reported the theft to General McDowell. In 1864 the government took the estate when Mrs. Lee could not appear in person to pay its taxes. Visiting shortly before her death in 1873, she wrote that it seemed but a dream of the past. [3] [1] [4]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Arlington House (NPS, 2009, rev. 2024), Summary p. 3

BEPA.summary:
A few blocks from the U.S. Capitol, at 144 Constitution Avenue NE, stands a brick federal-period house that the Park Service counts among the oldest residences in Washington, on land the Nacotchtank, or Anacostans, used for hunting and trading. Robert Sewall built the first house here in 1800, and Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin rented it from 1801 to 1813. On August 24, 1814, British troops burned it after, by Sewall’s later claim to Congress, Commodore Joshua Barney’s men, retreating from the Battle of Bladensburg, fired on them from inside; the house standing today was rebuilt on the spot by 1820. [1]

In 1929 the National Woman’s Party, founded by Alice Paul in 1916–17, bought the house from Senator Porter Dale with the help of its president and benefactor Alva Belmont, and made it the party’s fifth and final headquarters. From here, the 2017 foundation document says, the party targeted more than 600 discriminatory laws and won more than 300 legislative changes — in marriage, divorce and custody law, jury service, property rights and contracts, the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Paul helped lead the party from the house until she retired in 1972. [2] [3]

The party fought to save the house when construction of the Hart Senate Office Building threatened it in the 1960s; it was listed on the National Register in 1972 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1974. On April 12, 2016, after the party donated the property, President Barack Obama designated it a national monument. [1] [3]

black.html: For the March 3, 1913, suffrage parade on the eve of Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration, Paul, fearing she would alienate southern white women, tried to segregate Black marchers in a section at the rear; the 2021 resource study says it is unclear whether any actually marched there. The NAACP’s journal The Crisis counted about 40 Black women in the march, among them 25 Howard University students; Ida B. Wells-Barnett, reportedly told she could not march with the white Illinois delegation, waited at the side until the Chicago delegation passed, then stepped into the line with it. The study quotes historian Mary Walton’s judgment that Paul’s failure to welcome Black marchers left a permanent stain on her reputation. Mary Church Terrell marched in 1913 and later joined the White House pickets, while remaining critical of white suffragists’ disinterest in issues that mattered to Black women. [3]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study, Belmont-Paul Women's Equality National Monument (NPS, 2021), ch. 1, pp. 1-12 to 1-13 and 1-18

women.html:
On January 10, 1917, twelve party members began a silent vigil at the White House gates — reportedly the first people ever to picket it. After the United States entered World War I that April, spectators attacked the pickets; in June police began arresting them for obstructing traffic, and in July sixteen were sentenced to 60 days in Virginia’s Occoquan Workhouse. Officials abused the prisoners and held them in solitary confinement, the 2021 resource study records. Alice Paul, sentenced in October to seven months, the longest term, and Rose Winslow went on hunger strike and were force-fed. Publicity roused sympathy; the pickets were released in late November and their sentences invalidated in March 1918. [3]

The party then pursued an Equal Rights Amendment, drafted by its officers and lawyers after 1921 and rewritten by Paul in 1943. Introduced in every session of Congress from 1923, it passed in 1972 but was three states short of ratification at the 1982 deadline. [3]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study, Belmont-Paul Women's Equality National Monument (NPS, 2021), preface and ch. 1, pp. 1-18 to 1-21

BICY.name: Big Cypress National Preserve

photos.caption: A cypress swamp in Big Cypress National Preserve
photos.note: On-page caption: "Cypress swamps while appearing mysterious, are peaceful and serene." credit "NPS Photo". Resized from 5168x3448.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Big Cypress National Preserve archive page — overview (NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Big Cypress National Preserve, Florida (NPS, 2016)
Harvey & Harvey, A Question of Balance: Administrative History of Big Cypress National Preserve (NPS, 2024)

BICY.summary:
Water is the unifying force of Big Cypress: its 729,000 acres of largely freshwater wetland connect five habitats — hardwood hammocks, pinelands, prairies, cypress swamps and estuaries — and the preserve protects the flow of fresh water into the estuaries of Everglades National Park and the Ten Thousand Islands. By some accounts its watershed supplies more than half the surface water that reaches the Everglades from outside them. The preserve holds the largest dwarf cypress forests in North America and the largest old-growth South Florida slash pine forest, the ghost orchid, one of more than 30 native orchids, and the heart of the primary range of the Florida panther, one of the most endangered mammals in the world. [1] [2] [3]

In 1968 construction began on what was meant to be the world’s largest jetport, which would have devastated the natural flow of fresh water through the swamp. A coalition of conservationists, hunters, landowners and Seminole and Miccosukee people stopped it, and on October 11, 1974, President Gerald Ford signed the law creating Big Cypress as one of the nation’s first national preserves — a new kind of park where hunting, off-road vehicles, oil and gas extraction, private land and the customary uses of the Miccosukee and Seminole would continue alongside protection. Congress enlarged it by 147,000 acres in 1988. The land carries evidence of some 15,000 years of human use. [1] [2] [3]

black.html: Black workers helped cut the cypress forest of Big Cypress. A 2002 study prepared for the preserve by Frank and Audrey Peterman found that the railroad workers and Tamiami Trail builders who made the logging possible were overwhelmingly Black, and that the logging and sawmill labor pool was predominantly Black. Spurred in part by World War II’s need for durable timber, the Lee Tidewater Cypress Company alone shipped about 360 million board feet of cypress from 1944 to 1956. Copeland, a Lee Tidewater company town, had a Black side and a White side; the C. J. Jones company paid its workers in company scrip, good for rent and goods at its store, while Lee Tidewater paid in dollars. Frances Hodge, who in her 2002 interview said she came to Copeland in 1950 and who cooked at the company boardinghouse, serving white workers, for 50 cents an hour, remembered so much work that people slept on others’ porches — until the power saw came and the jobs were gone. The authors note how rarely the local papers of the day even mentioned these workers. [4]

sources.title: Frank & Audrey Peterman, African Americans and the Sawmills of Big Cypress — A Brief History (Earthwise Productions for NPS, Big Cypress National Preserve, 2002)

climate.html: The preserve’s 2016 foundation document records the change already under way: average annual temperature has risen at a statistically significant rate since 1950, sea levels and storm-surge heights have risen, and the preserve has been in or near 19 hurricane-strength storms over the past century. Rising seas and storm surge threaten loss of land and habitat, rising groundwater and saltwater intrusion into freshwater ecosystems, and an imbalance between salt and fresh water that can favor invasive species. The Gulf Coast region is already showing an enhanced hydrological cycle — more intense rain, stronger storms — and the preserve’s shallow waters are expected to track the warming closely. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Big Cypress National Preserve (2016) — FRV analyses and key issues on climate change

indigenous.html: The swamp was a refuge as well as a home. The 2024 administrative history recounts how U.S. troops pursued Seminole warriors into the Everglades during the Second Seminole War, and how in the Third the United States sought to remove the remaining Seminole from Big Cypress and the Everglades. Abiaka, a Miccosukee medicine man also known as Sam Jones, led warriors who defeated Zachary Taylor’s forces at Lake Okeechobee in 1837 and refused to relocate to Indian Territory. When fighting ended in stalemate by 1858, many Seminole, Billy Bowlegs among them, agreed to go to Oklahoma, but about 150, Abiaka included, stayed in the traditional villages of Big Cypress, where he remained based until his death in 1866. The Seminole population of Big Cypress grew through the late nineteenth century, and the Big Cypress Seminole Reservation now borders the preserve to the north. [3] In creating the preserve, Congress honored the customs and occupancy of the Miccosukee and Seminole peoples, whose villages stand in it today as they have for generations. [1]

sources.title: A Question of Balance (NPS administrative history, 2024), ch. 1, Prehistoric and Historic Background, pp. 9–11
NPSHistory.com: Big Cypress archive page — NPS brochure, 'Customary Uses'

women.html: Marjory Stoneman Douglas is remembered for saving the Everglades, but her newly formed Friends of the Everglades also played a major role in the coalition that turned back the jetport and won protection for Big Cypress, and her book The Everglades: River of Grass describes the swamp in detail. [1] [2] In the logging town of Copeland a generation earlier, Annie Mae Perry, a logger’s wife known far and wide as “Mother Perry,” served as midwife and delivered more than 500 babies in Copeland, Jerome, Immokalee, Everglades City and Naples; decades later she still gathered them every June. [4]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Big Cypress archive page — NPS brochure (Marjory Stoneman Douglas; the brochure spells her name 'Marjorie')
Foundation Document, Big Cypress National Preserve (2016), brief description
Peterman, African Americans and the Sawmills of Big Cypress (NPS, 2002), oral histories

BISC.name: Biscayne National Park
BISC.summary: Biscayne National Park in southeastern Florida protects 172,971 acres of marine and coastal environments, making it one of the largest marine parks in the National Park System. Ninety-five percent of the park is water, encompassing Biscayne Bay, the northernmost Florida Keys, and a portion of the third-largest barrier reef in the world. Originally established as Biscayne National Monument in 1968 after a citizen-led campaign blocked a proposed industrial seaport, it was redesignated as a national park in 1980. The park preserves mangrove shorelines, the shallow waters of Biscayne Bay, the undeveloped upper Florida Keys, and living coral reefs supporting over 600 species of fish.

BLRI.summary:
The Blue Ridge Parkway is a continuous 469-mile motor road through the central and southern Appalachians, linking Shenandoah and Great Smoky Mountains national parks. [1] For 355 miles it follows the Blue Ridge, the eastern rampart of the Appalachians; then it skirts the Black Mountains and weaves through the Craggies, the Pisgahs and the Balsams to the Great Smokies, ranging from 649 to 6,047 feet past tulip trees, dogwood, spruce and fir and dense thickets of catawba rhododendron. [1] The 2016 foundation document calls it the longest road planned as a single park unit in the United States, a road through 29 counties that is frequently the most heavily visited unit of the national park system. [1]

It was a Depression public works project. Congress allocated the first construction funds on June 16, 1933, under the National Industrial Recovery Act, and gave the Park Service its management on June 30, 1936. [1] New York landscape architect Stanley Abbott was hired to oversee the project, and construction began September 11, 1935, near Cumberland Knob, North Carolina — mostly by private contractors, with Works Progress Administration, Emergency Relief Administration and Civilian Conservation Corps crews as well. The last link, the Linn Cove Viaduct, opened in 1987, completing the continuous route. [1]

Along the way the parkway conserves what the foundation document calls examples of 19th- and 20th-century lifeways of the mountain communities — among them Mabry Mill, run by E.B. Mabry from 1910 to 1935, and the Blue Ridge Music Center, which celebrates the region’s music. [1] [1] It was also built in the Jim Crow South, and the Park Service’s 2009 historic resource study documents how segregation was planned into it. [1]

black.html: Segregated bathrooms appear in the parkway’s 1936 master plans for Bluff Park, Rocky Knob and Smart View, Rebecca Jones’s 2009 historic resource study finds. After an April 26, 1939 Washington conference with W. J. Trent, the Secretary’s adviser on Negro affairs, Superintendent Stanley Abbott’s annual report set out “provisions for Negroes”: shared gas stations and lunch counters, separate dining rooms, separate toilets, and separate cabin, camping and picnic areas in the large parks. At Cumberland Knob, a 1940 memo had rangers direct Black visitors to a five-unit picnic area, with “no sign” for direction. In August 1941 a Black family complained to NPS Director Newton Drury after a confrontation when they insisted on using the white area at Bluff Park. By 1941 Pine Spur, a 300-acre park for Black visitors near Roanoke, was well under construction, with 25 picnic units installed; it was never opened, and by the study’s account only a few curb stones and rotting outhouses remain. [1]

sources.title: Rebecca Jones, Historic Resource Study: African Americans and the Blue Ridge Parkway (NPS, August 2009)

labor_ccc.html: Abbott asked for nine Civilian Conservation Corps camps in 1937 and was granted four — Rocky Knob, Kelso and a camp near Galax in Virginia, and Laurel Springs in North Carolina — whose enrollees landscaped, controlled erosion, installed guard rails and worked on fire prevention. The Galax camp, NP-29, was a segregated company of Black enrollees that began work in December 1940; a June 1941 inspection counted 180 men, with classes four nights a week and a library of 856 books. That same month a memo reported that a subaltern’s “abusive tactics” had created a situation “bordering on insurrection,” and a separate June 4 disturbance between a cook and an officer led to three discharges. The camp closed in May 1942. The study found Black construction workers hard to trace because private contractors built the road; in December 1942 Abbott reported no permanent Black personnel and one Black temporary laborer. [1]

sources.title: Rebecca Jones, Historic Resource Study: African Americans and the Blue Ridge Parkway (NPS, August 2009)

slavery.html: The parkway passes a few African American communities, where folklorist Patrick Mullen identified families with roots in slavery. Lizzie Price, born enslaved in 1845, farmed at Pine Spur and sold her land to the parkway; Abbott later recalled bringing her the check, and the study records that she lived to 108. Graves believed to be of enslaved or free Black people lie at Meadows of Dan, near the graves of the Langhorne family, one of five slaveholding families there; by a 1960s account, above the Peaks of Otter visitor center; and in the Pine Spur cemetery. Mount Jefferson was once called “Negro Mountain” because, as the overlook sign says, runaway slaves supposedly hid there; in 1947 Superintendent Sam Weems, relaying information from Alfred Percy of Madison Heights, Virginia, wrote that stone fences at Humpback Mountain were built by enslaved people. [1] The parkway’s own cemeteries page notes that its burial grounds hold the graves of enslaved African Americans. [1]

sources.title: Rebecca Jones, Historic Resource Study: African Americans and the Blue Ridge Parkway (NPS, August 2009)
NPS, Cemeteries — Blue Ridge Parkway (nps.gov/blri)

BLSC.name: Blackwell School National Historic Site
BLSC.summary: Blackwell School National Historic Site in Marfa, Texas, was established on November 11, 2022, as the 423rd unit of the National Park System. The school operated from the 1880s through 1965 as the segregated school for Mexican American children in the Marfa Independent School District during the era of "Juan Crow" discrimination in Texas. Students were punished for speaking Spanish and faced systematic educational inequality. The site was championed by former students and their descendants — known as the Blackwell School Alliance — who preserved the remaining adobe classroom building and shared their oral histories to ensure this chapter of civil rights history would not be forgotten.

BRCA.summary:
Bryce Canyon is not a canyon. Below the east rim of Utah’s Paunsaugunt Plateau, frost and rain have carved more than a dozen horseshoe-shaped amphitheaters into the colorful, weak limestone of the Claron Formation, leaving fins, windows and spires called hoodoos. [1] On about 180 days a year temperatures swing between freezing nights and warm afternoons, so meltwater freezes and expands in the cracks again and again; the park’s 2016 brochure says the forces of weathering and erosion never rest, not even for a day. Its Pink Cliffs are the top step of the Grand Staircase, a sequence of rock layers recording 525 million years. [2]

For thousands of years, the 2014 foundation document says, Native peoples passed through, and more recent groups such as the Southern Paiute drew sustenance from the area. [1] Pioneer settlers followed: Ebenezer Bryce, who came to the Paria Valley settlement of Clifton in 1875 or 1876, dug a seven-mile irrigation ditch and built a timber road ending in the amphitheater locals called “Bryce’s Canyon,” then left for Arizona in 1880. In 1916 Forest Service supervisor J. W. Humphrey and his crew began publicizing the canyon, and Ruby and Minnie Syrett homesteaded nearby and began inviting friends from Panguitch to see it. [3] Bryce Canyon became a national monument under the Forest Service on June 8, 1923, and a national park in 1928. [2]

The park covers about 35,835 acres between 6,600 and 9,100 feet, spanning three climate zones from pinyon-juniper to spruce-fir forest. The foundation document calls it one of the darkest publicly accessible places in North America, where views often extend more than 100 miles. [1]

climate.html: Bryce’s long views depend on regional air quality, and the 2014 foundation document says air pollution comes principally from beyond the park’s boundaries, from regional sources; the park is a Class I area under the Clean Air Act, which gives the Park Service an affirmative responsibility to protect its visibility. From 2005 to 2009 average visibility was 3.7 deciviews above natural conditions, short of the park’s goal, and haze on the haziest days did not improve over 2000–2009. Temperature in the surrounding area rose significantly from 1901 to 2002, and the document warns that a warmer, drier climate could raise windblown dust and that more stagnant weather could increase ozone. [1] A 2025 assessment of the park’s East Creek water supply rated it moderately vulnerable to climate change; in a hot, dry future, runoff and recharge could fall by 41 percent, and the risk of severe wildfire is projected to increase. [5]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Bryce Canyon National Park (2014), Analysis of Fundamental Resources — Clean Air
Cognac, Willi, Mothes, Gilkerson & Lawrence, Water for People: Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment for Water Supplies at Bryce Canyon National Park (NPS/CSU, 2025)

indigenous.html: The 1985 historic resource study by Nicholas Scrattish, written in language now dated, says that as earlier peoples’ activity faded after A.D. 1200, Paiutes filtered into the area; their arrowheads and obsidian tools, found in relative abundance, imply hunting and gathering there. In 1936, by the study’s account, an elderly Paiute man of the Kaibab Reservation — recorded there as “Indian Dick” — told the Zion–Bryce park naturalist that before there were Indians the Legend People lived there; because they did something bad, Coyote turned them all into rocks, standing in rows, their faces still painted. The place, he said, is Angka-ku-wass-a-wits, translated by his nephew as “red painted faces.” He also said the Paiute never used a name for the canyon often cited as theirs. [3] The 2014 foundation document names the Southern Paiute among those who drew sustenance from the area, and says descendants of those who came before still make cultural connections to the landscape. [1]

sources.title: Scrattish, Historic Resource Study (1985), Prehistory and Paiute Place Names
Foundation Document, Bryce Canyon National Park (2014), Brief Description

labor_ccc.html: A 1994 National Register submission says Civilian Conservation Corps and relief crews were at work by October 1933 and that, with CCC labor, the park finished the last segments of the Rim Trail and part of the Fairyland Loop and completed the Under-the-Rim and Riggs Spring Loop trails. [4] According to the 1985 historic resource study, Bryce’s own camp, NP-3, opened in May 1934 when CCC Company 962 moved over from Zion; in 1934–36 the company summered at Bryce and wintered at Zion. In its first season its more than 200 enrollees took on campground improvement, 18 miles of roadside cleanup, an 18.8-mile fire trail below the rim from Bryce Point to Rainbow Point and 325 log check dams. In 1935 they began the park’s first CCC buildings, among them the Sunset Point comfort station, and in 1936 crews felled and burned 1,617 Douglas firs and 890 ponderosa pines to fight a bark beetle outbreak. [3]

BUIS.summary:
Buck Island rises out of the Caribbean a mile and a half off the northeast side of St. Croix: an uninhabited island of uplifted volcanic ash, two-thirds of it ringed by an elkhorn coral barrier reef whose branching corals push to 30-foot heights, with patch reefs shaped like haystacks rising nearly to the surface from as much as 40 feet below. Brown pelicans, least terns and hawksbill, leatherback and green sea turtles nest here. Today the 176-acre island and more than 18,000 acres of submerged reef and seafloor make up the monument. [2] [1]

The island was not always wild. Its tropical hardwoods, lignum vitae above all, were logged for timber and charcoal, and goats and sheep grazed it into the first quarter of the twentieth century; the 2012 management plan says that by 1948 grazing had reduced it to dry forest and desert scrub. Mongoose and rats brought by people may have eradicated the St. Croix ground lizard, the brochure says; the Park Service reintroduced the lizard in 2007, and the island is now its most secure refuge. [2] [3] [1]

The Virgin Islands government made Buck Island and its reefs a territorial park in 1948. President John F. Kennedy proclaimed the national monument on December 28, 1961, to protect a reef area the Park Service describes as one of the finest marine gardens in the Caribbean Sea, and on January 17, 2001, President Bill Clinton added 18,135 marine acres. The whole monument is now closed to fishing and collecting, one of only a few fully protected no-take marine areas in the national park system. [2] [3] [1]

climate.html:
The 2004 brochure warned that coral reefs worldwide are fast disappearing and that biologists see their plight as a planetary danger signal. The 2017 foundation document gives Buck Island figures: in the 1960s, 70 percent of corals were considered healthy; in the 1970s white band disease left only 5 to 10 percent of the elkhorn coral alive; and monitoring from the 1990s to 2016 found 2 to 5 percent live cover on two reefs. It counts bleaching, rising seas and ocean acidification among the threats and says climate change is likely to worsen the threat from storms. [2] [1]

A 2023 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists, with Park Service co-authors, found bioerosion dominant at 91 percent of reef sites surveyed in 2016, but concluded that significant elkhorn coral restoration, if successful, could let the reef crest keep pace with the roughly half-meter of sea-level rise expected by 2100 with moderate emissions cuts. [2] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Buck Island Reef National Monument archive page — overview (from the 2004 NPS brochure) and establishment block

indigenous.html: By about A.D. 400, according to the park’s history page, Amerindians living on St. Croix, who had come into the region through the Lesser Antilles from the lower Orinoco River and the Guyana coast, began to visit Buck Island to fish, catch lobsters and land crabs, gather conch and possibly collect turtle and bird eggs. They camped in the beach forest and left behind pottery and hearths. Charcoal and shell from hearths at West Beach have given two calibrated radiocarbon ranges, A.D. 410–600 and 510–700, and the pottery found on the island runs from Late Saladoid through Ostionoid styles. The 2017 foundation document reports that eroding shorelines are causing the loss of important archeological sites, among them the north shore Amerindian site. [2] [3] [1]

slavery.html:
Johann Diedrich (the park’s history page spells it Deidrich), Christiansted’s town clerk, controlled Buck Island from 1754 to 1773; between six and twelve enslaved Africans lived there at a time during his tenure, and three were listed in 1772. An 1841 Danish tax list names enslaved Africans there. Island-wide, the 2012 plan reports, enslaved people were more than 90 percent of St. Croix’s population before 1800, and in 1812 its 175 sugar plantations held 26,000 enslaved people. Emancipation came in 1848. [2] [1]

The 2001 proclamation records two slave ships under Liverpool captains wrecked in the waters it added: the Mary in March 1797, with 240 enslaved people, and the General Abercrombie in March 1803, with 339; both groups were brought to Christiansted. Such wrecks are rare in U.S. waters, the proclamation notes, and remnants lie in the monument. The Slave Wrecks Project, an NPS–Smithsonian partnership with universities, has drawn attention to them, the foundation document says. [2] [1]

Foundation Document, Cape Cod National Seashore, Massachusetts (NPS, 2018)

CACO.summary:
Cape Cod is a slender arm of sand and glacial debris curving some 60 miles into the Atlantic, one of the largest glacially formed peninsulas in the world. Wind and water never stop moving it: sand is torn from one stretch of shore and laid down on another, and the Great Beach on the ocean side is one of the longest uninterrupted sandy shorelines on the East Coast. Cape Cod National Seashore, authorized on August 7, 1961, protects about 44,000 acres along a 40-mile stretch between Chatham and Provincetown — beaches and dunes, kettle ponds, pine barrens, heathland and some 1,875 acres of salt marsh. [1] [1]

Archeological sites here record more than 9,000 years of human occupation, and by the 1600s the Wampanoag used or lived on all of the land now inside the seashore — use the Park Service says continues today. In 1620 the Cape was the Pilgrims’ first landfall and the place where they drafted the Mayflower Compact. Later Cape Codders took to whaling, fishing and shellfishing; lighthouses and lifesaving stations still line the outer shore; and the first transatlantic cable (1866) and the first exchange of transatlantic wireless messages (1903) went out from this coast. [1]

The Park Service’s own foundation document names what is at stake: the forces that shape the Cape are directly affected by climate change, and the seashore is a place to watch it happen. At the Marconi Station Site in Wellfleet, where the peninsula is only a mile wide, much of the high cliff has eroded since Guglielmo Marconi built his towers there in 1901. [1] [1]

climate.html:
The salt marshes are where rising seas show first. The 2018 foundation document finds evidence of sea-level rise in every one of the seashore’s salt marshes, which it says are getting wetter, and says their vegetation is changing rapidly in response. A 2020 Park Service study of marshes surveyed from 2003 to 2018 found both dominant marsh grasses (Spartina alterniflora and S. patens) declining, mostly from sea-level rise, crab grazing and wave erosion, and suggests that marsh migration is not keeping up with the losses; those marshes hold an estimated 18,000 metric tons of carbon. [1] [1]

On the ocean side, bluff erosion — a natural process the Park Service says is now being influenced by sea-level rise — has averaged 2.5 to 3 feet a year over a century, and the Nantucket tide gauge shows the sea rising faster here than the national average. Even the kettle ponds are warming: Gull Pond’s August surface water has grown warmer since 1980. [1] [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Cape Cod National Seashore (2018), Estuaries and Salt Marshes; Beaches, Barrier Islands and Spits (pp. 22–26)
Smith, Salt Marsh Vegetation Change at Cape Cod National Seashore between 2003 and 2018 (NPS NRR 2020/2157)
Resource Brief: Monitoring Climate Change at Cape Cod National Seashore (NPS Northeast Coastal and Barrier Network, December 2009)

indigenous.html:
When Samuel de Champlain mapped Nauset Bay in 1605 he saw a harbor bordered by wigwams and recorded about 150 people living around it, farming and fishing. That was a late chapter: Paleo-Indian projectile points indicate that people have lived on, or at least crossed, this land for 10,000 years. The Park Service’s archeological survey, begun in 1979, found shellfish being gathered at least 4,000 years ago, some people living on the Outer Cape year-round in the late Woodland period, and a community in sustained contact with other Native peoples of the Northeast. A communal burial at Indian Neck in Wellfleet held more than two dozen people and dates to about A.D. 880–1155. [1] [1]

After 1620 Plymouth colonists came to Nauset to buy corn and trade, spreading diseases against which the Nauset had no immunity; their population fell drastically. In 1639 about half the English at Plymouth moved to the Nauset area and founded what is now Eastham. [1] [1]

CACR.summary:
Creole culture took root along the Cane River in 18th-century Louisiana, at what the Park Service calls the borderlands between New France and New Spain — a culture nurtured by French and Spanish colonial ways, steeped in Africanisms and enriched by American Indian contact. The park preserves two plantations, Oakland and Magnolia, 10 and 20 miles south of Natchitoches: in the Park Service’s words the most intact French Creole cotton plantations in the United States, owned and continuously operated by the same families, the Prud’hommes and the LeComte–Hertzogs, since their establishment in the 18th century. They hold 70 historic structures, including eight rare brick slave quarters at Magnolia, and nearly 500,000 museum objects and archives. [n] [n]

Jean Baptiste Lecomte obtained the land grant that grew into Magnolia in 1753. Emmanuel Prud’homme’s land on the river became the core of Bermuda, later renamed Oakland; the brochure dates his grant to 1789, a family tradition the 2019 Historic Resource Study finds no evidence for. After the cotton gin’s invention in 1793 both families turned to cotton, and between 1818 and 1821 Prud’homme’s enslaved workers built his house. After the United States took Louisiana in 1803, the 2018 brochure explains, Anglo-Americans poured in with their English language, Protestant religion and their own enslaved workers; life grew more constricted for non-whites as U.S. law removed colonial-era rights such as self-emancipation by purchase. [n] [n]

Congress created the park on November 2, 1994, in the same law that created the 116,000-acre Cane River National Heritage Area — which the 2015 foundation document calls the only instance of a park unit and a heritage area being co-legislated. The Park Service says the park tells the story of oppressive plantation labor systems founded on slavery and replaced by tenant farming, sharecropping and day labor from Reconstruction through the 1970s. [n]

black.html:
After the war a Union commander, on June 5, 1865, told freed people to stay on the premises to which they belonged, and the initial labor contracts at Bermuda paid six to ten dollars a month for men and five to eight for women. Those contracts, the park’s brochure says, differed from slavery mainly in requiring the worker’s consent; sharecropping ranged from a relatively benign feudalism to virtual bondage, the chains of slavery replaced by endless debt at the plantation store. Many stayed and rebuilt a community around church and family, often in the quarters that had housed their enslaved ancestors. [n] [n]

The first sharecropper did not leave Oakland until 1949. At Magnolia the Hertzogs housed day laborers in the brick cabins from the Depression on; electricity reached the cabins in the 1940s; mechanical pickers replaced the field crews in the 1960s, and the last residents of the cabins, the Vercher family, moved out in the early 1970s. [n] [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)
NPSHistory.com: Cane River Creole NHP archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

indigenous.html:
Before there was a French post at Natchitoches, this valley was Caddo country. By the end of the 1400s the Caddo numbered about 200,000, and the Red River valley was among the most densely settled parts of their homeland. Then came European disease and a years-long drought: archaeological evidence cited in the 2019 Historic Resource Study suggests the population fell by about 95 percent between 1500 and the 1680s. The Natchitoches confederacy, smallest of three, lived in villages on the river terraces between today’s Oakland Plantation and Natchitoches. [n]

In 1835 the Caddo sold all their lands by a treaty signed near Shreveport, for $30,000 in goods and horses and a promise of $50,000 over five years, pledging never to return to live as a nation within the United States. They went to Texas and later to Oklahoma, where the Caddo Nation is based today. Some stayed or returned, and the tribe still holds the Natchitoches area as its spiritual homeland. [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)

slavery.html:
Between 1810 and 1860 the Prud’hommes held between 50 and 145 people, placing them in the top nine percent of Louisiana slaveholders. The LeComtes held 234 people in 1860 across Magnolia and their other properties, 112 of them in the Magnolia quarters, completed in 1845. In an 1836 cotton book, Phanor Prud’homme’s overseer listed the first names of 77 people who had worked seven days a week to bring in that year’s cotton; in April 1830 a Prud’homme cousin sold Phanor eight enslaved people for just over $3,000: a couple, Thibuad and Salinette, and their six children. The Historic Resource Study cautions that much of what was recorded about these lives was written by white planters and overseers. [n]

The brochure describes the cotton year: picking began in August and ran from first light until too dark to see, the hard bolls cut pickers’ hands, and the overseer expected each adult to pick at least 200 pounds a day. [n]

CAHA.summary:
A thin, broken strand of barrier islands curves out into the Atlantic and back again, sheltering North Carolina’s mainland coast and sounds. For thousands of years these islands of the Outer Banks have survived wind and sea; Cape Hatteras National Seashore protects their beaches, dunes, marshes and maritime forests of oak, cedar and yaupon holly. Offshore lie the shifting sand ridges of Diamond Shoals, in waters called the Graveyard of the Atlantic: more than 600 ships wrecked here, the park brochure counts, and in World War II German submarines sank so many Allied ships that the area was also called Torpedo Junction. Villagers served in the U.S. Life-Saving Service from the 1870s, kept the lighthouses — Ocracoke’s of 1823, Cape Hatteras’s of 1870, Bodie Island’s of 1872 — and buried the dead when rescues failed. [1]

Congress authorized Cape Hatteras as the first national seashore in 1937, and it was formally established on January 12, 1953. [1] [1] It stretches more than 70 miles across Bodie, Hatteras and Ocracoke islands; eight villages that predate the park lie among them but are not part of it. The park’s 2011 foundation document lists those who have made these islands home — Native Americans, farmers, watermen, enslaved people, lighthouse keepers and surfmen — and calls the seashore a living laboratory for the study of climate change and its effects on sea level. [1]

black.html: Slave ownership on the Banks was minimal but present; under Union occupation during the Civil War Hatteras Island held about 1,200 people, almost 100 of them enslaved, by historian David Stick’s count. [1] Richard Etheridge, born enslaved, who had served three years in the army’s 36th Infantry (colored), became on January 24, 1880, the first African American to command a life-saving station when he was named keeper of the Pea Island station, after its all-white crew was dismissed for negligence following an 1879 wreck. His all-Black crew — the only all-Black life-saving station in the country — rescued all nine people aboard the schooner E.S. Newman in a storm on October 11, 1896. The crew went unrecognized during the station’s years of service; on March 5, 1996, Etheridge and six surfmen were posthumously awarded Gold Lifesaving Medals. [1]

sources.title: Impact Assessment, Inc., Ethnohistorical Description of the Eight Villages adjoining Cape Hatteras National Seashore and Interpretive Themes of History and Heritage, Vol. 1 (NPS, November 2005)
Stover, Pea Island Life-Saving Station, Rodanthe, North Carolina, Coast Guard Station #177: Historic Resource Study (NPS, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, 2008)

climate.html: Most of the seashore’s barrier islands are less than 400 meters wide and lie entirely within the 100-year flood zone, and the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2005 assessment found relative sea level at Beaufort, about 75 kilometers southwest of Ocracoke, rising about 3.7 millimeters a year — roughly twice the global average — and rated 27 percent of the nearly 120 miles of shoreline it evaluated at very high vulnerability to sea-level rise and another 27 percent at high. [1] At Cape Hatteras, the 2003 cultural landscape report says, erosion had claimed about 1,800 feet of beach in front of the original 1803 tower by 1872; in 1999 the entire light station was moved southwest to a site about 1,600 feet from the shoreline. [1]

sources.title: Pendleton, Thieler & Williams, Coastal Vulnerability Assessment of Cape Hatteras National Seashore (CAHA) to Sea-Level Rise, USGS Open-File Report 2004-1064 (2005)
Vincent, Cape Hatteras Light Station Cultural Landscape Report (NPS Southeast Region, 2003)

indigenous.html: The first written account of the Outer Banks, Verrazzano’s of 1524, tells of many Native people meeting his crew off what was likely Hatteras Island; in David Stick’s 1958 retelling, they hauled a sailor tumbled by the surf onto dry sand and later sent him back to his boat. In 1590 John White speculated that the lost Roanoke colonists had joined the friendly Indians at Croatoan, now Hatteras Island — a theory never substantiated. The park’s 2005 ethnohistory reports that in the early 1700s about 80 Indians, likely Hatteras, lived in the Cape Woods along the sound; the archaeological record suggests theirs were the island’s only permanent settlements. Quoting Gary Dunbar (1956), it says they were described in 1715 as “in great poverty,” and that a 1733 cartographer counted “6 or 8” at Hatteras living among the English. Stick found the last reference to the Hatteras Indians in a 1788 deed from “Mary Elks, Inden, of Hatteras Banks.” [1]

sources.title: Impact Assessment, Inc., Ethnohistorical Description of the Eight Villages adjoining Cape Hatteras National Seashore and Interpretive Themes of History and Heritage, Vol. 1 (NPS, November 2005)

labor_ccc.html: In the early 1930s North Carolina planned three parallel lines of ocean-front dunes from the Virginia line to Ocracoke Inlet, and the work was turned over to the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Work Projects Administration. [1] Crews erected sand fences, piled brush from trees downed in the 1933 storm along the beach to trap sand, planted grass and dug roads and ditches; islanders recall camps at Rodanthe, near the Cape Hatteras lighthouse and on Ocracoke, where workers built theirs from lumber salvaged from the 1935 wreck of the Nomis. Some of the young men, paid $30 a month, married local women and stayed. [1] Near the lighthouse, the 2003 cultural landscape report finds, the CCC and WPA dunes of 1935–36 held the shoreline back for thirty years. [1]

sources.title: Impact Assessment, Inc., Ethnohistorical Description of the Eight Villages adjoining Cape Hatteras National Seashore and Interpretive Themes of History and Heritage, Vol. 1 (NPS, November 2005)
Impact Assessment, Inc., Ethnohistorical Description of the Eight Villages adjoining Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Vol. 2 (NPS, November 2005), §8.7 WPA/CCC
Vincent, Cape Hatteras Light Station Cultural Landscape Report (NPS Southeast Region, 2003)

photos.note: On-page caption: "Pictographs from the Great Gallery, Horseshoe Canyon Unit NPS/Neal Herbert". Resized from 2615x1782.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Canyonlands National Park archive page — overview (NPS brochure text) and establishment block
Schmieding, From Controversy to Compromise to Cooperation: The Administrative History of Canyonlands National Park (NPS, 2008) — Chronology and Introduction

CANY.summary:
Canyonlands is a wilderness of rock at the heart of the Colorado Plateau, where water and gravity have cut flat layers of sedimentary stone into hundreds of canyons, mesas, buttes, fins, arches and spires across 527 square miles. The Green and Colorado rivers divide it into Island in the Sky, The Maze and The Needles; below their confluence the combined river rushes 14 miles through the rapids of Cataract Canyon. John Wesley Powell, floating through in 1869, called it a strange, weird, grand region. When the park was established, the brochure notes, only Native Americans, cowboys, river explorers and uranium prospectors had dared enter it, and its roads are still mostly unpaved and its rivers free-flowing. [1]

Its path to protection was long. The Park Service proposed an Escalante National Monument of more than 6,000 square miles here in 1936; the plan drew harsh criticism in Utah, and a scaled-back version, repackaged as a recreation area, died in congressional committees in 1940. In April 1961 Interior Secretary Stewart Udall flew over the basin, responding to its beauty while Reclamation chief Floyd Dominy described the virtues of another dam site, what Samuel Schmieding’s 2008 administrative history calls a profound historical irony. Udall’s first concept was a one-million-acre park; after a three-year fight with Utah Republicans, President Lyndon Johnson signed a bill on September 12, 1964, creating the nation’s 31st national park at 257,400 acres. A 1965 master plan called for paved roads and deluxe lodging, and an aerial tramway was even considered for The Needles; the plan was shelved, and in 1971 the park grew by 87,000 acres, taking in The Maze, to 337,540 acres. [1]

climate.html: A 2023 NPS report used satellite images to follow vegetation in and near the park from 2000 to 2019. Multiple indicators, it says, suggest plant production rose across 58 percent of the area studied and fell across 2 percent; increases in annual precipitation may have caused some of the gain. By the end of the period the growing season was starting 12.6 days earlier and ending 11.2 days later, nearly 24 days longer on average. The report offers its findings to help managers plan for what it calls transitions imposed by climate change. [1]

sources.title: Landscape Phenology, Vegetation Condition, and Relations with Climate at Canyonlands National Park, 2000–2019 (NPS/NCPN/NRR—2023/2535), Executive Summary

indigenous.html:
People have occupied or passed through Canyonlands intermittently for about 12,000 years, according to a 2021 synthesis of park archeology by Alan Schroedl and Nancy Coulam. Seeds drew Archaic people here; their staples were cheno-ams, dropseed and Indian rice grass. Late Archaic people painted the Barrier Canyon Style figures of Horseshoe Canyon, life-sized forms the brochure dates to more than 2,000 years ago. Mesa Verde Anasazi farmers, Ancestral Puebloans, arrived after AD 1170, built masonry dwellings in The Needles and granaries elsewhere in the park, and by AD 1300 had left, probably moving south to join Pueblo IV villages. The authors reject a 1962 assertion that Fremont and Anasazi cultures came together here: none of the park’s structures were built by the Fremont. [1] [1]

Around AD 1600, the authors find some evidence, ancestors of the Southern Paiute or Ute, or possibly the Navajo, came into the park for resources such as salt. [1]

sources.title: Schroedl & Coulam, Archaic Foragers and Ancestral Puebloans of Canyonlands National Park (Canyonlands Archeological Project Report No. 5, P-III Associates, November 2021) — Part 2 synopsis and Final Summary
NPSHistory.com: Canyonlands archive page overview (The Maze, The Needles)

Foundation Document, Cane River Creole National Historical Park (NPS, September 2015)
Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)

CARI.summary:
Creole culture took root along the Cane River in 18th-century Louisiana, at what the Park Service calls the borderlands between New France and New Spain — a culture nurtured by French and Spanish colonial ways, steeped in Africanisms and enriched by American Indian contact. The park preserves two plantations, Oakland and Magnolia, 10 and 20 miles south of Natchitoches: in the Park Service’s words the most intact French Creole cotton plantations in the United States, owned and continuously operated by the same families, the Prud’hommes and the LeComte–Hertzogs, since their establishment in the 18th century. They hold 70 historic structures, including eight rare brick slave quarters at Magnolia, and nearly 500,000 museum objects and archives. [n] [n]

Jean Baptiste Lecomte obtained the land grant that grew into Magnolia in 1753. Emmanuel Prud’homme’s land on the river became the core of Bermuda, later renamed Oakland; the brochure dates his grant to 1789, a family tradition the 2019 Historic Resource Study finds no evidence for. After the cotton gin’s invention in 1793 both families turned to cotton, and between 1818 and 1821 Prud’homme’s enslaved workers built his house. After the United States took Louisiana in 1803, the 2018 brochure explains, Anglo-Americans poured in with their English language, Protestant religion and their own enslaved workers; life grew more constricted for non-whites as U.S. law removed colonial-era rights such as self-emancipation by purchase. [n] [n]

Congress created the park on November 2, 1994, in the same law that created the 116,000-acre Cane River National Heritage Area — which the 2015 foundation document calls the only instance of a park unit and a heritage area being co-legislated. The Park Service says the park tells the story of oppressive plantation labor systems founded on slavery and replaced by tenant farming, sharecropping and day labor from Reconstruction through the 1970s. [n]

black.html:
After the war a Union commander, on June 5, 1865, told freed people to stay on the premises to which they belonged, and the initial labor contracts at Bermuda paid six to ten dollars a month for men and five to eight for women. Those contracts, the park’s brochure says, differed from slavery mainly in requiring the worker’s consent; sharecropping ranged from a relatively benign feudalism to virtual bondage, the chains of slavery replaced by endless debt at the plantation store. Many stayed and rebuilt a community around church and family, often in the quarters that had housed their enslaved ancestors. [n] [n]

The first sharecropper did not leave Oakland until 1949. At Magnolia the Hertzogs housed day laborers in the brick cabins from the Depression on; electricity reached the cabins in the 1940s; mechanical pickers replaced the field crews in the 1960s, and the last residents of the cabins, the Vercher family, moved out in the early 1970s. [n] [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)
NPSHistory.com: Cane River Creole NHP archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

indigenous.html:
Before there was a French post at Natchitoches, this valley was Caddo country. By the end of the 1400s the Caddo numbered about 200,000, and the Red River valley was among the most densely settled parts of their homeland. Then came European disease and a years-long drought: archaeological evidence cited in the 2019 Historic Resource Study suggests the population fell by about 95 percent between 1500 and the 1680s. The Natchitoches confederacy, smallest of three, lived in villages on the river terraces between today’s Oakland Plantation and Natchitoches. [n]

In 1835 the Caddo sold all their lands by a treaty signed near Shreveport, for $30,000 in goods and horses and a promise of $50,000 over five years, pledging never to return to live as a nation within the United States. They went to Texas and later to Oklahoma, where the Caddo Nation is based today. Some stayed or returned, and the tribe still holds the Natchitoches area as its spiritual homeland. [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)

slavery.html:
Between 1810 and 1860 the Prud’hommes held between 50 and 145 people, placing them in the top nine percent of Louisiana slaveholders. The LeComtes held 234 people in 1860 across Magnolia and their other properties, 112 of them in the Magnolia quarters, completed in 1845. In an 1836 cotton book, Phanor Prud’homme’s overseer listed the first names of 77 people who had worked seven days a week to bring in that year’s cotton; in April 1830 a Prud’homme cousin sold Phanor eight enslaved people for just over $3,000: a couple, Thibuad and Salinette, and their six children. The Historic Resource Study cautions that much of what was recorded about these lives was written by white planters and overseers. [n]

The brochure describes the cotton year: picking began in August and ran from first light until too dark to see, the hard bolls cut pickers’ hands, and the overseer expected each adult to pick at least 200 pounds a day. [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)
NPSHistory.com: Cane River Creole NHP archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

photos.note: On-page caption: "the Castillo commands the northern edge of the heart of downtown St. Augsutine. NPS Photo"; alt text "Aerial view of the Castillo and the city of St. Augustine". Resized from 3005x1968.

photos.note: On-page caption: "Crossing a dry moat, this drawbridge was the only way into the Castillo. NPS Photo"; alt text "Drawbridge entrance to the Castillo de San Marcos". Resized from 2560x1920.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Castillo de San Marcos National Monument archive page — overview (from the 2017 NPS brochure), timeline and establishment block
Foundation Document, Castillo de San Marcos National Monument, Florida (NPS, 2016)
Raise and Rehabilitate the Seawall Environmental Assessment, Castillo de San Marcos National Monument (NPS, June 2025)

CASA.summary:
On the west bank of Matanzas Bay at St. Augustine stands the oldest masonry fort in the continental United States: a hollow square of locally quarried coquina stone, with a diamond-shaped bastion at each corner and only one way in. Spain broke ground on October 2, 1672, and finished it in 1695, replacing nine successive wooden forts that had guarded the town since its founding in 1565. For many years it was the northernmost outpost of Spain’s empire in the Americas, built to protect the town and the Gulf Stream route of the treasure fleets. [1] [1]

It held. English forces besieged it for 50 days in 1702, and British troops bombarded it for 27 days in 1740; the Park Service notes that the Castillo changed hands only by treaty, never in battle — to Britain in 1763, back to Spain in 1783, to the United States in 1821. The Americans renamed it Fort Marion and made it a prison for Native people: Seminoles in 1837, Plains Indians from 1875 to 1878, Apaches in 1886–1887. Proclaimed a national monument in 1924 and transferred to the Park Service in 1933, it had its Spanish name restored by Congress in 1942. [1] [1]

The Park Service defines the monument’s purpose as preserving the fort and interpreting more than 450 years of cultural intersections. Its seawall is now the lowest point in St. Augustine’s seawall network, which makes the fort the first place in the city to flood in a storm. [1] [1]

black.html: Africans were here from the start: Menéndez arrived in 1565 with about 50 Africans, free and enslaved, among his 800 colonists. When disease cut down the Native workforce building the Castillo, Governor Manuel de Cendoya asked Cuba for thirty enslaved Africans. In 1687 eleven people escaped slavery in Carolina by boat and reached St. Augustine; the governor refused to return them, and six of the men were paid to work on the Castillo. A 1693 royal decree offered freedom to those who fled British colonies and converted, and in 1738 Governor Manuel de Montiano granted the freedom seekers land two miles north of town. Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose — Fort Mose — was, the Park Service says, the first legally established free African settlement in North America, about a hundred people led by militia captain Francisco Menéndez. When Spain ceded Florida in 1763, its people left for Cuba. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Castillo de San Marcos: African Americans in St. Augustine 1565–1821 (nps.gov)
Palmer, Forgotten Sacrifice, Florida Historical Quarterly 80(4), 2002, p. 447

climate.html:
The 2025 environmental assessment for the seawall that fronts the fort is blunt. The wall is aging, eroding and storm-damaged, its low elevation worsened by subsidence, and coquina is porous: running water wears it, and acidic rain and seawater can dissolve the shell in the stone. Under the intermediate sea-level scenario the designers chose — about one meter of global rise by 2100 — the North and South Wall segments would be overtopped by Matanzas Bay even without a storm, with the potential to flood historic St. Augustine. Both of the Park Service’s action alternatives would raise the North and South wall segments to an elevation of +10.5 feet. [1]

The 2016 foundation document had already listed rising seas, rising groundwater, possible saltwater intrusion and more intense storms among the threats to the Castillo itself. [1]

sources.title: Raise and Rehabilitate the Seawall Environmental Assessment (NPS, June 2025), ch. 1 and alternatives
Foundation Document, Castillo de San Marcos (2016), Castillo de San Marcos threats (p. 12)

indigenous.html:
The fort was built with Native labor. Jason Palmer’s 2002 study documents Apalachee, Timucua and Guale men drafted under Spain’s labor system to quarry coquina on Anastasia Island and burn oyster shell for lime; the Apalachee quota rose from 100 to 300 men a year, and disease, hunger and exhaustion killed many. The walls, Palmer concludes, could not protect the people who built them. [1]

As Fort Marion it became an Army prison. In 1875, 74 prisoners chosen at Fort Sill — Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche, Arapaho and Caddo, many survivors of the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre — were brought here (the same Park Service page later gives the number as seventy-two). They were first kept in chains and shackles, which were removed after their jailer, Lt. Richard Henry Pratt, took charge; they were released in 1878. Their ledger drawings survive in the park collection. In 1886 came Chiricahua and Warm Springs Apaches, many of them women and children — more than 500 people, by Omega East and Albert Manucy’s 1952 account — crowded into some 130 tents atop the fort. The park now holds gatherings with the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes to honor those imprisoned here. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: Palmer, Forgotten Sacrifice: Native American Involvement in the Construction of the Castillo de San Marcos, Florida Historical Quarterly 80(4), Spring 2002, pp. 437–454
NPS, Castillo de San Marcos: Plains Incarceration (nps.gov)
Foundation Document, Castillo de San Marcos (2016), significance statements and fundamental resources (ledger art)
East & Manucy, Arizona Apaches as “Guests” in Florida, Florida Historical Quarterly 30(3), 1952

latino.html:
St. Augustine, founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés in 1565, is the oldest permanent European settlement in the continental United States, and for 235 years it was the political, military and religious capital of Spanish Florida. Its grid of narrow streets, plaza and patios may be the earliest example of community planning in the continental United States, and the brochure says the city’s character still reflects its Spanish heritage. The Castillo was laid out by the Spanish engineer Ignacio Daza; it was a presidio, and no one lived inside — soldiers lived in town with their families and came to the fort for 24-hour guard shifts. Spain’s Florida missions predate those of the American West by more than a century. [1]

The Park Service calls the fort a symbol of America’s first great melting pot, where Native people, European soldiers and settlers, and enslaved and free Africans met and clashed. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Castillo de San Marcos archive page — brochure text (2017): St. Augustine; A Guide to the Castillo
Foundation Document, Castillo de San Marcos (2016), interpretive themes
