sources.title: Foundation Document Overview, Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site, District of Columbia (NPS, 2016)
Pero Gaglo Dagbovie, “Willing to Sacrifice”: Carter G. Woodson, the Father of Black History, and the Carter G. Woodson Home — Historic Resource Study (NPS National Capital Region, April 2012)
NPSHistory.com: Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site archive page — overview, Woodson time line and establishment block

CAWO.summary:
At 1538 Ninth Street NW, in Washington’s Shaw neighborhood, stands a three-story brick row house, one of a block of nine with originally identical Victorian Italianate fronts. The foundation document and historian Pero Gaglo Dagbovie’s 2012 resource study date the row to 1872–74; an undated park brochure says the 1890s and dates Woodson’s residence from 1915. [3] By the foundation document’s account, from 1922 until his death in 1950 it was the home and workplace of Dr. Carter G. Woodson, known as the Father of Black History, and headquarters of the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, which he founded in 1915 (now the Association for the Study of African American Life and History). Here, in 1926, he created Negro History Week, which became Black History Month. [1] [2]

Woodson bought the house in July 1922 for $8,000. He lived on the third floor; the floors below held the association’s offices and the Associated Publishers, Inc., which the foundation document counts among the first publishers to print and distribute the works of African Americans, women and minorities. In 1923 he hung an 11½-foot sign out front reading “THE ASSOCIATED PUBLISHERS, INC.” Dagbovie calls this “office home” crucial to the early Black history movement. Woodson died there on April 3, 1950. [2] [1]

The house became a National Historic Landmark on May 11, 1976. Public Law 108-192, of December 19, 2003, authorized the Park Service to acquire it; it did so from the association in 2005, and the site became a park unit in 2006. The foundation document describes the home and two adjoining row houses, 1540 and 1542 Ninth Street, as undergoing rehabilitation for a visitor center and exhibits. [2] [3] [1]

black.html:
Woodson was born December 19, 1875, in New Canton, Virginia, to the formerly enslaved James Henry and Eliza Riddle. In 1892 he went to work in the coal mines of Fayette County, West Virginia, where a Black Civil War veteran, Oliver Jones, introduced him to books by self-trained Black historians. His 1912 Harvard Ph.D. made him only the second African American to earn one there, after W. E. B. Du Bois (1895), the foundation document notes. [1] During the “Red Summer” of 1919, when more than twenty-five major race riots swept U.S. cities, Woodson was in Washington for its July 20 riot and gave an affidavit about it. [2]

He timed the first Negro History Week, in February 1926, to the birthdays of Frederick Douglass and Abraham Lincoln. Race prejudice stemmed from the notion that Black people had contributed nothing of worth to world civilization, Woodson argued, Dagbovie writes; set the record straight in schools, and racism would be abolished. [2]

sources.title: Dagbovie, “Willing to Sacrifice” — Historic Resource Study, Carter G. Woodson Home NHS (NPS, 2012), preface, chs. 1 and 3, Appendix B chronology
Foundation Document Overview, Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site (NPS, 2016), Description

photos.caption: Lockhouse 16 atop a stone outcropping above the lock
photos.note: On-page caption: "Lockhouse 16 sits atop a stone outcropping above the lock. NPS photo"; alt text "A whitewashed lockhouse sits above a stone lock with wooden crib." Re-encoded JPEG, original dimensions.

photos.caption: The path leading to the Paw Paw Tunnel
photos.note: Contemporary park photograph. On-page caption: "Paw Paw Tunnel NPS"; alt text "A path leads up to a large stone tunnel carved into a mountain". Resized from 1683x1122.

sources.title: Foundation Document, Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park (NPS, 2013)
NPSHistory.com: Chesapeake and Ohio Canal NHP archive page — overview (from the 2011 NPS brochure) and establishment block

CHOH.summary:
The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal runs 184.5 miles along the Potomac River from Georgetown in Washington, D.C., to Cumberland, Maryland. Its 74 lift locks raised boats from near sea level to 605 feet, and works like the hand-built, 3,118-foot Paw Paw Tunnel and the Monocacy Aqueduct survive among more than 1,300 historic structures — by the 2013 foundation document’s account, one of the largest collections of 19th-century canal features in the park system. The park also preserves archeological evidence of 13,000 years of human habitation along the river, including prehistoric American Indian rock art. [1]

President John Quincy Adams broke ground on Independence Day, 1828, for a waterway meant to reach the Ohio River. By the time construction ended at Cumberland in 1850, the park brochure says, canals were obsolete; the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad completed the link to the West while the canal stopped far short of the Ohio. It survived as a carrier of coal until floods and debt ended it, and a major flood in 1924 finally stopped operations. The Park Service took over in 1938. In the early 1950s Supreme Court Justice William O. Douglas led a march to save the towpath from becoming a parkway, which he called “a long stretch of quiet and peace.” It became a national monument in 1961 and a national historical park on January 8, 1971. [2] [1]

black.html:
Black workers were on the canal from its first months: in December 1828 John Stubblefield, a free Black man, lost his left arm in a blasting accident and received $2 a month for a year. A company rule of 1857 barred Black boat captains, yet the boat register of January 1, 1878, lists at least four, among them Louis Roberson and Wilson Middleton; Andrew Jenkins captained boats from 1910 to 1923. [5]

A 2022 study prepared for the Park Service on the communities along the canal’s first 20 miles traces Black communities such as Herring Hill in Georgetown, St. Phillips Hill, Gibson Grove and Tobytown, and finds that the canal’s construction displaced African Americans, including the multiracial community of Sugar Hill in Georgetown. It notes that 1940, when the Park Service opened the canal as parkland, recurs as an end date for several Black enclaves, and asks what role the Service played in the displacement that followed. [7]

sources.title: Romain, “Difficulty on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal” (NPS, 2021), pp. 13 and 44–45
WSP USA, Historic Resources Study: African American Communities Along the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal, Washington, D.C., and Lower Montgomery County, Maryland (NPS, October 2022), Executive Summary

labor_ccc.html:
Thousands of immigrants found work building the canal. In August 1832 cholera reached the work camps near Harpers Ferry; a newspaper account quoted in Harlan Unrau’s historic resource study described the dead and dying lying together in crowded shanties, workers fleeing, and laborers who were “chiefly Irishmen.” Rivalries between Irish factions turned violent: on January 24, 1834, several hundred Longfords routed about 300 Corkonians near Dam No. 5 above Williamsport, and many of those overtaken in the pursuit were killed. [3] [2]

A century later the Civilian Conservation Corps did the heavy work of converting the canal’s first 22 miles into a recreational park. Josh Howard’s 2017 study notes that every enrollee in the two canal camps at Cabin John was an African American man, when, as of mid-1938, only one Black CCC camp existed in Maryland; by January 1942 the two companies had logged 83,800 and 74,900 man-days of work. [4]

sources.title: Harlan D. Unrau, Historic Resource Study: Chesapeake & Ohio Canal (NPS, prepared by Karen M. Gray, August 2007), monograph 3, Labor Force, pp. 123–130
Josh Howard, “Our Only Alma Mater”: The Civilian Conservation Corps and the C&O Canal — Special History Study, final draft (NPS, December 2017), Introduction
NPSHistory.com: C&O Canal archive page overview (2011 NPS brochure)

slavery.html:
In June 1830 the canal company’s directors and stockholders rejected President Charles Fenton Mercer’s request to purchase an enslaved workforce, but Sabrina Romain’s 2021 Park Service study finds that Black laborers, free and enslaved, were contracted to work on the canal throughout its construction, and by 1842 the company was relying on such contracts to cut costs. The canal also became a route out of slavery: Ben Addison, hired out to work in Georgetown, escaped on December 18, 1829; Charles Ringold, a blacksmith who had worked a long time on the canal, fled on April 30, 1838. [5]

At Ferry Hill Plantation, part of the park’s historic district, John Blackford held eighteen people in slavery when he died in 1839 — six men, four women and eight children; most were sold at his estate sale to unknown buyers. [6] [1]

photos.caption: The circa-1828 Lowcountry cottage at Snee Farm, now the park’s visitor center
photos.note: On-page caption (homepage slideshow, alt "1828 Lowcountry cottage and grounds"): "The historic house serves as the park's visitor center and features exhibits, film options, and a museum shop. NPS Photo". Resized from 3264x2448.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site archive page — overview (from the 2011 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document Overview, Charles Pinckney National Historic Site (NPS, January 2016)
Gibbs, African Americans at Snee Farm Plantation, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina (NPS Southeast Region, prepared 2001, printed 2006)

CHPI.summary:
Snee Farm, 28 acres in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, is the last undeveloped piece of a 715-acre Lowcountry plantation that Colonel Charles Pinckney bought in 1754. His son Charles, born in Charleston on October 26, 1757, inherited it in 1782 and used it as a country retreat; George Washington stopped there for breakfast in May 1791. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 the younger Pinckney attended every session and submitted a draft constitution that was never formally considered. The park’s foundation document credits him with more than 25 clauses in the final Constitution; the park brochure says his draft contained 30 or more provisions that were incorporated into the final document. [1] [1]

No building from the Pinckney era still stands. Most of his papers burned in Charleston’s 1861 fire, and the plantation was sold to pay his debts in 1817; the cypress-and-pine cottage on the site today dates from about 1828. What is known of the Pinckney years has come largely out of the ground: archeologists have recovered more than 150,000 artifacts, including the slave-made earthenware called Colonoware, and have located the kitchen, the well and two slave cabins. [1] [1]

The rest of the land was sold for housing development and a golf course in the early 1970s, and in 1986 a developer began grading roads across the remaining core. Local residents organized the Friends of Historic Snee Farm, Congress established the historic site on September 8, 1988, and the Park Service acquired the 28 acres in 1990. Its foundation document charges it with interpreting the lives of the farm’s inhabitants, “enslaved as well as free” — a place that was, in the park’s own words, home and livelihood to some and “a form of prison” to others. [1] [1]

black.html:
By 1790 the Lowcountry parishes were nearly 70 percent Black, and the HRS describes how the relative isolation of large plantations let enslaved people blend African traditions into the culture and creole language now called Gullah. After emancipation, African Americans kept working Snee Farm as tenants, sharecroppers and wage laborers. A 2001 park study by Tyson Gibbs of the University of North Texas anthropology department, built on oral-history interviews with former Snee Farm workers and their relatives, recorded Black foremen who ran the farm for its owners between 1943 and 1968 — Charlie Stroder, Billie Seabrook and members of the Kinsey family — and workers who moved freely between Snee Farm and Boone Hall across the road. [1] [1]

Gibbs found that African Americans, more than 75 percent of the area’s people at the first census, had fallen to about 7 percent of Mount Pleasant’s population, and warned of shrinking neighborhoods, developers’ demand for Black-owned land and the scattering of a culture. [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Kleine & Moffson, Historic Resource Study: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site (NPS, 2000), ch. 1, The Archeological Resources of Charles Pinckney NHS, 1754–1816
Gibbs, African Americans at Snee Farm Plantation, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina (NPS Southeast Region, prepared 2001, printed 2006)

slavery.html:
The park’s 2000 Historic Resource Study notes that a 1787 inventory listed forty enslaved people at Snee Farm, among them a gardener, carpenters, coopers and Cudjoe, a driver and sawyer; the 1810 census counted 58. They grew rice and indigo, and the study traces Lowcountry tidal-rice methods to West Africa and notes that planters relied heavily on enslaved people’s knowledge to produce the crop. The study finds archeological evidence that the “task” system prevailed at Snee Farm; shells, bones and a lead shot found in a cabin posthole hint at the food they caught for themselves. Their village of post-in-ground houses, one measuring 16 by 20 feet, stood about 250 yards from the planter’s house and was in use from about 1750 to 1841. [1] [1]

The same study notes that at the Convention Pinckney defended slavery against Northern delegates and fought for the three-fifths clause, for continuing the importation of enslaved Africans until 1808, and for the fugitive slave clause. When Snee Farm was sold in 1817, 43 people were enslaved there. [1]

Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Christiansted National Historic Site (NPS, 2021)

CHRI.summary:
On the harbor of St. Croix’s northeast coast, a three-block stretch of waterfront holds what the Park Service calls one of the most complete and best-preserved groups of 18th- and 19th-century Danish colonial buildings in the New World: Fort Christiansvaern, the Danish West India & Guinea Company Warehouse, the Customs House, the Scale House where hogsheads of sugar and puncheons of rum were weighed for export, and the Steeple Building, St. Croix’s first Lutheran church. The Danish company bought the island from France in 1733 and laid out Christiansted, named for King Christian VI, around a good harbor; a remarkably progressive 1747 building code shaped its orderly growth, and its neoclassical buildings still offer arcaded sidewalks and breezy galleries. [1] [1] [1]

The wealth in those walls was made by enslaved Africans. In 1803 St. Croix had 30,000 people, 26,500 of them enslaved, working cane on 218 plantations, and for a time it was one of the wealthiest sugar islands in the West Indies. The Park Service names the site’s central significance plainly: this is where tens of thousands of enslaved Africans were landed and sold at auction. Slavery was abolished in 1848. The United States bought the islands for $25 million in gold, and the transfer at Fort Christiansvaern and two other venues on March 31, 1917, created the U.S. Virgin Islands. [1] [1]

Civic-minded residents petitioned the federal government to protect the fort and its buildings, and the site was established as Virgin Islands National Historic Site on March 4, 1952. [1]

black.html: In slavery’s shadow a distinct class of Free Blacks grew up on St. Croix. Some were freed for service; others bought their freedom with money earned as artisans or from produce sold at the Sunday Market. They worked as merchants, fishermen, seamen, tailors, coopers and blacksmiths, filled the fire brigade and served in the militia, and many of the anonymous masons and carpenters who built Christiansted’s neoclassical town were Free Blacks. As early as 1747 a section of town, Neger Gotted — later Free Gut — was set aside for them to build their own houses. Their number more than doubled between 1791 and 1815, from 775 to 1,764, but not until 1834 were they granted full equality with whites. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Christiansted archive page — brochure text (2004): Free Blacks; In the West Indian Style; Regulars and Militia

indigenous.html: St. Croix’s first settlers came up the Lesser Antilles from South America. By 2,000 years ago there was a village at Salt River Bay on the north shore, and by 1300 it had the only ceremonial plaza and ball court so far found in the Lesser Antilles. On his second voyage, in 1493, Columbus named the island Santa Cruz and sent a boat ashore; it met Kalinago people (the brochure calls them Caribs) in a canoe, and the fight that followed, at what became known as the Cape of the Arrows, is considered the first armed resistance to European encroachment in the Americas. Over the next century the Spanish wiped out the island’s Kalinago population. The park’s museum holds what it calls a world-class archeological collection documenting St. Croix’s Amerindian cultures. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Christiansted archive page — brochure text (2004): Before the Danes
Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Christiansted NHS (2021), site history pp. 2–3
Foundation Document Overview, Christiansted NHS (2015), significance statements

slavery.html:
From settlement in 1734 until Denmark ended its slave trade — in 1803, by the park brochure’s dating — tens of thousands of Africans — the exact number is not known — were shipped to St. Croix. Survivors of the Middle Passage were auctioned at the Company’s compound — a warehouse complex built by enslaved Africans the Company owned, where, the Park Service says, people were sold in the courtyard until the 1750s. On the plantations they worked dawn to dark six days a week and around the clock at harvest, lived in masonry huts they built themselves in rows arranged for control, and kept African language, religion and foods alive. [1] [1]

Captured leaders of the 1733 uprising on St. John helped build the fort; in the early 1800s its prison held mostly enslaved plantation workers. Beside its doors, exposed ground marks the whipping post where enslaved people were publicly brutalized. The fort is now part of the National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument, Ohio (NPS, June 2014)
Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers Cultural Landscape (NPS, September 2019)
NPSHistory.com: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers National Monument archive page — overview (from an undated NPS brochure) and establishment block

CHYO.summary:
On a farm outside Wilberforce, Ohio, stands Youngsholm, the two-story brick house that Charles Young — soldier, diplomat and civil rights leader — called home. Built around 1854 in a simplified Italianate style, it was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1974, and on March 25, 2013, a presidential proclamation made the house and its adjoining farmland the 401st unit of the national park system. [1] The monument covers 59.656 acres of the original 79.14-acre farm that Charles Young acquired in two parcels in 1907; today fields, woodland and a farm pond surround the house. [2]

Young was born to enslaved parents in Kentucky in 1864, graduated from West Point in 1889 as only the third African American to do so, and served with the Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry. He became the first African American acting superintendent of a national park, at Sequoia and General Grant in 1903, the first military attaché to Haiti and the Dominican Republic, and, by the eve of World War I, the highest-ranking African American officer in the Army and the first to reach colonel. [1] The park’s brochure describes him overcoming stifling inequality in the face of racism and oppression. The monument tells his story together with that of the Buffalo Soldiers, the Black regiments Congress created in 1866. [3]

black.html: At West Point, which Young entered in 1884 as the ninth African American cadet, the park brochure says he faced constant racial insults and social isolation from cadets and instructors; his first posting, at Fort Robinson, was marked by isolation and hostility. [3] The 2014 foundation document notes no other African American graduated from West Point until 1936, and ties his medical retirement in July 1917 to the prejudices and political pressures, under which the War Department generally kept African Americans from leading Black regiments bound for France. He rode 500 miles on horseback from Wilberforce to Washington to prove his fitness; the decision was not reversed. He died in Lagos, Nigeria, on January 8, 1922, while serving as military attaché to Liberia, and in 1923 became the fourth soldier honored with a funeral service at Arlington Amphitheater. [1] The brochure adds that his body came home at the urging of his wife and other notable African Americans. [3]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: CHYO archive page — undated NPS brochure
Foundation Document, CHYO (2014), Brief Description

indigenous.html: The Park Service’s 2019 Buffalo Soldiers study says the name is thought to have arisen because, reportedly, Plains Indians compared the soldiers’ hair to a buffalo’s fur, while other sources credit their courage in combat, and more research is needed. As agents of the U.S. military, the study says, the Buffalo Soldiers facilitated westward expansion and carried out the army’s policies to “kill, subjugate, and displace native people,” though military records show infrequent instances in which they were enlisted to keep settlers off tribal lands. In the early national parks, Army soldiers restricted American Indians from using resources and holding ceremonies within parks, many of which had been their traditional homelands, and soldiers assigned to the parks enforced restrictions keeping them from returning; the study calls for that role to be explored. [4]

sources.title: NPS, Buffalo Soldiers Study (March 2019)

slavery.html: Young was born on March 12, 1864, near Mays Lick, Kentucky, to Gabriel and Arminta Young, both enslaved; shortly afterward Gabriel escaped slavery to fight in the U.S. Army. [2] The brochure says he joined the 5th Regiment, U.S. Colored Heavy Artillery, in Ohio in February 1865, and that after the war the family moved to Ripley, Ohio, where Charles studied under the African American abolitionist John Parker. [3] Laura Smith, a formerly enslaved woman, settled in Greene County with William Smith, a Mississippi plantation owner, who on July 14, 1858, filed manumission papers for her and their seven children; later that month she bought the house and 79.71 acres. She died in 1871, and the land stayed in her name until her heirs sold it. The Youngs’ two 1907 purchases effectively restored the boundaries of her farm, and local history holds that they may have been drawn by its connection to Smith and the Underground Railroad. [2]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers Cultural Landscape (2019), Chronology
NPSHistory.com: CHYO archive page — undated NPS brochure, 'Childhood: From Enslavement to Freedom'

women.html: While Charles served abroad, the 2019 cultural landscapes inventory says, his wife Ada oversaw the daily management of the household and farm, and around 1914 she directed construction of a bungalow on the property; in a 1914 letter from Liberia Charles discussed with his mother, Arminta, sending funds, hiring help and planning a new kitchen. Ada, who also taught at Wilberforce University, lived at Youngsholm until her death in 1953. After Charles died she sold the house and land in 1925 to family friend Claudia Harreld for $7,500, the appraisal, while the family went on living there. Struggling, she wrote in 1939 that pennies had been awfully scarce; in 1951 Harreld sold Youngsholm back to her for “$1 and other valuable consideration.” Their daughter Marie later taught French and music at Wilberforce. [2]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers Cultural Landscape (2019)

Foundation Document, Colonial National Historical Park, Virginia (NPS, May 2018)

COLO.summary:
Colonial National Historical Park holds both ends of British America on one Virginia peninsula: Jamestown Island on the James River, where 104 Englishmen came ashore in 1607, and the fields at Yorktown on the York, where Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. The Colonial Parkway runs between them through bald cypress, marsh and pine-hardwood forest, and about 6,000 of the park’s 8,677 acres are habitat for native plants and wildlife. People lived here for more than 11,000 years before the English arrived; the park’s 2018 foundation document says its resources evoke the interaction and conflict between the colonists and the Powhatan Paramount Chiefdom, the evolution of the colonies, and the development of lifelong African American slavery. [1] [2]

In 1619 the first elected representative assembly in English-speaking North America — 22 burgesses, subject to the governor’s veto — met in the church at Jamestown. The same year, 20 to 30 captive Africans were sold at Point Comfort. The park’s brochure puts the two side by side and draws the conclusion itself: Jamestown’s legacy includes representative government, but also slavery, a brutal institution that spread through the colonies. Congress authorized the park in 1930; the Park Service bought most of Jamestown Island in 1934, and in 1994 Preservation Virginia’s Jamestown Rediscovery project began the search that found the original James Fort, long believed lost to the river. [1] [2]

climate.html: Jamestown Island is low, sinking and surrounded by water. Sea level here rose an average of 0.18 inch a year between 1927 and 2013 and could stand 2.1 to 2.7 feet higher by 2100, and land subsidence on the island amplifies the rise. Recent assessments of more than fifty archeological sites on the island recorded dramatic losses to coastal erosion, many of them 40 to 50 percent. The park’s average temperature rose at a rate of 1.2 °C per century from 1950 to 2010, and the 2018 foundation document expects erosion and inundation to further damage and destroy archeological resources, storm surge to threaten the Jamestown collections storage and the parkway’s riverside stretches along the James and York, and rising seas to worsen scour at some parkway bridge abutments. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Colonial National Historical Park, Virginia (NPS, May 2018)

indigenous.html: The English landed inside the chiefdom of Wahunsenacawh, known as Powhatan, who ruled subordinate tribes from Werowocomoco. The foundation document says he first tried to absorb the colony as one more tributary “tribe,” then to contain rather than destroy it; a key source of conflict was the colonists’ demand for food the tribes could not spare, after drought-induced crop failures that NPS-sponsored tree-ring analyses of Jamestown’s cypresses have since revealed. When more English arrived, Powhatan cut off the maize and besieged the fort, and the Starving Time of 1609–10 followed. His brother Opechancanough led attacks in 1622 and 1644, by which time disease and English attacks had set the confederacy’s power in decline. After Opechancanough was captured and killed in 1646, his successor’s treaty made the confederacy’s tribes tributaries of the English king and established one of the earliest Indian reservations; after Bacon’s Rebellion, the 1677 Treaty of Middle Plantation added tributary tribes and formalized a reservation for the Pamunkey and Mattaponi, a treaty the foundation document says is still in effect. The Pamunkey and the Catawba Indian Nation are the park’s traditionally associated tribes. [2] [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Colonial National Historical Park, Virginia (NPS, May 2018)
NPSHistory.com: Colonial National Historical Park archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

slavery.html: Tobacco, which John Smith said passed in Virginia as current silver, demanded labor. At first the colony relied on indentured servants, and the earliest Africans faced conditions closer to theirs; some bought their freedom and became planters. The foundation document traces how that changed: the number of enslaved Africans in Virginia rose from 300 in 1650 to 13,000 in 1700; after 1662 a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life; and after Bacon’s Rebellion, in which many Black indentured servants fought, new laws were meant to divide poor whites and Blacks. The 1705 Slave Code, in the brochure’s words, stripped all rights from people of color. At the New Town home site of planter-merchant William Pierce, archeologists are uncovering the story of a woman named Angelo or Angela, the only one of the first Africans whose name is known, who lived in his household in 1625. [2] [1]

Foundation Document, Cumberland Gap National Historical Park, Kentucky, Tennessee and Virginia (NPS, 2016)

CUGA.summary:
From Alabama to Canada the Appalachian Mountains rise in parallel ridges between the seaboard and the continent’s interior, and for anyone traveling by horse or on foot the crossing points were few. Cumberland Gap is one of them: a notch in the Cumberland Mountains (carved by wind and water, in the 2016 foundation document’s words; caused by a fault block cutting across the range, according to the 2024 historic resource study) that migrating bison used first and American Indians followed. Their Warrior’s Path ran through it. [1] [1] [1]

Dr. Thomas Walker, staking out an 800,000-acre grant beyond the Blue Ridge, explored the gap in 1750, and in 1775 the longhunter Daniel Boone was commissioned to blaze a road through it. Boone’s trace became the Wilderness Road, the primary way west until 1810. The 2008 park brochure counts 200,000 to 300,000 people crossing (dating the stream from 1780 in its text and 1776 in its timeline); the 2016 foundation document says nearly 300,000 between 1775 and 1810, and that some 40 million Americans can trace their history to the crossing. In the Civil War both sides thought the gap strategic; it changed hands several times but saw no major action. [1] [1]

Congress authorized the park on June 11, 1940, and it was established in 1955. U.S. 25E then ran through the gap; the highway was moved into the Cumberland Gap Tunnel, opened in 1996, and the gap was restored toward its appearance around 1810. The park now covers 24,547 acres in three states, more than 14,000 of them recommended for wilderness. [1] [1]

black.html: The 2024 historic resource study traces Black history in the towns beside the park, Cumberland Gap and Middlesboro. After the Civil War, freed people from the Cumberland Gap area settled at Tiprell, the former home of Confederate Maj. G. B. Cockrell, until his return forced them off the land. Many went back to Cumberland Gap and joined a Black community growing up around the old grist mill; the 1870 census counted 45 Black residents in the town. In industrializing Middlesboro, nearby, there were 447 Black residents at its 1890 charter, and in 1891 Berea College graduate George W. Bell opened the first school there for Black children, later Lincoln High School, where he taught with his wife, Elgetha. Later, the study finds, the region’s Black community declined as industrial jobs moved away and coal mining fell sharply in the 1920s, part of a wider exodus from the Appalachian coalfields to industrial centers such as Pittsburgh, Cleveland and Akron. [1] [1]

sources.title: North Wind Resource Consulting, Historic Resource Study, Volume One: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park (NPS, September 2024)
NPSHistory.com: Cumberland Gap NHP archive page — overview (from the 2008 NPS brochure), timeline and establishment block

indigenous.html:
The park’s 2024 historic resource study puts human use of the region at more than 12,000 years, though only ten of nearly 90 sites known in the park by 2005 had prehistoric components. Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw and Muscogee (Creek) peoples to the south and Shawnee, Wyandotte and Delaware to the north reached hunting grounds on a trail first worn by elk and bison, which the Shawnee called Athiamiowee, the Path of the Armed Ones (the brochure spells it Athawominee). In 1750 Walker saw crosses and figures carved by Indigenous people on laurel trees near the gap. [1] [1]

In the 1774 Treaty of Camp Charlotte the Shawnee gave up their hunting grounds south of the Ohio, and in March 1775 a Cherokee council at Sycamore Shoals, despite opposition, most notably from Dragging Canoe, approved the sale of some 20 million acres. The study describes the wars of 1776–1794 as fighting against colonists who kept violating treaties protecting tribal lands. [1]

sources.title: North Wind Resource Consulting, Historic Resource Study, Volume One: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park (NPS, September 2024)
NPSHistory.com: Cumberland Gap NHP archive page — overview (from the 2008 NPS brochure), timeline and establishment block

slavery.html: The people who crossed the gap, the foundation document notes, ranged from merchants and doctors to servants and enslaved people. Near the gap itself slavery took a different shape than in the lower South, according to the 2024 historic resource study: its small, self-sufficient farms were not heavily dependent on enslaved labor, most small farmers in the region enslaved fewer than five people, and the enslaved typically worked alongside their enslavers as farmers, craftspeople, cattle herders and merchants. A few large landowners — Robert Crockett, Daniel Huff and James Patterson — each held 20 to 30 enslaved people before the Civil War, and the 1850 census listed 33 slaveholders in or near the gap. When John G. Newlee took over the iron furnace at Cumberland Gap in 1841, he brought several enslaved Black workers who were employed in running it. [1] [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Cumberland Gap National Historical Park, Kentucky, Tennessee and Virginia (NPS, 2016)
North Wind Resource Consulting, Historic Resource Study, Volume One: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park (NPS, September 2024)

women.html:
The foundation document says modern travelers can hardly imagine what the men, women and children crossing the gap endured: hunger, cold, injury, disease, loneliness and uprooted families. A traveler’s 1803 journal quoted in the park brochure describes four or five hundred people on the road, many nearly naked and barefoot, with a single horse for two or three children. [1] [1]

A century later, on Brush Mountain inside today’s park, the families of the Hensley Settlement lived what the 2024 historic resource study calls a primitive existence reminiscent of the region’s earliest settlers. In December 1903 Eunice “Nicey” Hensley and her husband Sherman became the first of the family to move there; at its peak in the 1930s about 120 people lived in the settlement. According to the 2024 historic resource study, women did most of its domestic labor — preserving food, making quilts and serving as midwives. Sherman Hensley was the last to leave, in 1951. [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Cumberland Gap National Historical Park, Kentucky, Tennessee and Virginia (NPS, 2016)

photos.caption: Nearly 18 miles of undeveloped beach, nesting area for birds and sea turtles

Page last updated July 30, 2024. Resized from 5184x3456.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Cumberland Island National Seashore archive page — overview (from the 2012 NPS brochure) and establishment block
NPS, Foundation Document, Cumberland Island National Seashore, Georgia (2014)

CUIS.summary:
Cumberland Island is the largest and southernmost of Georgia’s barrier islands: 17.5 miles long, up to 3 miles wide and 36,415 acres, nearly half of it salt marsh, mudflat and tidal creek. Live oak forest draped in Spanish moss gives way to interdune meadows, freshwater ponds where alligators bellow in spring, rear dunes up to 45 feet high at the north end and almost 18 miles of beach, where loggerhead sea turtles nest in the most significant numbers on the Georgia coast. The ocean is the dominant force here, constantly building and eroding the shore. [n] [1]

People have used the island for more than 4,000 years, and the brochure lists what they left: shell middens, Spanish pot shards from the mid-1500s, a standing row of slave cabin chimneys, and the ruins of mansions. Revolutionary War general Nathanael Greene bought land here in 1783; his widow Catherine built the four-story tabby house called Dungeness; and from 1881 Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy acquired most of the island for winter estates. Carnegie family members, government officials, conservation groups and the Park Service worked together to create the national seashore on October 23, 1972, and Congress designated wilderness on the island in 1984, now the largest designated wilderness on any East Coast barrier island. [n] [1]

black.html: Union forces occupied Cumberland Island on March 2, 1862. Island tradition, recorded in a 1978 National Register nomination, holds that freedpeople driven off the Stafford, Rayfield and Dungeness plantations settled at the north end as squatters. In 1890 Mason Burbank, part-owner of the High Point hotel, bought five acres at Half Moon Bluff, divided them into 42 lots, and sold them to Black residents, some of them former slaves or their descendants; the nomination suggests the hotel owners wanted assurance of long-term employees. A log building serving as church and school went up in 1893, and the present First African Baptist Church was built in 1937. The foundation document describes the Settlement as home to several African American families who staffed the island’s hotels and estates. [n] [n] [1]

sources.title: Torres, Historic Resource Study, Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Historic Structure Report, Historical Data Section of the Dungeness Area (NPS, November 1977)
National Register nomination, High Point–Half Moon Bluff Historic District (Martin’s Half Moon Bluff Tract/High Point), Cumberland Island (NPS Southeast Regional Office, January 1978)
NPS, Foundation Document, Cumberland Island National Seashore, Georgia (2014)

climate.html: The 2014 foundation document expects climate change to bring more frequent and intense storms and rising seas, likely causing more shoreline erosion and the loss of archeological resources, and projects significant effects on coastal areas from inundation and higher temperatures. A 2004 U.S. Geological Survey assessment of nearly 30 kilometers of the island’s shoreline rated 22 percent at very high vulnerability to sea-level rise and 28 percent at high vulnerability; the nearby Fernandina Beach tide gauge had recorded relative sea-level rise of about 2 millimeters a year over 103 years. [n] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Foundation Document, Cumberland Island National Seashore, Georgia (2014)
Pendleton, Thieler & Williams, Coastal Vulnerability Assessment of Cumberland Island National Seashore (CUIS) to Sea-Level Rise, USGS Open-File Report 2004-1196

indigenous.html:
Shell middens across the island are, in the 2014 foundation document’s words, the most conspicuous clues to a complex American Indian population that once prospered here. Indians knew the island by names including Tacatacuru, according to the 1977 historic resource study, whose author calls its people Timucuans. In 1587 the Franciscan Baltasar López founded the mission of San Pedro de Mocama, probably at the south end (Mocama meant “on the sea” in Timucua), and a second mission, San Pedro y San Pablo de Porturiba, followed in the north, probably after 1595. In 1602 López counted 792 Christian Indians on the island. [n] [1]

The missions did not last. As the English pushed south from Carolina, Creek allies of the English struck missions as far south as Jekyll Island in 1680; amid revolts and an exodus of Indians to the English, Spain’s governor ordered all missions north of Amelia Island removed in 1686, and those on Cumberland were abandoned. [1]

sources.title: NPS, Foundation Document, Cumberland Island National Seashore, Georgia (2014)
Torres, Historic Resource Study, Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Historic Structure Report, Historical Data Section of the Dungeness Area (NPS, November 1977)

slavery.html:
By the late 1700s, the foundation document says, a plantation system built on enslaved Africans had taken root on Cumberland. After Nathanael Greene’s death in 1789, Catherine Greene and her second husband Phineas Miller sold live oak timber for the first ships of the U.S. Navy, and sea island cotton became the island’s most profitable crop. The number of enslaved Africans rose from about 200 in 1835 to 455 in 1850 as cotton production grew, while the white population probably never exceeded 60; by 1860 the island had about 13 plantations. [n] [1]

At Robert Stafford’s plantation, famous for sea island cotton, the slave quarters stood about a kilometer east of the main house. A 2003 Park Service report counts the remains of 26 chimneys of tabby and brick there, 19 still standing. After the Civil War, according to writers the 1977 study cites, Stafford burned the quarters and sent away the freedpeople who had returned. [n] [1]

photos.note: On-page figcaption: "The Paul Laurence Dunbar House Historic Site in Dayton, Ohio. NPS / Tom Engberg"; alt "A two-story home with peaked gray roof and two chimneys with green shutters around the windows". Resized from 5184x3456.

DAAV.summary:
Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park is a partnership park of six sites and 111 acres in and around Dayton, Ohio, preserving the places of inventors Wilbur and Orville Wright and poet Paul Laurence Dunbar. At South Williams and West Third streets stand the fourth Wright Cycle Company building, the only one left of the brothers’ bicycle business, and the Hoover Block, where they ran a print shop on the second floor from 1890 to 1895. On the 84-acre Huffman Prairie, now inside Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, they proved in 1904 and 1905 that the airplane was a practical invention; by October 1905 they could stay aloft for 39 minutes and 24 miles. In 1910 the Wright Company opened the first factory in the United States designed for building airplanes. [1] [2]

Dunbar and Orville Wright were in the same class at Dayton’s Central High School, and the Wrights printed Dunbar’s short-lived newspaper, the Dayton Tattler, which catered to the neighborhood’s African American population, along with tickets for his poetry performances. The park was established on October 16, 1992. Its foundation document calls the Dunbar house the first publicly administered site to commemorate an African American. [1] [2] [3]

black.html:
Dunbar was born in Dayton in 1872 to parents who had both lived in slavery. Denied newspaper jobs in Dayton because of his race, he ran an elevator, scribbling notes and poems in quiet moments, and published his first book, Oak and Ivy, in 1892. He lived in the west Dayton house from 1904 until his death in 1906 at 33; the foundation document says it represents the success he reached in an era of increasing racial segregation. [1] [2] [3]

By 1960, the 2022 administrative history reports, 95 percent of Dayton’s African American residents lived in West Dayton, the result of continuing housing discrimination. Some residents questioned the motives of the mostly European American group proposing the park and asked for help upgrading their properties instead. The administrative history says the park’s local backers “acknowledged West Dayton’s concerns but ultimately disregarded them,” while acquiescing to the wealthy suburb of Oakwood, whose opposition kept Hawthorn Hill out of the park. [1]

sources.title: Susan Ferentinos with Hannah Craddock Mossman, Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park: An Administrative History (NPS, September 2022), ch. 1 and ch. 4, pp. 18–20, 78–80, 199
NPSHistory.com: Dayton Aviation Heritage NHP archive page — NPS brochure, ‘Paul Laurence Dunbar: Dayton’s Beloved Poet’
Foundation Document, Dayton Aviation Heritage NHP (2017), significance statement 2

women.html: The park’s 2018 interpretive plan describes Paul as raised by a single mother who was formerly enslaved. Matilda Dunbar kept the house much as he knew it and lived there until her death in 1934. The plan says the State of Ohio’s 1936 purchase, which made it the nation’s first state-owned African American historical site, validated decades of work by Matilda Dunbar and Dayton’s citizens to preserve his legacy. The 2022 administrative history says that Dunbar married fellow writer Alice Moore (later known as Alice Dunbar Nelson) in 1898, “but Dunbar proved to be abusive, and Alice left him four years later.” Katharine Wright designed Hawthorn Hill with her brothers; in 1914 she, Orville and Milton Wright moved in. [1] [2] [3]

DEWA.summary:
At the Delaware Water Gap the river twists in a tight S-curve through Kittatinny Mountain, cutting a pass about 1,200 feet deep and a mile wide between New Jersey’s Mount Tammany and Pennsylvania’s Mount Minsi. The view made the gap a renowned resort area in the 1800s. Today the park covers 67,210 acres, by the foundation document’s count, and 40 miles of the Delaware, which the 2014 foundation document calls the longest undammed river in the eastern United States; it draws more than 5.2 million visits a year, largely from the New York and Philadelphia metropolitan areas. [1] [2]

The park began as recreation land around a reservoir that was never built. After Hurricanes Connie and Diane in August 1955 — nearly 100 people died along Brodhead Creek alone — Congress asked the Army Corps of Engineers to study dams on the Delaware, including one at Tocks Island that would have backed up a reservoir roughly 40 miles long. Some 600 families and property owners were displaced, some from land their families had worked for centuries. Congress created the recreation area in 1965 around the planned reservoir. As costs rose and grassroots opposition grew, the Delaware River Basin Commission voted in 1975 to discontinue the project; the acquired land passed to the Park Service, 40 miles of free-flowing river were protected in 1978, and the dam was deauthorized in 1992. The foundation document credits the fight for a free-flowing Delaware with contributing to the movement that led to Earth Day and the National Environmental Policy Act. [3] [2]

indigenous.html:
The foundation document counts about 11,000 years of human use here and nearly 500 documented American Indian archeological sites — the best-preserved such complex in the Northeast, it says, with ongoing significance to American Indian tribes. The Park Service’s Lenape page says archeology begun in 1959, to salvage sites before the planned reservoir flooded the valley, revealed more than 10,000 years of history, consistent with Lenape oral traditions of living here since time immemorial. [2] [4]

Minisink — a Delaware word translated as “Hilly Country” or “Island” — was, by its National Historic Landmark nomination, the most important Munsee Indian community for much of the 1600s and 1700s. Pennsylvanians claimed the entire west bank of the Delaware under the Walking Purchase of 1737, which the nomination calls still controversial; Munsee people who refused to move were ordered off their land in 1742 by Iroquois acting at Pennsylvania’s request. Most had left Minisink by 1755, when war broke out. [5]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Delaware Water Gap NRA (NPS, 2014), significance statement 6 and Rich Archeological Heritage

It is the largest masonry structure in the Americas, and is composed of over 16 million bricks." credit "NPS Photo / Maria Belen Farias". Resized from 5616x3744. Caption here omits the page's superlatives.

NPSHistory.com: Dry Tortugas National Park archive page — NPS brochure text and establishment block

DRTO.summary:
Almost 70 miles west of Key West, seven keys of coral reef and sand — the Dry Tortugas — lie within roughly 101 square miles of shoals and open water at the far end of the Florida Keys. Ponce de León named them Las Tortugas, the turtles, in 1513; mariners’ charts soon read “Dry Tortugas,” because the islands offered no fresh water. Wind, waves and storms keep reshaping them, and hurricanes have made a few of the smaller keys disappear and reappear. Between February and September as many as 100,000 sooty terns gather to nest on Bush Key, and green and loggerhead sea turtles nest on the beaches. [1] [1]

The keys sit beside the main shipping channel between the Gulf of Mexico, the western Caribbean and the Atlantic, and their reefs made the area one of the nation’s principal ship graveyards. On Garden Key, construction of Fort Jefferson began in 1846 and was never finished; the park brochure calls it the nation’s largest 1800s masonry fort. During the Civil War it served as a military prison, holding Union deserters and four men convicted of complicity in Lincoln’s assassination. Franklin D. Roosevelt proclaimed Fort Jefferson National Monument on January 4, 1935, and Congress redesignated it Dry Tortugas National Park on October 26, 1992, broadening its purpose to include the islands’ marine ecosystems. [1] [1]

black.html: How emancipation came to Fort Jefferson, the 2019 study says, was far from straightforward. In summer 1862 the fort’s commander, Col. Joseph S. Morgan, declared the enslaved workers at Forts Jefferson and Taylor “independent” of their owners; the Fort Taylor engineer protested. Because the Keys were under Union control, the study notes, the Emancipation Proclamation did not strictly apply there; Key West slaveholder James Filor wrote Lincoln seeking an exemption, arguing that U.S. government agents had induced Key West citizens to buy slaves for work on the forts, and failed. In 1863 the fort’s Black labor force became freedmen and women; the study found no known documentation of them specifically. From September 1865 to January 1866, companies of the 82nd U.S. Colored Infantry, organized in Louisiana in 1864, garrisoned the fort. [1] [1]

sources.title: Pirtle, Smith & Reed (New South Associates), The African American Experience at Fort Jefferson, 1847–1876, prepared for the NPS (2019)
Smith, Engineering Slavery: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and Slavery at Key West, Florida Historical Quarterly 86(4), 2008

climate.html: The park’s 2017 foundation document records warmer ocean temperatures, increasing acidification of seawater, and coral bleaching and disease at the Dry Tortugas, and states that the associated effects of climate change have all been documented there. It lists sea-level rise and shoreline erosion as threats to island habitat and to turtle nesting beaches, rising temperatures as affecting sex ratios in sea turtles, and increasing storm intensity and frequency as a challenge to the ecosystem’s health and resilience. [1]

sources.title: NPS, Foundation Document, Dry Tortugas National Park (2017), fundamental resources analysis

slavery.html: From 1847 to 1863 enslaved men leased by the Army Corps of Engineers, mostly from Key West, formed the core of Fort Jefferson’s labor force, alongside seasonal white workers, mostly Irish immigrants; enslaved women were brought to cook and do laundry. A 2019 study for the Park Service calls the practice industrial slavery and concludes that its use at Fort Jefferson and nearby Fort Taylor would solidify slavery’s hold on Key West. Historian Mark A. Smith (2008), assuming Fort Jefferson used a share similar to Fort Taylor’s roughly 9 percent, suggests that about 17 percent of Key West’s enslaved people worked for the engineers between 1845 and 1860. On July 10, 1847, seven men — Jerry Mason, Jack English, George English, John Thompson, and Ephraim, Howard and Robert Mallory — slipped away by night in four boats, bound for the Bahamas. They were brought back days later, and a guard was posted. [1] [1]

sources.title: Pirtle, Smith & Reed, The African American Experience at Fort Jefferson, 1847–1876 (NPS, 2019), ch. 2
Smith, Engineering Slavery, Florida Historical Quarterly 86(4), 2008, pp. 498–503

Foundation Document, Effigy Mounds National Monument, Iowa (NPS, March 2014)
HRA Gray & Pape, Figures on the Landscape: Effigy Mounds National Monument Historic Resource Study (NPS Midwest Region, August 2003)

EFMO.summary:
Along the 400-foot bluffs above the Mississippi River in northeastern Iowa, low rises on the landscape resolve into shapes: bears, birds and other animals raised in earth. The NPS brochure says American Indians built these effigies between 850 and 1,400 years ago, and that only in the upper Midwest did a culture regularly build mounds seemingly shaped like birds, turtles, lizards, bison and, most often, bears. The monument holds 206 known prehistoric mounds, 31 of them animal effigies; the Great Bear Mound is 137 feet long. People have lived in eastern Iowa for more than 10,000 years, and the oldest mounds in the area, round conical burial mounds, date back about 2,500 years. Why the effigies were made remains, in the brochure’s word, a mystery; they were possibly religious sites or clan symbols. [1] [2]

Surveys of northeastern Iowa in the 1800s and early 1900s counted more than 10,000 mounds of all types; within a century fewer than 1,000 survived, as farmers plowed many low mound groups under. Official support for a park dates from 1909, when a state legislator’s proposal won the backing of Ellison Orr, then president of the Iowa Forestry and Conservation Association. In 1939, through the aid of state Conservation Commissioners Margo Frankel and Louise Parker, the Iowa Conservation Commission acquired the land needed to meet the Park Service’s 1,000-acre requirement. President Harry Truman proclaimed the monument on October 25, 1949. By 2014 it spanned 2,526 acres in four units, including the 1,045-acre Heritage Addition of 2000 and the Sny Magill unit, which holds half of all its mounds. [1] [2] [3]

indigenous.html:
A 2001 cultural affiliation study for the Park Service concluded that Oneota peoples probably derived from earlier Woodland peoples, including the effigy builders, though the link is difficult to prove; that Oneota is ancestral to a number of Siouan-speaking groups; but that a shared group identity between the mounds and specific tribes cannot be established. It also found a consistent theme among members of several Siouan groups, notably the Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) and Iowa, that their ancestors built the effigy mounds. [1]

In 1832 the United States forced the Sauk and Fox to cede land that included today’s monument, and moved the Winnebago into the “Neutral Ground” as a buffer between the feuding Sioux and Sauk and Fox; in June 1848 the Winnebago were removed north of the Minnesota River. The 2014 foundation document says the monument is identified by members of its traditionally associated tribes as a sacred landscape. [1] [2]

sources.title: Green, Zimmerman, Lillie, Makes Strong Move and Sly-Terpstra, Effigy Mounds National Monument Cultural Affiliation Report, Vol. I (University of Iowa for NPS, 2001), ch. 9
Figures on the Landscape: Effigy Mounds NM Historic Resource Study (2003), ch. 4, pp. 36–37
Foundation Document, Effigy Mounds National Monument (2014), significance statements

women.html: Emma Big Bear Holt (1869–1968), a Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) woman, lived for years around what is now the monument — in a wickiup in winter and a tent in summer near Waukon Junction, three miles north, later beside the river at McGregor. The Park Service remembers her as one of the last Ho-Chunk living a traditional life in northeast Iowa. Her husband, Henry, helped prepare black ash logs, and she sold her baskets to locals and tourists; they are now collectors’ pieces, identifiable in part by their counter-clockwise rotation. The park writes that she and her family likely witnessed the destruction of some mounds as farm fields and towns expanded. [1]

sources.title: NPS, Effigy Mounds National Monument: “Emma Big Bear” (nps.gov, last updated July 27, 2021)

EVER.name: Everglades NP

photos.caption: An aerial view of the landscape transition from sawgrass to Florida Bay
photos.note: Homepage header gallery figcaption: "An aerial view of the landscape transition from Sawgrass to Florida Bay." credit span "NPS Photo". Resized from 3008x2000.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Everglades National Park archive page — overview (from the 2014 NPS brochure) and establishment block
NPS, Foundation Document, Everglades National Park, Florida (October 2017)
Blythe, Wilderness on the Edge: A History of Everglades National Park (NPS / Organization of American Historians, September 2017)

EVER.summary:
The Everglades is a river so gently sloping that no point in the park stands more than eight feet above sea level: a shallow, 50-mile-wide flow of fresh water that historically began in Lake Okeechobee and still moves slowly toward Florida Bay and the Gulf of Mexico. Marjory Stoneman Douglas named it the River of Grass in the 1940s. The park’s 1.5 million acres hold freshwater sloughs and prairies, pine rocklands, tropical hardwood hammocks, mangrove estuaries and the seagrass meadows of Florida Bay, more than 400 bird species, and the largest legislated wilderness east of the Rocky Mountains. It is the only place in the United States that is at once an International Biosphere Reserve, a World Heritage Site and a Wetland of International Importance. [n] [1]

Its archeological and historic sites span about 6,000 years. Congress authorized the park in 1934, but the land had to be donated, and President Harry S Truman did not dedicate it until December 6, 1947. It was the first national park set aside for its biological resources rather than its scenery or history. [n] [1]

The Park Service’s 2014 brochure describes what has happened since. Canals and levees shunt off water before it reaches the park, agricultural runoff and mercury pollute it, and wading birds nesting in southern Everglades colonies have declined 93 percent since the 1930s, from 265,000 to about 18,500. Congress has authorized the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, which the brochure calls the world’s largest environmental restoration project. [n] [1]

climate.html: The park’s 2017 foundation document reports sea-level rise already evident in estuarine and freshwater wetland gauges and saltwater intrusion and sea-level rise increasing, at a rate it says is rising because of climate change. It warns that rising seas and salt water could accelerate peat collapse and the loss of Everglades soils and marsh elevation, turning wetlands into open estuary; that stronger storm surges could overtop the marl ridge and threaten the Cape Sable wetlands; and that rising seas and larger storms threaten the park’s cultural resources. An earlier Park Service climate brochure noted that two-thirds of the park lies below three feet in elevation, and that under some sea-level scenarios the park’s pinelands, which hold most of South Florida’s remaining pineland habitat, could disappear. [n] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Foundation Document, Everglades National Park, Florida (October 2017)
NPS South Florida Natural Resources Center, Climate Change and South Florida’s National Parks: portrait of a changing landscape (undated, after the 2005 hurricane season)

indigenous.html: The Spanish met the Calusa, a chiefdom built on fishing, hunting and gathering rather than farming, and the Tequesta. Disease, war and upheaval took a horrendous toll, Blythe’s 2017 park history says; many historians believe the last of them left for Cuba with the Spanish in 1764, though some may have stayed. Most of the people who became known as Seminoles were Muskogee-tradition people from farther north. In the Second Seminole War (1835–1842) soldiers killed Chekika at a hammock now inside the park and strung up his body; almost 3,000 Indians and associated Black people were removed west. After the Third Seminole War, 100 to 150 people held out, ancestors of all of today’s Seminole and Miccosukee in Florida. Officials then agreed to replace a 99,200-acre Seminole reservation inside the proposed park with land elsewhere; Blythe found no evidence the Indians were consulted. The 2017 foundation document recognizes the park as ancestral territory of Florida tribes. [n] [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Wilderness on the Edge: A History of Everglades National Park (NPS / Organization of American Historians, September 2017)
NPS, Foundation Document, Everglades National Park, Florida (October 2017)

women.html: The Florida Federation of Women’s Clubs, led from 1914 by May Mann Jennings, won 960 acres of Royal Palm Hammock from the legislature in 1915, added a 960-acre exchange of land donated by Henry Flagler’s widow, and opened Florida’s first state park in 1916, running it with limited state funding until 1947. Marjory Stoneman Douglas, a writer and early park supporter, published The Everglades: River of Grass in November 1947, a month before the dedication, drawing on U.S. Geological Survey scientist Garald Parker; the first printing of 7,500 copies sold out by Christmas. During the fight against a proposed jetport she became president of the new Friends of the Everglades. In 1997 Congress renamed the park’s wilderness the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Wilderness; she was 106. [n] [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Wilderness on the Edge: A History of Everglades National Park (NPS / Organization of American Historians, September 2017)

FIIS.name: Fire Island National Seashore
FIIS.summary: Fire Island National Seashore, established in 1964, protects a 26-mile stretch of barrier island off the southern shore of Long Island, New York — one of the last remaining undeveloped barrier beaches on the Atlantic Coast. The national seashore was created after a fierce conservation battle to prevent large-scale resort development on the island. The park includes the Sunken Forest, a rare 300-year-old maritime holly forest growing behind the dunes, and the Fire Island Lighthouse, first constructed in 1826 and rebuilt in 1858. The William Floyd Estate, the ancestral home of a signer of the Declaration of Independence, is also part of the seashore. Fire Island has historically served as a significant cultural refuge for LGBTQ communities, particularly the communities of Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines.

FODA.name: Fort Davis National Historic Site
FODA.summary: Fort Davis National Historic Site in the Davis Mountains of West Texas preserves one of the best surviving examples of a frontier military post in the American Southwest. Established in 1854, the fort guarded emigrants, mail coaches, and freight wagons on the San Antonio–El Paso road through Limpia Canyon. After the Civil War, the post was garrisoned by troops of the 9th and 10th U.S. Cavalry and the 24th and 25th U.S. Infantry — the famed Buffalo Soldiers, African American troops who played a vital role in the frontier Army during the Indian Wars period. The fort was active until 1891 and was designated a national historic site in 1963. Over two dozen original and restored buildings remain, making it one of the most intact frontier forts in the West.

FODO.summary:
In January 1862 a Union reconnaissance concluded that the weakest points in the Confederacy’s western defense line were two earthen forts guarding the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers. On February 6 Flag Officer Andrew Foote’s gunboats pounded Fort Henry into submission; almost 2,500 of its garrison escaped a dozen miles to Fort Donelson, on the Cumberland near Dover, Tennessee. There, on February 14, the Confederate river batteries drove off Foote’s ironclads in a 90-minute duel. A Confederate breakout the next day briefly opened an escape route before confused commanders ordered their men back to the trenches, and on February 16 Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant answered a request for terms: no terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender. An estimated 13,000 Confederate soldiers were shipped north to prison camps. [1]

It was the North’s first major victory of the war. The South gave up southern Kentucky and much of Middle and West Tennessee, and the rivers became Union supply lines into the Confederate heartland. The park’s foundation document adds that the campaign saw the war’s first use of inland ironclad gunboats and its first joint Army–Navy operation, and that the Union presence drew enslaved people to seek freedom, leading to Free State, which it calls one of the first freedmen’s communities in Tennessee, and perhaps the nation. Fort Donelson became a national military park on March 26, 1928, and a national battlefield on August 16, 1985. [1] [1]

black.html: After the surrender, enslaved people from nearby plantations came into the Union lines. Ten days after it, Grant issued General Orders No. 14, which barred slaveholders from his lines; he would not return people to their enslavers, and he sought government work for those who had built the Confederate fort. Freedom seekers kept coming. Their settlement southwest of the Union fort became known as Free State, probably one and the same as the army’s contraband camp, whose men built the new Union Fort Donelson in 1863 and enlisted as United States Colored Troops; teachers from Indiana opened a school there in March 1864 that by May had 100 pupils. The brochure says an estimated 300 enslaved people wintered at Fort Donelson in 1864; the study quotes an 1867 description of Free State as numbering about 300. Free State lasted for decades and became an African American neighborhood of Dover. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Fort Donelson NB archive page — overview (from the NPS brochure) and establishment block
Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)

indigenous.html: The park’s 2013 ethnographic overview places the Cumberland valley in a region that archeologists have posited was largely abandoned around 1450–1550; by the 1600s it was a borderland used by at least three tribal nations for hunting and seasonal camps. The Shawnee were among its first occupants, so many that the Cumberland was known as the Rivière des Chaouanons, the Shawnee River; Stewart County was likely a seasonal hunting ground. Around 1714–1715 the Cherokee and Chickasaw drove a large contingent of Shawnee out of the valley. The 1785 Treaty of Hopewell compelled the Cherokee to cede land south of the Cumberland, and in 1805 the Chickasaw reaffirmed a boundary on the ridge between the Cumberland and Tennessee rivers while the Cherokee ceded their lands north of it. By the end of the 1830s the Southeastern nations had been forced to cede their lands east of the Mississippi and remove to Indian Territory, where their governments remain. [1]

sources.title: Lee, Greer & Lee, Fort Donelson National Battlefield: Ethnographic Overview and Assessment, Final Report (Earth Search for NPS, September 2013)

labor_ccc.html: Depression relief programs worked on the park itself. From December 1933 to April 1934, 398 Civil Works Administration laborers, among them African Americans and three women, worked on seven projects in the park, graveling roads, planting and controlling erosion. A crew of four Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees helped historian W. W. Luckett excavate a caved-in magazine at the water batteries; the restored magazine, completed in 1940, is a CCC-built interpretive reconstruction, and the 2020 historic resource study recommends that the park’s National Register listing stop describing it as an original feature. [1]

sources.title: Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)

slavery.html:
Before the war, the iron furnace companies were Stewart County’s largest slaveholders. The park’s 2020 historic resource study reports that in December 1852 the iron makers on the Cumberland employed 1,395 white workers and 1,910 enslaved laborers, and in 1859 the owners of the Cumberland Iron Works, John and Jane Bell, held 417. Enslaved people made up nearly a quarter of Stewart County’s residents. When rumors of a revolt started at one or more of the furnaces around Christmas 1856 — reports the study calls full of inaccuracies — it was reported that eighty enslaved people were arrested; enslaved furnace workers were beaten to force confessions, and approximately six or seven, possibly more, were killed in Stewart County — though, the study notes, there was no proof of any rebellion. [1]

The fort itself was built by Confederate soldiers and enslaved laborers, who also built more than 400 log huts as the garrison’s winter quarters. [1]

sources.title: Brent, Spurlock, Heavrin & Poole, Historic Resource Study, Fort Donelson National Battlefield (Cultural Resource Analysts for NPS, March 2020)
NPSHistory.com: Fort Donelson NB archive page — overview (from the NPS brochure) and establishment block

women.html:
Enslaved women worked at the iron furnaces, cooking, cleaning, laundering and farming for the works, and the 2020 historic resource study notes that enslaved and free white women also did physically demanding work alongside men at the furnaces; the 417 people held at the Cumberland Iron Works in 1859 included 58 women. After the battle, the brochure notes, women like Mary Ann Bickerdyke nursed sick and wounded soldiers though they were not officially recognized as nurses. [1] [1]

In the contraband camp, women commonly worked as cooks and laundresses, and in March 1864 two women teachers from Wayne County, Indiana, arrived with Ira B. Hutchens to open its school, teaching children and adults to read. [1] [1]

Foundation Document, Fort Frederica National Monument, Georgia (NPS, 2016)

FOFR.summary:
On St. Simons Island, Georgia, at a sharp bend in the Frederica River between salt marsh and live oaks hung with moss, lie the remains of Frederica, the fort and town James Oglethorpe laid out in 1736 to hold Britain’s southern frontier against Spanish Florida. The first settlers — 44 men, mostly skilled workers, and 72 women and children — built palmetto huts and then houses of wood, brick and tabby, a concrete of burnt oyster shell, along a 75-foot-wide Broad Street shaded by orange trees. At its height the town held about 500 people by the 2009 park brochure’s count, more than 800 by the 2016 foundation document’s. [1] [2]

Frederica was born of war. In early 1740 “the aggressive Oglethorpe,” as the 2009 brochure calls him, set out to capture St. Augustine with 900 troops and 1,100 Indian allies, and failed. In July 1742 a Spanish force landed on the island; British troops beat back one column within sight of the town and ambushed another at Bloody Marsh. Casualties were light, but within a week the Spanish withdrew, ending, in the Park Service’s judgment, Spain’s claim to Georgia and the Carolinas. Peace undid the town: the regiment was disbanded in 1749, and a visitor in 1755 found houses without inhabitants and streets overgrown with weeds. [1] [2]

Congress created the national monument on May 26, 1936. Its roughly 282 acres in two units protect a largely intact archeological record — the subject of more than 40 investigations since 1936, with more than 227,000 objects in the park’s collections — and tabby ruins such as the King’s Magazine that now stand in the path of an eroding riverbank. [2]

black.html: Just outside the town wall lies a small cemetery of freed people from the late 1860s and 1870s. One of them is Thomas Abbott, whom Charles Stevens — a coastal shipper who held nineteen people in slavery in 1860 and whose family owned much of the old townsite — had enslaved; another is Celia Abbott. Many freed people, the park notes, still worked for former enslavers after emancipation, often on the same land. Thomas Abbott’s son Robert, born on St. Simons, founded The Chicago Defender, a paper that aided African Americans during the Great Migration and exposed lynching; in 1928 he paid $1,500 for a monument to his ancestors. Ground-penetrating radar in 2017 and 2019 and a 2019 excavation, guided by a church map marking a “Colored burial lot,” confirmed the cemetery’s location. The monument, the 2016 foundation document says, links the park to the island’s African American community and the early struggle against racial prejudice. [6] [2]

sources.title: NPS, Fort Frederica NM: Reconstruction Era History at Fort Frederica (nps.gov, last updated August 1, 2024)
Foundation Document, Fort Frederica NM (NPS, 2016), Other Important Resources and Values: Monuments

climate.html: The river beside which Oglethorpe placed Frederica is now eroding it. The 2016 foundation document warns that shoreline erosion along the Frederica River is an increasing threat, especially to the King’s Magazine, and that a rising water table and more frequent and intense storm surges tied to climate change could disturb buried archeological deposits. Salt marshes on the Georgia coast, it notes, may shrink by 20 to 40 percent this century as sea level rises. The document calls for working with Georgia’s Department of Natural Resources on a Living Shoreline project to stabilize the bank, and one of its interpretive themes concerns conserving and restoring the island ecology that shaped the lives of the people who lived there. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Fort Frederica NM (NPS, 2016), Interpretive Themes; Analysis of FRVs (Archeological Resources, Historic Structures, Frederica River and Salt Marsh); Key Issues: Climate Change

indigenous.html: Before Frederica there was a Guale village on the same ground, allied to Spain through trade and conversion to Catholicism; two Spanish missions stood on the island. The park’s history describes how English traders armed Native slave raiders — the Westo were the largest such group from 1679 into the early 1700s — and how British colonists and their allies attacked the coastal missions to enslave the Guale; in 1683 the village and missions were abandoned, their people following the Spanish south or forcibly removed. Half a century later the Yamacraw, a people of mixed Creek and Yamasee descent, served as treaty negotiators between Oglethorpe and the Creek, allowing Frederica’s peaceful founding in February 1736. Oglethorpe laid out the town lots on a field the Indians had planted in corn, and townspeople traded with Creek and Yuchi people outside the town gate. [3] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Fort Frederica NM: The People Before Frederica (nps.gov, last updated September 12, 2024)
NPSHistory.com: Fort Frederica archive page — 2009 NPS brochure (“Defending Utopia”, “Touring the Park”)

slavery.html: Frederica’s settlers farmed with their own hands, because Georgia banned slavery. The park attributes the ban both to the Trustees’ ideals and to fear: an enslaved person’s quickest way to freedom ran down the Frederica River to Spanish Florida, where accepting Catholicism and fighting for Spain could bring liberty. Colonists petitioned against the ban soon after Frederica’s founding; in 1751 Parliament allowed slavery. By 1775 nearly 18,000 people were enslaved in Georgia; St. Simons came to hold more than 14 plantations. In 1803 John Couper and Thomas Spalding bought 75 Igbo people in Savannah; on the voyage south, the park recounts, they overpowered their captors, took the ship into Dunbar Creek two miles from Frederica, and walked into the water rather than be re-enslaved. Long told as legend — the park notes details vary by source — the event is documented in letters to Pierce Butler, one recording bodies salvaged at ten dollars a head. [1] [5]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Fort Frederica archive page — 2009 NPS brochure (“Defending Utopia”, “The Battle of Bloody Marsh”)
NPS, Fort Frederica NM: Igbo Landing (nps.gov, last updated September 9, 2024)

women.html: Coosaponakeesa, known as Mary Musgrove, was born at Coweta on the Ocmulgee River in 1700, the daughter of British trader Edmund Griffen and of a sister of the Lower Creek leader Brim. When Oglethorpe met the Yamacraw chief Tomochichi in 1733 she interpreted, and the colony paid her one hundred pounds sterling a year. She helped negotiate treaties, recruited warriors against Spain, supplied the struggling colonists with meat and bread, and in 1742 influenced the Creeks to aid the British on St. Simons. She owned three trading posts, and her third husband, Thomas Bosomworth, pressed claims to Sapelo, St. Catherine’s and Ossabaw islands granted to her by the Creeks — making her, in the park’s telling, the largest landowner in colonial Georgia. [4]

sources.title: NPS, Fort Frederica NM: Mary Musgrove (nps.gov, last updated October 20, 2022)

FOMC.name: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine
FOMC.summary: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine in Baltimore, Maryland, is the birthplace of the American national anthem. During the Battle of Baltimore on September 13–14, 1814, British naval forces bombarded the star-shaped fort for 25 hours during the War of 1812. The fort's successful defense inspired Francis Scott Key, who watched the bombardment from a truce ship in the harbor, to write the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry," which was later set to music and became "The Star-Spangled Banner," officially adopted as the national anthem in 1931. Designated as a national park in 1925 and redesignated in 1939, Fort McHenry is the only unit in the National Park System designated both a national monument and a historic shrine.
