Foundation Document, George Washington Memorial Parkway, District of Columbia–Maryland–Virginia (NPS, 2014)

GWMP.summary:
George Washington Memorial Parkway runs along the Potomac River through Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia, protecting the river’s landscape and natural shoreline while offering scenic vistas of Washington, D.C., and the Great Falls of the Potomac. Congress established it on May 29, 1930, through the Capper-Cramton Act. Its first leg, the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway, opened in 1932, the bicentennial of Washington’s birth; the 2014 foundation document calls it the first comprehensively designed modern motorway built by the federal government, a pioneer of limited access, grade-separated intersections and cloverleaf interchanges. The northern section was completed in 1962, and the Maryland side was renamed Clara Barton Parkway in 1989. [1] [1]

The park covers 7,600 acres by the park brochure’s count (7,374 in the foundation document) and more than 25 sites. [1] At Great Falls, the largest waterfall on the Potomac, the river rushes over jagged rocks into Mather Gorge beside the remnants of the Patowmack Canal, whose construction Washington presided over; the 15-mile Potomac Gorge is, in the foundation document’s words, one of the most biologically diverse natural areas in the national park system. Fort Hunt Park, once part of the Mount Vernon estate, had batteries that defended the river during the Spanish-American War; in World War II, as the site of P.O. Box 1142, it served as a prisoner-of-war camp and the interrogation center for many high-profile German prisoners. [1]

The parkway’s lands hold prehistoric American Indian sites, and it also manages Theodore Roosevelt Island, a Civil War training area for the Union Army that included the first United States Colored Troops, and Clara Barton National Historic Site at Glen Echo. [1]

black.html: In 1863 the island, then called Analostan or Mason’s Island, became Camp Greene, where the 1st Regiment of United States Colored Troops was mustered. The Emancipation Proclamation had opened Union enlistment to African Americans that January, but Black soldiers could not rise to officer rank and were paid seven dollars a month against thirteen for white soldiers of equal rank. The District of Columbia mustered the regiment in May 1863, and some 3,500 Black men from the District enlisted by the war’s end. Walt Whitman visited and called it the pleasantest camp he had yet seen. On July 30, 1863, the regiment left the island for the siege of Richmond and Petersburg, later fought at Wilmington, and lost 185 enlisted men before it was decommissioned in 1865. [1]

sources.title: NPS, Camp Greene (nps.gov/this, last updated May 23, 2024)

indigenous.html: Theodore Roosevelt Island lies in a stretch of the Potomac valley that people have used for over 15,000 years, a Park Service history of the island explains. Projectile points about 9,000 years old are its earliest archeological record; people came to fish, hunt, gather shellfish and nuts, and, archeologists suspect, revisited such camps over generations. Around 4,000 years ago people of the Savannah River Culture brought soapstone bowls, and settlement on the island peaked in the Middle Woodland period (700 B.C.E.–1000 C.E.). By the Late Woodland the region’s tribes included the Powhatan coalition in Virginia and the Piscataway and Nanticoke in Maryland, and John Smith’s map of 1607–08 records the nearby settlements of Namoraughquend and Nacotchtanck. English encroachment disrupted the economies and social structures of Virginia tribes, the history notes, yet many Native people still live in the Potomac valley. [1] The foundation document records American Indian archeological sites along the parkway, including on the bluff at Clara Barton’s house. [1]

sources.title: NPS, A History of Native American Life on Theodore Roosevelt Island (nps.gov/this, last updated May 23, 2024)
Foundation Document, George Washington Memorial Parkway, District of Columbia–Maryland–Virginia (NPS, 2014)

labor_ccc.html: In May 1933 about 3,000 delegates to a second Bonus March of World War I veterans were bused to Fort Hunt, where Eleanor Roosevelt visited them; when Franklin Roosevelt offered places in the new Civilian Conservation Corps, 2,657 enrolled. CCC Camp NP-6 opened there on October 17, 1933, with 200 enrollees of Company 1241 from New York and Virginia, who cleared dead timber, built bridle paths and landscaped the capital’s parks. A third march camped at Fort Hunt in May 1934, including 270 African American delegates, and 565 more veterans joined the Corps. Company 2387, which replaced it in 1937, planted trees and shrubs along the parkway, and between 1933 and 1938 some 20 enrollees built relief maps and models of parks in Fort Hunt’s “Model Laboratory.” [1] On Theodore Roosevelt Island, CCC crews from 1935 graded paths and, with the Historic American Buildings Survey, excavated the Mason House foundation in 1936. [1]

sources.title: Matthew R. Laird, “By the River Potomac”: An Historic Resource Study of Fort Hunt Park (NPS, August 2000), ch. 5
NPS, Civilian Conservation Corps at Theodore Roosevelt Island (nps.gov/this, last updated May 23, 2024)

women.html: Clara Barton’s house at Glen Echo, Maryland, went up in 1891 on land given by developers Edward and Edwin Baltzley, who also supplied the labor and some of the materials, hoping her fame would sell lots around their Chautauqua. Barton — Civil War nurse, women’s rights suffragist, and founder and first president of the American Red Cross — lived there briefly in 1891 and again from 1897 until her death in 1912, kept a small farm of cows, horses, chickens and goats, and presided over the Chautauqua’s Women’s Executive Committee. [1] The house was the Red Cross’s first permanent headquarters from 1897 to 1904. The foundation document notes that Barton won international recognition at a time when women were not given the same opportunities as men, and that the site, established in 1974, was one of the first national historic sites dedicated to the accomplishments of an American woman. [1]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Glen Echo Park–Clara Barton House (NPS, 2011)

HAFE.name: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park

photos.caption: Lower Town Harpers Ferry seen from Maryland Heights
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "View of Lower Town Harpers Ferry as seen from Maryland Heights" with credit span "NPS Photo/Shenandoah Sanchez" (park homepage carousel). Resized from 3068x2048.

photos.caption: John Brown’s Fort in winter
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "John Brown's Fort in Winter" with credit span "NPS Photo/Holden Mills" (park homepage carousel). Resized from 3650x2452.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park archive page — overview (from the 2015 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Harpers Ferry National Historical Park (NPS, 2016), pp. 3–6

HAFE.summary:
At Harpers Ferry the Potomac River cuts through the Blue Ridge and takes in the Shenandoah, leaving a V-shaped water gap that Thomas Jefferson called perhaps one of the most stupendous scenes in nature, worth a voyage across the Atlantic. That gap made the place a crossroads from the earliest human habitation onward: American Indians first, then European settlers, and in 1747 Robert Harper’s ferry across the Potomac. Congress authorized a federal armory here on June 15, 1796; when production began in 1801 it was the nation’s second, and in its workshops new ideas about interchangeable parts were tried and tested while large-scale manufacturing turned a quiet rural village into one of the leading industrial centers of its day. [1] [2]

In October 1859 John Brown and his followers seized the armory, determined to arm enslaved people and spark a rebellion; the raid failed, but his trial and execution, in the park brochure’s words, propelled the nation toward civil war. Harpers Ferry then changed hands eight times, and in September 1862 Stonewall Jackson captured nearly 12,700 Union soldiers here — the largest surrender of U.S. troops in the war. After it, Storer College opened on Camp Hill in 1867 as a school primarily for formerly enslaved people, and in 1906 hosted the second conference of the Niagara Movement, where W. E. B. Du Bois demanded equality and civil rights. Congress authorized Harpers Ferry National Monument in 1944; it became a national historical park in 1963 and now covers 3,745 acres in West Virginia, Maryland and Virginia. [1] [2]

black.html:
During and after the war, people escaping slavery, called “contrabands,” poured into Harpers Ferry; by the mid-to-late 1860s about 700 African Americans lived in town, double the prewar number. Freewill Baptists opened a school for refugees in the armory paymaster’s Lockwood House in 1864, and on October 2, 1867, Storer College began classes there with nineteen students. Students were bullied by local residents and at times had to be escorted into town by hired militiamen. For 25 years Storer was the only institution in West Virginia offering African Americans secondary and post-secondary education; Frederick Douglass was among its first trustees. [3] [2]

In August 1906 the Niagara Movement held its second conference at Storer, and participants walked from the college to John Brown’s Fort, then standing on the Murphy Farm, going barefoot as they approached it to commemorate Brown; the conventions led to the founding of the NAACP in 1909. Storer closed in 1955, after the State of West Virginia withdrew its support. [3] [2]

sources.title: Bailey, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry NHP (NPS, 2017), pp. 27, 47–49, 107, 140
Foundation Document, Harpers Ferry National Historical Park (NPS, 2016), pp. 4, 6

indigenous.html: People first lived in the Shenandoah Valley in the Paleoindian period, roughly 11,000 to 9,600 B.C. A 1989–1990 excavation in Lower Town recovered 1,585 artifacts — ceramics, stone tools, postholes and hearths — from Late Archaic and Early Woodland occupations around 1200 to 500 B.C. By the time Europeans arrived about 1600, the valley had held no permanent villages for nearly a century; Tuscarora and Shawnee people lived there in temporary settlements, and Iroquois raiding parties used it as a route to attack southern nations such as the Catawba and Cherokee. A series of treaties pushed Native nations west; in the 1744 Treaty of Lancaster the Iroquois sold their land claims to the Virginia Colony and moved west of the Allegheny Mountains. The 2017 ethnographic overview could identify no Native American groups with ties to the park’s resources, quotes an earlier park study that there are no federally recognized tribes in the vicinity, and acknowledges that the park has generally devoted more of its resources to the town’s historic remains than to its pre-contact past. [3]

sources.title: Bailey, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry NHP (NPS, 2017), ch. 2, Native American Presence, pp. 15–18

labor_ccc.html: The armory began in 1801 with 28 armorers who turned out 293 flintlock muskets that year; by 1810 it employed almost 200 workers in 28 buildings. Its earliest workforce was mostly highly skilled gunsmiths using hand tools, each able to make an entire gunstock or forge and assemble a whole musket lock, and the Ordnance Department’s drive to impose factory discipline met resistance. When Superintendent Thomas Dunn posted strict rules and inspections that cut piece-work wages, a disgruntled former worker Dunn had refused to rehire, Ebenezer Cox, murdered him in his office in early 1830; Cox’s execution, the park’s 2006 study says, made him a folk hero to the armorers. In 1842, after Major Henry Craig imposed a fixed workday enforced by a clock, the entire workforce struck for a week and sent a delegation to President John Tyler protesting that they were being made into “mere machines of labor.” The protest failed: Congress passed, and Tyler signed, a law placing military superintendents over all U.S. armories and arsenals. [4]

sources.title: Lee, The U.S. Armory at Harpers Ferry: Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2006), pp. 12, 23, 30, 42–43

slavery.html:
Harpers Ferry sat in Jefferson County, Virginia, which in the first half of the nineteenth century held twice as many enslaved people as any other county in present-day West Virginia: 4,157 in 1840, 4,341 in 1850, and 27 percent of the population by 1860. In Harpers Ferry and Bolivar most owners held one or two people. Newspaper accounts cited in the 2017 ethnographic overview show people bought and sold frequently; an 1857 notice reported free Black people sold by court order in front of the Charles Town courthouse for remaining in the state contrary to law; and escapes toward Pennsylvania were frequent enough that the Virginia Slave Insurance Company was formed in Charles Town to insure against them. [3]

On October 16, 1859, Brown led 21 men against an arsenal holding 100,000 arms. The first man killed was Heyward Shepherd, an African American baggage handler for the B&O Railroad. By noon on October 17, the park’s own 2006 armory study records, drunken vigilantes encircled the armory and several captured raiders were brutally executed; U.S. Marines took Brown at daybreak on October 18. [3] [4]

sources.title: Bailey, An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry National Historical Park (NPS, 2017), pp. 23, 43–45
Lee, The U.S. Armory at Harpers Ferry: Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2006), ch. 7, pp. 57–59

HOBE.name: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park
HOBE.summary: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park in east-central Alabama preserves the site of the decisive battle of the Creek War. On March 27, 1814, forces led by General Andrew Jackson, including U.S. Army regulars, Tennessee militia, Cherokee allies, and Lower Creek warriors, attacked the fortified camp of the Red Stick Creek faction at a horseshoe-shaped bend on the Tallapoosa River. Approximately 800 of the 1,000 Red Stick warriors were killed in the battle — one of the deadliest defeats suffered by Native Americans in U.S. history. The resulting Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek Nation to cede roughly 23 million acres — half of present-day Alabama and part of southern Georgia — to the United States. The park was established in 1956.

HOFU.name: Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site

HOFU.summary:
In 1771, as relations between England and its American colonies came apart, Mark Bird, already an important figure in the colonial iron industry, built Hopewell Furnace in eastern Pennsylvania. It took an acre of woodland to make enough charcoal to run an iron furnace for a single day. When the Revolution came, Bird turned from casting stove plates to supplying cannon and shot to the Continental Army and Navy; afterward trouble collecting debts from the new nation, a postwar depression and a 1786 flood added to his financial woes, and Hopewell was sold at a sheriff’s sale in 1788. [1]

The furnace’s best years came under resident manager Clement Brooke, from 1816 to 1831, when its iron went up and down the East Coast. The Panic of 1837, the Bessemer steel process and the rise of urban steel mills ended that, and Hopewell went out of blast for the last time on June 15, 1883. Around it had lived what historians call an “iron plantation”: miners, woodcutters, colliers, teamsters, moulders and farmers whose lives the furnace governed, African Americans among them, enslaved at first and later free. [1]

The federal government bought the property in 1935, and on August 3, 1938, 214 acres of furnace lands were set aside as a national historic site — according to the park’s 2004 historic resource study, the first industrial complex the Park Service established as a historic site. The 2017 foundation document describes an iron-making village that operated from 1771 to 1883, whose buildings, landscape and people illustrate the American industrial past, and whose surviving company records reveal the daily business and the activities of the people who lived and worked there. [1] [1] [1]

black.html:
An African American community grew up along Six Penny Creek, in what is now French Creek State Park; an 1860 map shows about a dozen families there. Peter Jones and Joseph Tolbert, of two of those families, probably worked at Hopewell — Jones as early as 1818 — and the 2004 historic resource study judges the community likely to have been formed by people who escaped slavery. By 1856 it had its own church, Mount Frisby African Methodist Episcopal, on land owned by Isaac Cole; it served as a stop on the Underground Railroad. Cole and James Jackson, both Union Army veterans, are buried in its cemetery, which the study calls the oldest African American cemetery in Berks County. Furnace records name many other African Americans, among them Bill Jacobs, who spent nearly 100 years at Hopewell as teamster, coachman and gardener. [1]

In 1988 superintendent Derrick Cook began an annual Black History Month program at the site. [1]

sources.title: Robinson & Associates, Historic Resource Study: Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site (NPS, December 2004)
Glaser, Administrative History: Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site (NPS Northeast Region, August 2005)

labor_ccc.html:
Before the government had finished buying the land for the French Creek Recreational Demonstration Area, a Depression program to give poor city dwellers outdoor recreation, Civilian Conservation Corps Company 2213, 200 unemployed young men, arrived at Camp SP-7 on December 10, 1934. In little more than six months they replaced roofs and stabilized five structures of the old iron plantation for their own use. In April 1935 CCC architect Gustavus Mang reported on the site’s history and recommended preserving the furnace buildings. [1] [1]

The 2004 historic resource study is frank about the cost: enrollees used slag piles and stones from the East Head Race walls to build roads, regraded ground near the Ironmaster’s House, reportedly removed artifacts and disposed of some furnace records — perhaps, it says, the most damaging act. The Park Service adds that CCC workers stabilized the furnace stack, built Route 345 and served as some of the site’s first tour guides. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Hopewell Furnace NHS archive page — overview (from the 2011 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Robinson & Associates, Historic Resource Study: Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site (NPS, December 2004)
NPS, “The Civilian Conservation Corps,” Hopewell Furnace NHS website

slavery.html:
When Pennsylvania passed its emancipation act in 1780, Mark Bird held 18 enslaved workers, which the park’s 2004 historic resource study says made him the largest slaveholder in Berks County. Some of them worked at his Birdsboro forges, and tradition holds that enslaved laborers dug the furnace’s East Head Race. The study notes this was not unusual: travelers reported that enslaved African Americans did much of the work at Maryland’s ironworks, and enslaved workers were known at furnace jobs in southeastern Pennsylvania in the 1750s. [1]

The park brochure traces the change over time: African Americans worked the furnaces enslaved at first, later as temporarily employed runaway slaves and as free Black workers. The 2017 foundation document lists enslaved people, the Underground Railroad, abolition and emancipation among the stories of the park’s interpretive themes. [1] [1]

sources.title: Robinson & Associates, Historic Resource Study: Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site (NPS, December 2004)
NPSHistory.com: Hopewell Furnace NHS archive page — overview (from the 2011 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site, Pennsylvania (NPS, 2017)

women.html:
The furnace’s workforce was not only men. The park brochure says the cleaners who finished cast products were often women and children, that women added to family incomes by sewing, lodging and boarding single workers and laundering, and that some earned extra income as woodcutters and miners. The 2017 foundation document calls for showing women at Hopewell in roles ranging from traditional nineteenth-century ones to work directly involved in iron making. [1] [1]

Elizabeth Disrude, superintendent from October 1975 to February 1988, was the Mid-Atlantic Region’s first female superintendent. Glaser’s 2005 administrative history reads her appointment as part of the Park Service’s response to the women’s rights movement, and notes that the 1970s living-history program brought in women’s roles, though usually closer to the period celebrated by the Bicentennial than to the site’s own period of interpretation. [1]

HUTR.summary:
Hubbell Trading Post sits at 6,325 feet beside the Pueblo Colorado Wash on the edge of Ganado, Arizona, in a valley the Navajo call Lók’aah niteel, Wide Reeds, and in the middle of the Navajo Nation. People lived along this wash long before any trader: Wide Reed Ruin, a pueblo with kivas and plazas inside the site, was built in A.D. 1276–77 by tree-ring dating, and, by the administrative history’s account, the general area was largely abandoned about 1300 because of a drought that had begun in the 1270s. [1] [1] [1]

John Lorenzo Hubbell, born in Pajarito, New Mexico Territory, in 1853, began trading in the Ganado valley in 1876 and, by the park’s administrative history and foundation document, bought a trading post on this spot — William Leonard’s, the administrative history says — in 1878 (the 2010 park brochure dates the purchase to 1876). He came as the Navajo struggled to adjust to reservation life after the Long Walk. In 1883 he built a new post of uncoursed sandstone, today divided into a bullpen store, jewelry room and rug room beside a wareroom, and a U.S. post office opened there in the 1880s. At various times Hubbell and his sons owned more than 30 trading posts. He died in 1930 and lies in an unmarked grave on Hubbell Hill, following Navajo custom. [1] [1] [1]

Congress authorized the historic site on August 28, 1965, on the understanding that it would stay a working business, and Dorothy Hubbell sold it to the Park Service in 1967. It is the oldest continuously operating trading post in the Southwest: artisans still bring in rugs, jewelry, pottery and baskets, neighbors still buy groceries, and the museum collection holds more than 450,000 items. [1] [1]

indigenous.html:
In 1864 the U.S. Army forced more than 8,500 Diné (Navajo) on the Long Walk to Hwééldi — Bosque Redondo, at Fort Sumner, New Mexico Territory — for four years of imprisonment. When they came home in 1868 their hogans, herds and crops were gone, and many came to depend on traders for food. The Navajo leader Totsonii Hastiin, Ganado Mucho, invited Hubbell to the valley; when smallpox swept the reservation in 1886 Hubbell turned his home into a hospital. Traders wrote letters and served as pawnbroker and banker; the Manchesters’ 1993 administrative history counts them among the most important acculturating forces in Navajo history. [1] [1] [1] [1] [1]

The park brochure says Navajo learned weaving from Spanish, Mexican and Pueblo weavers and surpassed them, and dates blankets of Spanish Churro-sheep wool to the 1650s; Navajo-Churro ewes still lamb at the post each spring. Hubbell urged weavers toward older patterns in gray, black, white and red, the style now called Ganado Red. Daghaa Neezi, Friday Kinlicheenie, came to work at the post around 1915, kept its garden for some 70 years and, as a medicine man, performed a Blessing Way there. [1] [1] [1]

latino.html: Hubbell came from a Hispanic New Mexican family on his mother’s side. His father, James Lawrence Hubbell, came from Connecticut; his mother, Julianita Gutierrez (so spelled in the administrative history; the park brochure has “Gutierriez”), was of Spanish descent. He worked as a clerk and Spanish interpreter at forts and trading posts before he traded, married Lina Rubi of Cebolleta, New Mexico Territory, in 1879, and was known to local Hispanics as Don Lorenzo — “Don,” the administrative history notes, being a Spanish term of respect — and to the Navajo as Naakaii Sani, Old Mexican. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Hubbell Trading Post NHS archive page — overview (from the 2010 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Manchester & Manchester, Hubbell Trading Post National Historic Site: An Administrative History (NPS Southwest Cultural Resources Center, 1993), Introduction — History of the Site to 1957

women.html: Born Dorothy Elizabeth Smith in Indiana, Dorothy Hubbell came west in 1920 to teach the Hubbell children and soon married their widowed father, Roman. By 1957, with Roman gradually paralyzed by strokes and the family company in bankruptcy, she was running the post while caring for him. That July she asked the Museum of Northern Arizona whether it could acquire and preserve the place; it could not, but the administrative history dates the movement for a national historic site to that year. She was appalled when one prospective buyer said he would sell off the contents and put in a liquor store, and the Manchesters credit her “vision, determination, and patience” for bringing the collection to the American people intact. [1] [1] [1]

INDE.name: Independence National Historical Park

photos.caption: Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were signed

NPS Photo". Resized from 5883x3922.

photos.note: On-page caption (homepage slideshow, alt "Color photo of the Liberty Bell with Independence Hall in the background."): "Recognizable for its crack, the Liberty Bell remains significant today for its message of liberty. NPS Photo". Resized from 3000x2000.

Foundation Document, Independence National Historical Park (NPS, September 2017)

Mooney, Levin, Wuebber, Jeppson, Roberts, LaRoche & Brauer, The Archeology of Freedom and Slavery: Excavations at the President’s House Site in Philadelphia (URS/NPS/City of Philadelphia, 2009; rev. 2023)

INDE.summary:
Independence National Historical Park covers more than 51 acres of downtown Philadelphia, and at its center stands the old Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall. In its Assembly Room the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776; four days later the Declaration was read aloud to the public for the first time in the square outside. In 1787 fifty-five delegates were sent to Philadelphia, and in the same Assembly Room they created the Constitution — a document, the park’s own brochure says, that failed to adequately address slavery. Congress sat in nearby Congress Hall from 1790 to 1800, while Philadelphia was the nation’s capital, and the First Continental Congress had gathered at nearby Carpenters’ Hall in 1774. [1] [1]

The bell that hung in the State House steeple was first heard in 1753; its inscription reads “Proclaim Liberty throughout All the land unto All the Inhabitants Thereof.” In the 1830s anti-slavery groups named it the Liberty Bell; it cracked around 1846. The park’s brochure calls the crack a reminder that liberty is imperfect, hopefully evolving to include those denied full participation. [1] [1]

Congress created the park on June 28, 1948. The park was made by creating public parks and open green space around the founding-era landmarks, clearing later commercial buildings, drawing on the City Beautiful movement and the colonial revival of Williamsburg, and in the 1950s and 1960s park architects, archeologists and historians working on Independence Hall developed restoration methods the Park Service still treats as a model. Independence Hall was named a World Heritage Site in 1979. [1] [1] [1]

black.html: Ona Judge hid among the free Black Philadelphians she had befriended — part of a city the brochure describes as home to people fleeing slavery and free people of African descent. The house itself was torn down in 1832, and for some fifty years after Independence Mall was built the site lay under a lawn and a women’s restroom, marked only by a small brass plaque. In 2002 independent scholar Edward Lawler Jr. showed that Washington had ordered a smokehouse on the lot altered as housing for his “stablepeople.” Lawler judged it most likely that the order was carried out and the building housed enslaved stable workers, and he pointed out that visitors would pass over that site on entering the new Liberty Bell Center; in the controversy that followed, attorney Michael Coard founded the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition, and on July 3, 2002, some five hundred mostly African American protesters demanded a memorial. The 2007 excavation uncovered the kitchen where Hercules cooked and drew more than 300,000 visitors in four months; the park then built its first community-based exhibit there, interpreting race and slavery. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: Mooney, Levin, Wuebber, Jeppson, Roberts, LaRoche & Brauer, The Archeology of Freedom and Slavery: Excavations at the President’s House Site in Philadelphia (URS/NPS/City of Philadelphia, 2009; rev. 2023)
NPSHistory.com: Independence National Historical Park archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Independence National Historical Park (NPS, September 2017)

slavery.html: Partly beneath today’s Liberty Bell Center stood the President’s House, the executive mansion of George Washington (1790–1797) and John Adams (1797–1800). The Washingtons brought nine enslaved Africans from Mount Vernon to work there at various times: Austin, Christopher Sheels, Giles, Hercules, Joe Richardson, Moll, Ona (Oney) Judge, Paris and Richmond. Under Pennsylvania’s Gradual Abolition Law of 1780, the park’s 2009 excavation report (revised 2023) explains, enslaved people became free after a six-month stay in the state, so Washington rotated them back to Virginia — a practice the report says itself violated Pennsylvania law, which was not enforced. In the spring of 1796 Ona Judge walked out while the family sat down to dinner and escaped to New Hampshire; she died free in 1848. Hercules, the chef, escaped from Mount Vernon on February 22, 1797. Adams, the brochure notes, never owned slaves. [1] [1]

sources.title: Mooney, Levin, Wuebber, Jeppson, Roberts, LaRoche & Brauer, The Archeology of Freedom and Slavery: Excavations at the President’s House Site in Philadelphia (URS/NPS/City of Philadelphia, 2009; rev. 2023)
NPSHistory.com: Independence National Historical Park archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

women.html: Lucretia Mott and other activists of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society wrote for The Liberty Bell, the Boston abolitionist annual that in 1839 first gave the bell its name in print and for twenty years used it as an anti-slavery symbol, John Paige’s special history study for the park records. On July 4, 1876, Susan B. Anthony gave the first public reading of a women’s declaration of rights here, urging suffrage. And on August 2, 1954, the General Federation of Women’s Clubs gave the Park Service $209,541.82 raised nationwide to restore and refurnish the first floor of Independence Hall — by the park’s account the largest single sum ever applied to the building to that time. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: Paige, The Liberty Bell of Independence National Historical Park: A Special History Study (NPS Denver Service Center, undated, c. 1985), ch. on the bell as an abolitionist symbol
Foundation Document, Independence National Historical Park (NPS, September 2017)

INDU.name: Indiana Dunes National Park (National Lakeshore)
INDU.summary: Indiana Dunes National Park on the southern shore of Lake Michigan in northwestern Indiana protects 15,349 acres of dunes, wetlands, prairies, rivers, and forests. The park's origins trace to the early 20th-century conservation campaign led by botanist Henry Cowles, whose groundbreaking studies of plant succession on the Indiana dunes helped establish the modern science of ecology. Despite being surrounded by one of the most heavily industrialized regions in North America, the park supports remarkable biodiversity — over 1,100 native plant species, the fourth-highest count of any national park unit. Originally designated as Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, it was redesignated as a national park in 2019.

JELA.name: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve

photos.caption: The American rampart and cannons at Chalmette Battlefield, site of the 1815 Battle of New Orleans
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "Chalmette Battlefield's American rampart and cannons still guard the site of the Battle of New Orleans in 1815." credit span "NPS Photo" (park homepage). Resized from 2048x1536.

photos.caption: Spanish moss and wetland vegetation in Barataria Preserve
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "Spanish moss and lush vegetation provide glimpses of Louisiana's wild wetlands at Jean Lafitte's Barataria Preserve." credit span "NPS Photo" (park homepage). Resized from 3872x2592.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Jean Lafitte NHP&P archive page — overview (2017 and 2014 NPS brochures) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve (NPS, 2015), pp. 3–6

JELA.summary:
This land is the creation of the Mississippi River. At the end of its journey it drops sediment scoured from 40 percent of the continental United States, and the ground beneath the New Orleans region is less than 4,000 years old — marsh, slow bayous, cypress swamp and forested natural levees in a restless interplay of land and water. American Indians settled the delta as it formed, some 2,500 years ago; from the 1720s European settlers and enslaved Africans took their place among them, and the park’s brochure traces how French colonists, the Chitimacha, Houma and other tribes, enslaved West Africans, Spanish-speaking Isleños, free people of color from the Caribbean and Acadians each shaped the delta’s culture. [1]

On January 8, 1815, on the Chalmet plantation below New Orleans, Andrew Jackson’s mixed force of regulars, militia, volunteers and Jean Lafitte’s Baratarian privateers stopped a British assault in less than two hours; more than 2,000 British soldiers were killed, wounded or captured and American casualties numbered fewer than 20. Chalmette National Historical Park, created in 1939 to preserve part of that field, was the first national park unit in Louisiana. Congress expanded it into Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve on November 10, 1978, and in 1988 added three Acadian cultural centers, for six sites in all. The land itself is now going: human engineering has blocked sedimentation and increased coastal erosion, and rising seas due to climate change are accelerating the loss, by the brochure’s count a football field’s worth of land every 45 minutes. [1] [2]

black.html: Around 1867, Jean Pierre Fazende, a free man of color before emancipation, began selling lots on part of the old Chalmet plantation to freedmen. Fazendeville grew into a close-knit Black working-class village of about 40 houses, a church, stores, a school and benevolent societies, sitting between the battlefield monument and the national cemetery, which for generations drew its laborers from the village. Blythe’s 2012 administrative history records that NPS managers believed from the start that the community would have to be obliterated to provide a meaningful visitor experience of the historic scene. A 1962 law authorized the federal government to acquire every property in the village, and by 1964 the community was lost. The taking came, Blythe notes, while Black residents of St. Bernard Parish were struggling to register to vote, and some of those displaced saw the two as connected. The same history notes that throughout the Jim Crow era park managers and the major New Orleans media often overlooked the free men of color who helped win Jackson’s victory. The NPS placed a wayside about Fazendeville on the battlefield in 2008. [3] [2]

sources.title: Blythe, Administrative History of Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve (NPS, 2012), ch. 3 pp. 35–36; ch. 4 pp. 57–58
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte NHP&P (NPS, 2015), p. 4

climate.html: The delta was always in motion: over 3,500 years the Mississippi built five major deltas, the newest only 500 years old, while subsidence and erosion balanced the new land it laid down. Human engineering, from artificial levees to jetties, has upset that balance. The park’s 2015 foundation document says parts of this landscape have the highest rate of relative sea-level rise and land loss in North America — a historical average of 0.36 inches a year at Grand Isle from 1947 to 2012, with NOAA-based projections for 2100 of 3.30 to 7.62 feet. In Barataria Preserve, scientists have already documented species lost from the natural levee ridges, more flooding and land loss, and the document names the climate-driven rise of ocean influence over the delta and its people the park’s major cross-cutting concern. [1] [2]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Jean Lafitte archive page — 'Shaping a New Land' (2017 NPS brochure)
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte NHP&P (NPS, 2015), pp. 7, 12, 32

indigenous.html: People lived in the Barataria basin as soon as the river formed it, and by the Marksville period (about 100 B.C. to A.D. 300) were building large villages, growing corn and probably beans and squash to a moderate extent while hunting and gathering remained their most important source of food. Prehistoric shell middens from that long occupation remain part of the preserve’s landscape. At French contact their descendants were the Washa, Chawasha and Chitimacha (“Sitimachas” on an early French map after Guillaume Delisle). France’s Indian allies waged a twelve-year war on the Chitimacha, and, Holmes writes, Chitimacha bands contributed many Indian slaves to the French colony; the 1718 peace forced the Chitimacha to abandon Bayou Lafourche and settle near New Orleans. By 1739 the Washa and Chawasha together numbered only thirty warriors, which, Holmes writes, probably reflects significant population loss from disease. [4] [2]

sources.title: Holmes, Historic Resources Study: The Barataria Unit (NPS, 1986), ch. II, The Indigenous Occupation, pp. 31, 35; ch. VI, p. 129
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte NHP&P (NPS, 2015), p. 7 (Barataria Cultural Landscape)

latino.html: Spain took over Louisiana in 1763, and its colonial government built the public road it named El Camino Real de Barataria, the royal road, a remnant of which survives in the preserve. In 1778 the first settlers from the Canary Islands — the Isleños — arrived, brought by the Spanish governor to strengthen Spain’s presence and provide a barrier against British and American aggression. In 1779 the Spanish government settled a group of about 150 on a grant that took in the meeting of Bayou des Familles and Bayou Barataria; John McDonogh, who later bought the abandoned grant, said the bayou was called “des Familles” after the Canarian families placed there. Repeated floods from hurricanes and river crevasses, and a gradual drift of settlers to other Canarian settlements, wore the settlement down over some sixteen years, until a crevasse that opened in or before 1796 ruined the last five families’ crops and livestock and the government moved them to Terre aux Boeufs, in today’s St. Bernard Parish. [1] [2] [4]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Jean Lafitte archive page overview (2017 NPS brochure)
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte NHP&P (NPS, 2015), p. 9 (El Camino Real de Barataria)
Holmes, Historic Resources Study: The Barataria Unit (NPS, 1986), ch. III, Canary Islanders Settlement, pp. 57–58

slavery.html: Before the Civil War the Barataria region near New Orleans was worked as sugar plantations. In 1850, Holmes’s 1986 historic resource study counts 1,176 people living there: 504 enslaved, 15 free people of color and 657 white, with 79 percent of the enslaved owned by planters and living on the plantations. In 1856 the Mavis Grove plantation inventoried houses for 156 enslaved people alongside a steam-powered sawmill and seventy mules; the Andrew Hodge estate, almost entirely Mavis Grove, was valued at $226,914.61. Enslaved workers usually labored six days a week for their owners, and every day during the October-to-December harvest and sugar making. Earlier, from 1805 to 1813, Jean Lafitte, who the park’s foundation document says navigated these swamps smuggling contraband and enslaved people, built a commercial empire in the basin and, Holmes writes, dared to openly advertise an auction of contraband slaves there. [4] [2]

sources.title: Holmes, Historic Resources Study: The Barataria Unit of Jean Lafitte NHP (NPS Southwest Cultural Resources Center Professional Papers No. 5, 1986), pp. 59, 88–89
Foundation Document, Jean Lafitte NHP&P (NPS, 2015), p. 3

KIMO.name: Kings Mountain National Military Park

photos.caption: The U.S. Monument in the fall
photos.note: On-page caption: "US Monument in the Fall NPS Photo". Contemporary park photograph. Resized from 2400x3585.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Kings Mountain National Military Park archive page — overview (NPS brochure text, 2013) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Kings Mountain National Military Park, South Carolina (NPS, 2017)

KIMO.summary:
Kings Mountain — named for an early settler, not for King George III — is a rocky spur of the Blue Ridge rising 150 feet above the surrounding country, its forested slopes cut by ravines. On October 7, 1780, Maj. Patrick Ferguson waited on its summit with 1,000 loyalist militia and 100 Provincials. Some 900 patriot riflemen, many of them over-mountain men from the valleys of the Holston, Nolichucky and Watauga, rode through a night of rain, encircled the ridge and fought their way up from tree to tree. In little over an hour Ferguson, the only Briton in the battle, was dead and Cornwallis had lost his entire left flank; even after a white flag went up, patriots kept firing on the surrendering loyalists for several minutes. [1]

The park’s 2017 foundation document counts among its stories that the Revolution was, in many circumstances, a civil war, and says both sides recognized the battle as a turning point; Thomas Jefferson called it the turn of the tide of success. [1] The field then lay neglected for years. In 1815 Dr. William McLean, a former patriot surgeon, had soldiers’ bones exposed by erosion reburied and dedicated a monument; about 15,000 people came for the 75th anniversary in 1855. Congress established Kings Mountain National Military Park on March 3, 1931. [1]

The park’s 3,945 acres in York and Cherokee counties, South Carolina, take in the entire battlefield, its landscape little changed since 1780, the foundation document says. It is the southern end of the Overmountain Victory National Historic Trail and adjoins Kings Mountain State Park, most of whose land the Park Service conveyed to South Carolina in the 1940s. [1]

black.html: African Americans joined the chase after Ferguson, the park brochure says, and Essius Bowman, a free man, is one of the men said to have shot Ferguson. [1] The 2017 foundation document names African American participation in the battle, on both sides, as one of the park’s interpretive topics. [1] The park’s own buildings carry a later history: the stone Administration Building completed in March 1941 had basement restrooms originally restricted to African Americans. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Kings Mountain National Military Park archive page — overview (NPS brochure text, 2013) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Kings Mountain National Military Park, South Carolina (NPS, 2017)
Blythe, Carroll & Moffson, Kings Mountain National Military Park Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, May 1995)

indigenous.html: Before European-American settlers arrived, the Kings Mountain area lay in a buffer zone between the Catawba and Cherokee nations, the park’s 1995 historic resource study explains: the Catawba had villages to the east along the Catawba River, the Cherokees had villages to the west in the mountains, and both hunted here without settling permanently. In 1780 the region’s rough roads sometimes followed Native American trails. The study also notes that many of the militiamen were veterans of combat with Native Americans, and that Isaac Shelby and John Sevier each left roughly half their counties’ able-bodied men at home to defend against what the study calls the Cherokee threat. [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Carroll & Moffson, Kings Mountain National Military Park Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, May 1995)

labor_ccc.html: Under Park Service direction, Civilian Conservation Corps labor did most of the development work at Kings Mountain between 1937 and 1942, the 1995 historic resource study says. [1] Two CCC camps were set up — MP-1 for the military park and SP-7 for the proposed state park — but while land-purchase money was held up, the men were limited to fire prevention and boundary surveys. CCC guides trained by Rogers W. Young met visitors at a contact station on the ridge. [1] After all the acreage was acquired, the CCC built a lake, campgrounds, roads, a bathhouse and picnic shelters in the recreation area, and at the battlefield concentrated on road work and brush clearing; it began building the superintendent’s residence in September 1940. [1] With the war, enrollment fell from an average of 205 men to about 50, and on March 15, 1942, the CCC’s work at Kings Mountain ended; the superintendent reported many jobs left in semi-chaotic condition. [1]

sources.title: Massey, An Administrative History of Kings Mountain National Military Park (NPS Southeast Region, 1985)
Blythe, Carroll & Moffson, Kings Mountain National Military Park Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, May 1995)

slavery.html: The stone house that Henry Howser, a German stonemason from Pennsylvania, built on Kings Creek in 1803 still stands in the park, along with seven outbuilding foundations. The 1810 census shows Howser enslaving three people, one of six slaveholders in the area; by 1820 he enslaved four. The 1995 historic resource study suggests he likely built one or more dwellings for the people he enslaved, though little is known of the outbuildings. After his son’s death in 1842, the son’s widow Faithy Howser ran the farm for forty years; in 1860 she held three enslaved people, quartered in two houses. [1] [1] [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Carroll & Moffson, Kings Mountain National Military Park Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, May 1995)
Massey, An Administrative History of Kings Mountain National Military Park (NPS Southeast Region, 1985)
Foundation Document, Kings Mountain National Military Park, South Carolina (NPS, 2017)

women.html: Many wives and children came to Sycamore Shoals in September 1780 to see the militia off. [1] In 1899 the Kings Mountain chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution took over the neglected ground, receiving the land the Centennial Association had bought, and campaigned for local interest, more land and national recognition. [1] [1] Their efforts, administrative historian Gregory De Van Massey wrote in 1985, led Congress to appropriate $30,000 in 1906 for a new monument, and their role in the park’s creation “cannot be overemphasized.” The 83-foot U.S. Monument was dedicated in 1909, and the DAR, local officials and activists kept pressing until the 1930 sesquicentennial and the park’s creation the next year. [1] [1]

sources.title: Blythe, Carroll & Moffson, Kings Mountain National Military Park Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, May 1995)
NPSHistory.com: Kings Mountain National Military Park archive page — overview (NPS brochure text, 2013) and establishment block
Massey, An Administrative History of Kings Mountain National Military Park (NPS Southeast Region, 1985)

LECL.name: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail

photos.caption: Beacon Rock along the Columbia River in Washington
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "Beacon Rock along the Columbia River in Washington. NPS Photo"; alt "Water in the foreground with large conical rock on shore". Contemporary park photograph. Resized from 5184x3888.

photos.caption: Sunset over the Missouri River headwaters
photos.note: On-page figcaption: "Sunset over Missouri River headwaters NPS Photo / Alex Wiles". Resized from 5938x3964.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail archive page — overview (NPS brochure, 2016) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail (NPS, 2012)

LECL.summary:
The Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail runs about 3,700 miles to the mouth of the Columbia River near Astoria, Oregon, through 11 states and many tribal lands; the 2012 foundation document places its start at Wood River, Illinois, while the 2016 brochure says Hartford, Illinois. Congress established it in 1978 as one of the four original national historic trails, and the Park Service administers it through partnerships with agencies, tribal nations, nonprofits and private landowners. Along the route are the junction of the Knife and Missouri rivers, where the Corps wintered near the villages of the Mandan and Hidatsa, the Great Falls of the Missouri, Lemhi Pass on the Continental Divide, the Bitterroot Mountains, and Beacon Rock, where Clark saw the first sign of tidal water. [1] [2]

The NPS brochure says the Corps of Discovery would not have reached the Pacific and returned without the help of tribes like the Mandan and Hidatsa, Shoshone, Nez Perce and Clatsop, who provided food, trade, knowledge of the country ahead and guides. In September 1805, near starvation, the party came out of the Bitterroots near today’s Weippe, Idaho, and was fed and cared for by the Nez Perce. Only once, with Piegan Blackfeet in July 1806, did an encounter turn violent; two Blackfeet were killed. [1]

The trail’s 2012 foundation document acknowledges that some call the expedition an epic event leading to a young nation’s growth, while others characterize it as having huge disruptive impacts on rich Indigenous cultures. It says tribal oral histories, with the journals’ descriptions, substantiate, validate and enrich understanding of the tribes the expedition met. [1]

indigenous.html:
The federal government later flooded many of the expedition’s water routes. According to the trail’s 2018 administrative history, fifteen dams rose on the Missouri alone between 1890 and 1963; the Pick-Sloan Plan, approved in 1944, flooded more than 550 square miles of tribal land in North and South Dakota and forced more than 900 American Indian families from their homes. [1]

Many tribes were wary of the expedition’s bicentennial. Superintendent Gerard Baker, who grew up on the Fort Berthold Reservation, promised them they could tell their stories without censorship, edits or curation; historians Jackie Gonzales and Emily Greenwald write that the NPS had a long history of making such promises to tribes that it later broke. In October 2000 Allen Pinkham led the first tribally run planning meeting, at Lewiston, Idaho; eleven tribes there chose to take part, and the Circle of Tribal Advisors grew to about forty tribes, two-thirds of those Lewis and Clark documented. [1]

sources.title: Jackie Gonzales and Emily Greenwald, Commemoration and Collaboration: An Administrative History of the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail (NPS, 2018), pp. 24, 158–162

slavery.html: York, the brochure says, was a Black man held in slavery by William Clark. A Park Service page, as captured in December 2024, described him as a skilled frontiersman, likely the first African American to cross North America, born into a system that considered him property. His presence, with Sacagawea’s and her baby’s, was a curiosity to the tribes, and in November 1805 he too voted on where to winter. After the return the men received double pay and 320 acres; York, the NPS page said, was denied his payment and his freedom. During the bicentennial, Louisville unveiled a bronze statue of York on its Ohio River waterfront, and living history actor Hasan Davis portrayed him at a 2006 Corps II signature event in New Town, North Dakota. [1] [2] [3]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Lewis and Clark NHT archive page — NPS brochure (2016)
NPS, Lewis & Clark National Historic Trail: “York” (nps.gov, Wayback Machine capture of December 9, 2024)
Gonzales and Greenwald, Commemoration and Collaboration (2018), ch. on Corps II signature events, pp. 221, 225

women.html:
Sacagawea, a 16-year-old Shoshone, joined the Corps at Fort Mandan with her husband, the trapper Toussaint Charbonneau; their son Jean Baptiste, born in February 1805, traveled the whole route. She recognized Beaverhead Rock near her people’s homeland, met her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader, and in November 1805 voted with the Corps on where to winter. [1]

A century later, the administrative history recounts, suffragist Eva Emery Dye’s 1903 novel recast her as a heroine for the women’s suffrage movement, and Dye and other Portland Women’s Club members raised $7,000 for a statue unveiled at Portland’s 1905 Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition. In 2006 Stephenie Ambrose Tubbs wrote that Sacagawea’s history had been replaced with “almost 80 percent myth, legend, and fantasy,” and that her greater genius would seem to be her memory for landscapes, her skill as a translator and her ability to harvest foods. [1] [2]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Lewis and Clark NHT archive page — NPS brochure (2016), Corps of Discovery and timeline
Gonzales and Greenwald, Commemoration and Collaboration (2018), ch. 1, Commemorating Sacagawea, pp. 19–20
Stephenie Ambrose Tubbs, “Heartily Tired of the National Hug: Why Sacagawea Deserves a Day Off,” Columbia 20, no. 4 (Winter 2006–07)

LIBI.name: Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument

photos.caption: Headstone markers on the Little Bighorn battlefield
photos.note: NPSHistory.com park-archive banner photo; on-page credit (div.image-credit) reads "NPS photo"; alt text "Park Photo"; no caption on page — caption describes only what is visible (white headstone markers in grass), and the page's brochure text describes the Army's 1890 battlefield markers. Re-encoded JPEG at original dimensions. nps.gov Indian Memorial photos were rejected because their credits carry © Cathleen Cutschall.

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument archive page — overview (NPS brochure, 2016) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, Montana (NPS, March 2015)

LIBI.summary:
Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument is 765 acres of ridgelines, coulees and native prairie above the Little Bighorn River in southeastern Montana, in two parcels inside the exterior boundaries of the Crow Indian Reservation. On June 25 and 26, 1876, twelve companies of the 7th U.S. Cavalry under Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer, with Arikara and Crow scouts, fought allied Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho people camped along the river under the spiritual leadership of Tatanka-Iyotanka (Sitting Bull). Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated the regiment. Custer and every member of his immediate command, about 210 men, were killed, and another 53 died in the companies under Maj. Marcus Reno and Capt. Frederick Benteen. [1] [2]

The NPS brochure traces the battle to the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty: gold was found in the Black Hills, the heart of the reservation, in 1874, thousands of gold seekers swarmed in in violation of the treaty, and in December 1875 the commissioner of Indian Affairs ordered the tribes to return before January 31, 1876, or be treated as hostiles. The Indians won the battle, the brochure says, but subsequently lost the war against the military’s efforts to end their independent, nomadic way of life. The park’s 2015 foundation document says the outcome shocked the nation and heightened threats to the cultural survival of all Indian peoples. [1] [2]

The battlefield was established as a national cemetery in 1879, and in 1890 the Army set 249 headstone markers where Custer’s men fell. In 1991 Congress renamed Custer Battlefield National Monument as Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument and authorized a memorial to the Indian participants; since 1999 the Park Service has placed red granite markers at known Cheyenne and Lakota warrior casualty sites. The foundation document calls it sacred ground, contested ground and shared ground. [1] [2]

indigenous.html:
The 2003 Indian Memorial dedication program counts about 7,000 Sioux, Cheyenne and Arapaho people camped in the valley of the Greasy Grass, and 35 Arikara and six Crow scouts riding with Custer. The program adds that Arikara scouts killed in the valley fight, among them Bloody Knife, were buried where they fell and later reburied with the cavalry dead in the mass grave at Last Stand Hill, and that Sioux and Cheyenne relatives placed stone cairns where their people had been killed or wounded. [1]

In 1988, protesting the lack of an Indian memorial, American Indian Movement members cemented a plaque near the cavalry’s mass grave. The 1991 law authorized one, and it was dedicated on June 25, 2003, under the theme “Peace Through Unity,” identified by Cheyenne elder Austin Two Moons and Oglala Lakota elder Enos Poor Bear Sr. The Crow’s rights to the battlefield land passed to the United States in 1930. [1] [2]

sources.title: “Peace Through Unity”: Indian Memorial Dedication program, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument (NPS, June 25, 2003)
Foundation Document, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument (2015), appendix A

women.html:
The park’s 2015 foundation document credits Elizabeth Bacon Custer’s efforts to enshrine her husband’s memory, along with the battle’s famous personalities, with profoundly shaping how film, theatre, art and literature portrayed it; in 1939 Congress authorized a museum and accepted her collection. [1]

In 1925 Nellie Beaverheart, daughter of the Cheyenne Lame White Man, who was killed in the battle, wrote to the War Department asking for a marker where her father died and was buried. The Army never responded. The Park Service placed a wooden marker for him on Battle Ridge in 1956 and replaced it with red granite on June 25, 1999. [1]
