ROCR.summary:
Rock Creek Park follows a 9.6-mile stretch of Rock Creek from the Maryland line to the National Zoo, a forested valley of deciduous woods, meadows, wetlands and floodplains inside the capital where 180 species of birds have been recorded. Congress established it on September 27, 1890, as a public park or “pleasure ground” whose timber, animals and curiosities were to be kept as nearly as possible in their natural condition; the 2015 foundation document calls it one of the first federal park units and, among them, unique for lying beside a city. Today the park administers 2,749 acres in 99 areas, among them the Rock Creek and Potomac Parkway, the Old Stone House, Meridian Hill Park and nine of the Civil War Defenses of Washington, including Fort Stevens. [1] [2]

Peirce Mill, rebuilt in 1820 by Isaac Peirce and his stonemason son Abner with granite quarried nearby, was the last of eight mills in the valley; its main shaft broke in 1897, ending the milling there. Two years after the park was created the government condemned the mill property, and in 1934 Interior Secretary Harold Ickes proposed restoring it as part of the Depression-era improvements to the park. [2]

black.html: Meridian Hill Park, an 11.88-acre park managed by Rock Creek Park and colloquially called Malcolm X Park, sits on land with a long Black history. Elise Elder’s 2019 Park Service study reports that during the Civil War the Union Army’s Camp Cameron there offered food, shelter and work to freedmen and people escaping slavery, and that a Black community grew up afterward along today’s 15th Street. When the government acquired the land for the park, most of those homes were condemned, and by 1912 all of the residents had been forced to move; Black laborers were then hired to build the park. In the 1960s Black activist groups held rallies there, and after Malcolm X was assassinated in 1965 Black Washingtonians began a drum circle in his memory that the study, in 2019, called a weekend fixture ever since. [4]

sources.title: Elise Elder, Meridian Hill Park — African American Experiences Since the Civil War: A Special Resource Study (NPS National Capital Region with the Organization of American Historians, September 2019), Executive Summary, pp. 1–4

indigenous.html: William Bushong’s 1990 historic resource study says human occupation of what is now the District probably dates back 10,000 to 20,000 years; fluted spear points found in Anacostia and northwest Washington have been dated to between 9,000 and 9,500 B.C. Inside the park, the Piney Branch quartzite quarry was, archeologists interpret, a work site for extracting stone for tools and weapons between about 3,000 and 1,100 B.C.; the foundation document notes that it supplied important evidence in the debate over the history of human presence in the Americas. Park Service archeologists found two more sites along Rock Creek in 1985, hunting base camps where people processed meat and nuts, worked hides and made stone tools. Nearby, on the Anacostia’s east bank, lived the Nacostins (anglicized as Anacostians); when the English trader Henry Fleet sought a Potomac fur monopoly in the early 1630s, Bushong writes, they were already the middlemen in the beaver trade with interior tribes. [3] [1]

sources.title: William Bushong, Historic Resource Study: Rock Creek Park (NPS, August 1990), ch. 1, pp. 7–12
Foundation Document, Rock Creek Park (NPS, 2015), Brief Description

labor_ccc.html: Bushong calls the 1930s an important transitional decade for the park. Between 1934 and 1938, Public Works Administration grants paid for new bridges and buildings, the restoration of Peirce Mill, the completion of Piney Branch Parkway and the paving of park roads; in May 1934 an average of 136 laborers and 3 stonemasons a day were building the parkway and its retaining walls. Civilian Conservation Corps crews riprapped the creek, planted trees, built two miles of bridle trails and demolished the old Brightwood Reservoir. In September 1938 a CCC camp, NP-14, opened just north of Fort DeRussy with 154 enrollees; it closed when the program ended in 1942. [3]

sources.title: Bushong, Historic Resource Study: Rock Creek Park (NPS, 1990), New Deal chapter, pp. 133–144

slavery.html: The Peirce family, who built Peirce Mill, held people in slavery. Bushong’s historic resource study, which spells the name Pierce, reads Isaac Pierce’s wealth in the census: the 1820 count, Bushong suggests, shows two enslaved families who worked as house servants, mill workers and field hands, and by 1840, a year before his death, he enslaved fourteen people, many of them children. His son Abner, who inherited the farm in 1842, also held enslaved people; the 1850 census Bushong cites lists nine children among them. Abner’s nephew Pierce Shoemaker, the next owner, held twenty people in slavery before Congress abolished slavery in the District of Columbia on April 16, 1862. [3]

sources.title: Bushong, Historic Resource Study: Rock Creek Park (NPS, 1990), pp. 28–29

SAAN.name: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
SAAN.summary: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park in San Antonio, Texas, preserves four of the five Spanish colonial missions established along the San Antonio River in the 18th century: Mission Concepción, Mission San José, Mission San Juan, and Mission Espada. Together with the Alamo (Mission San Antonio de Valero), these missions represent the largest concentration of Spanish colonial missions in North America. Founded between 1718 and 1731 by Franciscan friars, the missions served as centers for converting and acculturating Native American peoples into Spanish colonial society. The park was established in 1978 and the missions were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 — the first World Heritage Site in Texas — recognized for their outstanding example of the interchange of Spanish and Coahuiltecan cultures.

SAJH.name: San Juan Island National Historical Park
SAJH.summary: San Juan Island National Historical Park in Washington State preserves the sites of the 1859 Pig War confrontation between the United States and Great Britain over possession of the San Juan Islands. The dispute began when an American settler shot a British-owned pig and escalated into a military standoff with both nations deploying forces on the island. The conflict was resolved through 12 years of joint military occupation and ultimately settled by international arbitration in 1872, when Kaiser Wilhelm I of Germany ruled in favor of the United States. The park preserves both the American Camp and English Camp — the respective military installations — and the island's prairie, forest, and shoreline ecosystems. The park was established in 1966.

SAJU.summary:
San Juan National Historic Site protects the stone defenses of San Juan Bay: Castillo San Felipe del Morro on the cliffs above the harbor entrance, Castillo San Cristóbal to the east, El Cañuelo across the bay on Isla de Cabras, and most of what remains of the wall around Old San Juan — in the foundation document’s words, the oldest and largest Spanish fortification system in the United States. [1] Trade winds and ocean currents carried sailing ships here from Europe, and Puerto Rico was the first major island with water, shelter and supplies on that route. Over ten generations and 250 years Spain built a system of defense in depth to guard its access to the wealth of the Americas: El Morro grew from a promontory with cannon into a six-level fortress, and Castillo San Cristóbal, built over 150 years against attack by land, is called by the park brochure the biggest European fortification in the Americas. [1]

The brochure’s timeline records English attacks on San Juan in 1595 and 1598, a Dutch attack in 1625 and a British attack in 1797. After the Spanish-American War, the 1898 Treaty of Paris transferred the forts and 210.86 acres to the U.S. military, which named the post Fort Brooke in 1943. In 1949 the Secretary of the Interior designated part of it a national historic site — on February 24, according to the foundation document; NPSHistory’s establishment list gives February 14. In 1983 UNESCO named it, with La Fortaleza, a World Heritage Site. [1] [1]

The park’s 75 acres are the largest open green space in Old San Juan. Its masons, trained in traditional techniques, preserve the stone fortifications, and the foundation document expects rising seas and stronger storm surges to contribute to the ongoing weathering of its centuries-old structures in a coastal environment. [1]

indigenous.html: Before European colonization the island was home to the Taíno, who called it Boriquén; Columbus and Juan Ponce de León stopped in 1493 and Columbus named it San Juan Bautista, the 2021 National Register documentation records. [1] Under Ponce de León, who began the colony in 1508, Spain displaced the Taíno, and the park brochure’s timeline marks a Taíno revolt in 1511. [1] The first stone fort, La Fortaleza (1533–1539), faced chiefly landward; the Register documentation reads that orientation as protection against attacks from the Taíno and from Carib people raiding from the Lesser Antilles. It also names Native Taíno among the peoples — with African, Spanish, Italian, Irish, English and others — who contributed to the design and construction of the fortifications themselves. [1]

sources.title: Bulger & Schiappacasse, National Register of Historic Places Registration Form: San Juan National Historic Site (Update), June 22, 2021
NPSHistory.com: San Juan National Historic Site archive page — overview (from the 2011 NPS brochure), timeline and establishment block

latino.html: The 2021 National Register documentation finds the forts significant as a symbol of Puerto Rican identity. Under U.S. rule, it explains, Spanish architecture took on new meaning: elites disenfranchised by American colonial policy turned to the island’s Hispanic legacy, and the independence movement increasingly looked to the Spanish past. In 1912, when rat-infested walls were blamed for an outbreak of bubonic plague and the Army still declined to repair them, Governor George R. Colton urged that walls not needed for defense pass to the “People of Puerto Rico.” In 1926–27 engineer Martín Paniagua and the newspaper El Mundo attacked Army Corps of Engineers repairs in Portland cement, and the contractors agreed to reface the concrete with coral blocks. [1] The foundation document calls the site a potent symbol of cultural heritage linking Puerto Rico’s history to Hispanic culture and providing a common identity with other Latin American countries. [1]

SAND.summary:
Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site lies on the grassland plains of southeastern Colorado, about 170 miles southeast of Denver. In winter, Big Sandy Creek offered firewood, shelter and water; people of many tribes paused here on the Smoky Hill Lodgepole Trail. At dawn on November 29, 1864, approximately 675 soldiers of the 1st and 3rd Regiments, Colorado Volunteer Cavalry, under Col. John M. Chivington attacked a village of Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho people who believed they were safe on their 1861 treaty lands; a U.S. flag and a white flag flew at Peace Chief Black Kettle’s lodge. Over seven hours the soldiers killed more than 230 people. Women, children and elders fled up the dry creek channel with soldiers following, shooting, and dug pits and trenches along the streambed. Afterward the troops mutilated the dead and took body parts as trophies. [1] [2]

Capt. Silas Soule and Lt. Joseph Cramer ordered their companies to stand down, and their written accounts shocked national and military leaders. An Army judge condemned the “cowardly cold-blooded slaughter,” yet Chivington was never formally charged. In the 1865 Little Arkansas Treaty the United States took responsibility for the massacre and promised reparations to survivors; the NPS brochure says they have never been fulfilled. The 2017 foundation document finds that by eliminating most Cheyenne advocates for peace, the massacre hardened resistance and escalated warfare on the plains. [1] [2]

Site-location research sought to reconcile Cheyenne and Arapaho history and cultural authority, historic documentation and archeology, and gathered oral histories from massacre descendants. Congress authorized the site on November 7, 2000; it was established effective April 27, 2007. Of its 3,025 acres, 1,465 are held in trust for the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes. Its stated purpose includes helping to minimize the chances of similar incidents in the future. [1] [2]

climate.html:
The cottonwoods along Big Sandy Creek are part of the massacre landscape, and individual trees, living and dead, carry cultural and spiritual significance for their association with the encampments and the massacre. A 2006 tree-ring study of some 110 trees dated none definitively to 1864, though the evidence suggests several were alive then as seedlings or saplings; most of the main gallery forest took root in 1949–1960, and very few trees have established since 1965. [1]

A 2013 Park Service climate brief found mean annual temperature at nearby Eads rising 0.18 °F per decade from 1895 to 2011, fastest in winter and spring, and projected a further 4–5 °F by mid-century; summer precipitation may decrease 10 to 15 percent. [1]

sources.title: Jeff Lukas and Connie Woodhouse, Riparian Forest Age Structure and Past Hydroclimatic Variability, Sand Creek Massacre NHS, Final Report (INSTAAR for NPS, October 2006)
Nicholas Fisichelli, Climate Change Trends for Planning at Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site (NPS Climate Change Response Program, April 18, 2013)

indigenous.html:
For the Cheyenne and Arapaho, the NPS brochure says, even speaking of the massacre is sacred, and the site is forever hallowed because the spirits and blood of the victims are intermingled with the earth. The site’s 2024 administrative history explains that the tribes do not consider the interment of returned ancestors here a reburial but the first burial, since the dead were not buried after the massacre. Interments in the site’s repatriation area began on June 8, 2008, with ancestors returned by the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, History Colorado and the University of Nebraska; tribal members keep an all-night vigil before each burial. [1] [2]

In November 1999 Laforce “Lee” Lone Bear, a Northern Cheyenne descendant of survivors, organized a 173-mile run from the massacre site to the Colorado State Capitol. The Northern Cheyenne still coordinate the Spiritual Healing Run with the Northern Arapaho and the Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho. [1]

SARI.summary:
On the north coast of St. Croix, an upland watershed drains into Salt River Bay, a bay fringed with some of the largest mangrove forests left in the Virgin Islands and with coral reefs, opening onto a submarine canyon as deep as 350 feet, carved by an ancestral river 30,000 years ago when the sea stood 300 feet lower. Beyond it the seafloor falls away into the Virgin Islands Trough. The bay’s waters were designated a National Natural Landmark in 1980 and are home to 27 species listed as rare, threatened or endangered. [1]

Congress created the 1,015-acre park on February 24, 1992, to be managed jointly by the National Park Service and the Government of the Virgin Islands. Its foundation document calls it a confirmed site where members of Columbus’s second voyage landed on what is now U.S. territory in 1493, and the scene of the earliest recorded armed resistance by Amerindians to European colonization. Fort Salé, first built in 1641 to guard the inlet, is in its words one of the earliest and few surviving European earthen fortifications in the New World. [n] [1]

The park’s own account is that every major period of human habitation in the Virgin Islands is represented here, from several South American Indian cultures, among them the Taíno and Island Caribs, through the 1493 encounter, European colonization and enslaved West Africans and their descendants, a story revealed by more than a dozen major archeological investigations since 1880 and by historical research. [1]

climate.html: Salt River ran year-round when Columbus anchored here; it now flows only after heavy or sustained rain, which the brochure attributes to centuries of land use and regional climatic change. The bay’s mangroves are still recovering from Hurricane Hugo in 1989, and the 2021 landscape inventory lists sea-level rise, coastal erosion and hurricanes among the natural stressors on them; Hurricane Maria damaged park buildings in 2017. The 2015 foundation document projects sea level at the park rising 0.33 to 1.57 feet by 2050 and 0.59 to 4.92 feet by 2100, which, with stronger storms, could threaten the park’s archeological and historic sites. [n] [n] [1]

indigenous.html:
South American hunter-gatherers reached the Virgin Islands about 4,500 years ago, the 2006 brochure says; by 2,000 years ago the first of three pottery-making peoples lived at Salt River Bay, and after 700 the Taíno gradually absorbed the Igneri. Their ball court, unearthed in 1923, is the only one known in the Lesser Antilles, the brochure says. The Taíno called the island Ay; the Kalinago (the brochure’s Caribs) called it Cibuqueira. [n] [1]

On November 14, 1493, over twenty armed men from Columbus’s fleet visited a Kalinago village and seized enslaved Taíno women and children they claimed to have liberated, then fought villagers in a canoe; each side lost a man, and Columbus named the place Cape of the Arrows. The brochure reports a 1512 Spanish royal decree ordering the extermination of St. Croix’s Caribs, and disease helping depopulate the island by 1590; the park’s website now calls this the Spanish capture and removal of Amerindian peoples. [n] [n] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Salt River Bay NHP & Ecological Preserve archive page — overview (from the 2006 NPS brochure) and establishment block
NPS, Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve (2021)

slavery.html:
Denmark ruled St. Croix from 1733 to 1917 and made it a major sugar-producing island; the Danish West Indies Company built sugar and cotton plantations and a trade that included enslaved people transported from West Africa. Colonists cleared the dense forest around the bay for cotton, tobacco and sugar, and the Danish period left at least six sugar plantations in the Salt River Bay area. A brick and coral-block well tower, built about 1780–1800 for Estate Morningstar, used wind to draw water to irrigate the estate’s crop lands. In 1788 the Danes built a customs post to stop sugar, molasses and rum being smuggled out through the bay. [n] [1]

Across St. Croix, enslaved people made up more than 90 percent of the population before 1800, and in 1812, the peak year, 175 sugar plantations held 26,000 enslaved people, according to a 2012 Park Service plan for nearby Buck Island; emancipation came in 1848. [1]

SCBL.summary:
Scotts Bluff towers 800 feet over the North Platte River valley floor in the Nebraska Panhandle, a sandstone and siltstone landmark that wind and water are dismantling grain by grain. The monument’s 3,003 acres of prairie, bluffs and badlands protect Scotts Bluff, South Bluff, Mitchell Pass and remnants of the Oregon-California Trail. The valley has been a prairie pathway for at least 10,000 years, leading American Indians to places where bison came to drink, and the bluff’s size and badlands gave it the name Me-a-pa-te, “hill that is hard to go around.” [1] [2]

It takes its present name from Hiram Scott, a fur trader who died on an 1828 journey east from the Rockies; how he died remains a mystery. In 1850 anonymous laborers filled gullies and built ramps through Mitchell Pass, and from 1851 it was the main route, cutting about eight miles. In 1852, the peak year, up to 50,000 people passed. Travelers called the bluff “a Nebraska Gibraltar.” The Pony Express and the transcontinental telegraph later used the same gap; the railroad’s completion in 1869 greatly reduced emigrant travel. [1] [2]

Local leaders petitioned for protection, and President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed the monument on December 12, 1919 — according to the 2015 foundation document, the first time the Antiquities Act was used to preserve a landscape based on the westward expansion movement. That document warns that the prairie is changing rapidly: cheatgrass occupies most of the monument, and the region is projected to warm 4 to 5 °F by 2050, with more intense storms and more heat waves. [1] [2]

indigenous.html:
In the early 1990s archeologist Caven P. Clark identified another 51 sites here, all but two prehistoric, with finds ranging from perhaps 8,000 years before present to 1450; he concluded its springs were “of undoubted significance to the prehistoric settlement system.” From perhaps the 1500s to the early 1800s the region was a favorite bison hunting ground of the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho. [1] [2]

Plains peoples traded game, moccasins and bison robes to emigrants for flour, cloth and tobacco, and acted as paid guides. But emigrant livestock, Indian herds and an 1848–1862 drought depleted the corridor’s grasses; that decline and increased hunting drove bison from between the Platte and Arkansas rivers, and the tribes, Greenwald writes, drawing on Elliott West, became more dependent on the United States for food. After the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty, the foundation document says, the Pawnee, Cheyenne and Sioux were forcibly removed to reservations. The foundation document notes that the 10 affiliated tribes are all off site. [1] [2]

sources.title: Greenwald, “A Nebraska Gibraltar” HRS (2012), ch. 2 American Indian Habitation and Use; ch. 5 Human and Environmental Change in the Platte River Corridor
Foundation Document, Scotts Bluff National Monument (2015), Brief Description and appendix D

labor_ccc.html: The visitor center, Summit Road and administrative buildings were primarily built in the 1930s by the Works Progress Administration and the Civilian Conservation Corps, the foundation document says. [1] In 1935, CCC Company 762 — 200 men whose orders to the Ozarks were changed at the last minute — set up Camp NM-1 in the badlands between the bluff and the river, raising barracks of adobe bricks they made on site. Enrollees built the first unit of the Oregon Trail Museum, worked on the Summit Road, which opened September 19, 1937, laid a water system and fences, and in 1936 cleaned and restored Scotts Spring, by then a muddy cattle water hole. An NPS landscape architect explained in 1936 that Chief Architect Vint recommended adobe not because it was appropriate for the area but because it was the only way to build comparatively long-lasting headquarters under Emergency Conservation Work limits. The CCC left in 1938. [1]

sources.title: Greenwald, “A Nebraska Gibraltar” HRS (2012), ch. 7, New Deal Construction, 1933–1939

SEMO.summary:
The Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail follows the 54-mile route of the 1965 voting rights marches: from Brown Chapel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Selma, over the Edmund Pettus Bridge and east along U.S. Highway 80 through Dallas and Lowndes counties to the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery. Along the highway, the 2015 foundation document notes, row-crop fields, pastures and woodlots remain largely intact, reflecting the agrarian land use of 1965. Congress established the trail by a law signed on November 12, 1996. [1]

Selma became the focus because of what had been done to its voters. African Americans made up about half of Dallas County’s voting-age population, but since 1901 the county and state had kept them from the polls with literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation; in 1961 only 156 of the county’s 15,000 voting-age African Americans were registered. The 2008 park brochure calls the final march the climactic event of the modern civil rights movement, and the foundation document names the marches an important catalyst for the Voting Rights Act, signed August 6, 1965. [1] [1]

The trail also marks what the right cost. The foundation document records that many suffered from violent opposition and some were murdered, and that after the act passed many Lowndes County tenant farmers were evicted for exercising their right to vote. It defines the trail’s purpose as inspiring all citizens to be vigilant in protecting their constitutional rights. [1]

black.html:
In January 1965 the Southern Christian Leadership Conference joined the Selma campaign. Sheriff Jim Clark directed would-be registrants to an alley, then let no one register; by February 5 more than 3,000 had been arrested. On February 18 in Marion a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson as he tried to defend his grandfather; a call to carry his body to Montgomery became the march. [1] [1]

On March 7 about 600 marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams were tear-gassed and beaten by state troopers and the sheriff’s posse beyond the Edmund Pettus Bridge, opened in 1940 and named, the Historic American Engineering Record notes, for a Confederate general and Alabama senator who also served as a grand dragon in the Alabama Ku Klux Klan. The final march, under federal protection, left Selma on March 21 and reached the Capitol on March 25, some 25,000 strong by the brochure’s count. [1] [1] [1]

women.html: On January 19, 1965, when Amelia Boynton of the Dallas County Voters League was slow to obey Sheriff Clark’s order to move, he grabbed her by the collar and shoved her toward a patrol car; with the photograph of her treatment in major newspapers, the 2008 park brochure says, the media turned its eye on Selma. On the night the march ended, Viola Liuzzo, who had come from Detroit to help, was shot and killed by Klansmen after driving marchers back to Selma; her memorial overlooks the route. The park’s 2015 foundation document warned that Boynton’s Selma home was in disrepair and under threat of demolition. [1] [1]

SITK.summary:
Tlingit people had thrived for countless generations on the island they called Shee, in a land of forest, rivers and sea where a warm current keeps Sitka’s harbor free of ice all year. Salmon came in staggering numbers on the spawning runs; from cedar and other conifers of the rain forest they built multi-family plank houses and carved canoes up to 60 feet long. At the mouth of the Indian River, where the park now lies, the river, the ocean and the coastal rain forest meet in a habitat rich enough that pink salmon runs sometimes pack the river with more than 1.3 million fish. [1]

Russian fur traders, called Anooshi by the Tlingit, pushed into Southeast Alaska under Alexander Baranov of the Russian-American Company. In 1802 Tlingits, especially the Kiks.ádi clan of Shee At’iká, attacked his new outpost north of Sitka and killed most of its Russian and Aleut inhabitants. In 1804 Baranov returned with Russians, Aleuts and the warship Neva; the Kiks.ádi, led by their war chief K’alyaan, held a fort at the mouth of the Indian River, repulsed a landing and wounded Baranov, then withdrew after a siege when their gunpowder ran out. Russia made Sitka the company’s headquarters, and in 1867 sold Alaska to the United States. [1]

In 1890 the federal government reserved the Indian River site as a public park; it became Sitka National Monument in 1910, and in 1972 Public Law 92-510 enlarged it, added the Russian Bishop’s House and made it Sitka National Historical Park. The 2012 foundation document calls it the site of a major armed resistance of Alaska Native people to Russian colonization. [1] [1]

climate.html: A 2017 Park Service assessment found that the land at Sitka is rising through tectonic uplift, so relative sea level near the park is falling, about 2.29 millimeters a year by NOAA’s trend, and every park asset lies outside the projected 2050 sea-level rise zone. The hazard it singles out is tsunami: the park lies just east of the Fairweather fault system, which has tremendous potential to generate tsunamis. Across the five coastal hazards it scored, eight totem poles are the only structures rated highly vulnerable, and all four highly vulnerable transportation assets are trails, including the Totem Walk. In a separate tsunami case study, 65 percent of the park’s assets, worth over $26 million, have high tsunami vulnerability. [1]

sources.title: Peek et al., Sitka NHP Coastal Hazards & Sea-Level Rise Asset Vulnerability Assessment & Tsunami Vulnerability Case Study (NPS 314/154045, December 2017)

indigenous.html: Thornton’s 1998 study for the Park Service describes the Indian River as Kiks.ádi territory: the clan possessed it and kept seasonal subsistence camps on the lower river until the late 1800s. Its 1804 fort, Shís’ḵ’i Noow (best translated “Green Wood Fort”), stood on a new kind of fort site, designed to defend against large Russian ships and their weaponry; shallow tidelands kept keeled vessels off. From the Kiks.ádi perspective, Thornton writes, the battle was an unwarranted attack on their sovereignty; memorials for the dead began perhaps as early as 1806, and the withdrawal is now retraced as the Kiks.ádi Survival March. The 1910 proclamation listed the graves of Russians killed in the battle but not Tlingit ones. The Alaska Native Brotherhood, founded in Sitka in 1912, proposed the Southeast Alaska Indian Cultural Center, opened in the park in 1969. Thornton concludes that Tlingit social and symbolic ties to the park remain strong, while subsistence ties have been largely severed. [1]

sources.title: Thornton (with Hope), Traditional Tlingit Use of Sitka National Historical Park, final report to NPS (July 31, 1998)

women.html: According to Herb Hope, as Thornton reports, women gathered kelp to make the green palisade logs slippery. Oral history handed down to Herman Kitka credits a woman interpreter, apparently married to a Russian officer, with warning Katlian (the brochure’s K’alyaan) that the Castle Hill fort would not stand up to cannon fire — the reason, in that account, the Kiks.ádi built in the forest at Indian River. In the 20th century Ellen Hope Lang (later Hayes), a Kiks.ádi woman and former resident of The Cottages, the Presbyterian Model Cottage Settlement, was a member of the Alaska Native Brotherhood, the craft center board and the park staff, eventually as superintendent; Thornton credits her with helping bring the cultural center to life. [1]

sources.title: Thornton (with Hope), Traditional Tlingit Use of Sitka National Historical Park, final report to NPS (July 31, 1998)

SLBE.name: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore
SLBE.summary: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore on the northeastern coast of Lake Michigan in Michigan protects 35 miles of shoreline, massive perched sand dunes rising up to 450 feet above the lake, pristine inland lakes, dense beech-maple forests, and two offshore wilderness islands — North and South Manitou. The national lakeshore was established in 1970, and in 2011 viewers of ABC's "Good Morning America" voted its beaches the "Most Beautiful Place in America." The park's name derives from a Chippewa (Ojibwe) legend in which a mother bear and her two cubs swam across Lake Michigan to escape a forest fire; the mother bear waited on the bluff for her cubs, who drowned and became the Manitou Islands, while she became the Sleeping Bear Dune. The park's diverse ecosystems support endangered piping plovers and over 100 species of migratory birds.

STON.summary:
Stonewall National Monument is a 7.7-acre site in Greenwich Village, New York City: the 0.12-acre Christopher Park, donated by the city, together with the privately owned Stonewall Inn across the street and the surrounding streets and sidewalks. West of 6th Avenue the street grid is a relic of the 18th century, narrow streets meeting at odd angles; in June 1969 that labyrinth helped demonstrators who knew the neighborhood evade riot-control police who were not from the local precinct. [1]

At about 1:15 a.m. on June 28, 1969, undercover police raided the Stonewall Inn, by then one of the city’s most popular LGBTQ bars. Police told customers — many of them transgender women and drag performers, the foundation document says — that anyone who refused to show identification would have to go into a bathroom where police could verify their sex; the patrons refused. The crowd outside shouted “Gay Power!”, and as it grew angrier the officers retreated into the bar and locked themselves inside; 13 people were arrested. Protests continued nightly in Christopher Park and the nearby streets through July 3. [1]

President Barack Obama proclaimed the monument on June 24, 2016; the Stonewall Inn, Christopher Park and parts of the neighborhood had been a National Historic Landmark since 2000. The proclamation calls the uprising a watershed moment for LGBT civil rights and a transformative event in the nation’s civil rights movement, on par with Seneca Falls in 1848 and the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery march, and describes the nation’s march toward equality and respect for LGBT people as not yet finished. [1] [1]

lgbtq.html:
Through the 1960s, the park brochure says, almost everything about living openly as a lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender person was a violation of law, rule or policy (the foundation document says this of the years before 1960). In New York people were arrested for same-sex dancing or kissing or for wearing clothes of the perceived opposite gender; police raided bars for serving “homosexuals.” By the 1960s Christopher Park drew LGBTQ youth, many of whom had run away from or been kicked out of their homes. [1] [1] [1]

The park brochure names street kids among the first to fight, and Marsha P. Johnson, one of the most outspoken members of the city’s transgender community, among the first to fight back. With Sylvia Rivera she co-founded STAR, the Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries, in the early 1970s. Within a year, the 2016 proclamation records, the number of LGBT organizations in the country grew from around 50 to at least 1,500. [1] [1]

women.html: Barbara Gittings organized the New York chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis and in the 1960s organized some of the first protests against the federal ban on employing homosexuals; she helped lobby until the American Psychiatric Association declassified homosexuality as a mental illness in 1973. The New York Daughters of Bilitis joined the Mattachine Society and Philadelphia’s Janus Society to picket Independence Hall on July 4, 1965, and on four successive July 4ths, under a strict dress code meant to present homosexuals as “presentable and employable.” Inside the Stonewall Inn, the foundation document notes, only a very small number of lesbians were among the patrons; in later commemorations, it says, butch lesbians were among the more marginalized members of the community who claimed their place. [1] [1]

STRI.summary:
In the cedar woods, rocks and cotton fields outside Murfreesboro, Tennessee, armies totaling 81,000 men fought from December 31, 1862, through January 2, 1863, in one of the Civil War’s bloodiest encounters. Each side lost nearly one-third of its men: 13,249 Union and 10,266 Confederate casualties. On the last afternoon, 57 Union cannon massed above McFadden’s Ford killed or wounded more than 1,800 Confederates in less than an hour, and the Confederate army limped away. The victory, the park brochure says, together with the Emancipation Proclamation that took effect on January 1, shifted the war’s aims from restoring the Union to remaking the nation. [1]

Union soldiers and hundreds of formerly enslaved men then built Fortress Rosecrans, a 200-acre fort and supply depot ringed by three miles of earthworks — one of the largest Civil War earthen fortifications, in the 2014 foundation document’s words — and Murfreesboro stayed under Union occupation until 1877. Hazen’s brigade raised its monument on the field in 1863, one of the oldest intact Civil War monuments, the foundation document says, and more than 6,100 Union soldiers, 2,500 of them unknown, lie in the national cemetery. [1] [1]

Congress created Stones River National Military Park on March 3, 1927; it became Stones River National Battlefield on April 22, 1960. It preserves a small part of the original battlefield, in six separate parcels, along with cedar glades whose plant community is found only in Rutherford County, including the endangered Pyne’s ground plum. Its 2014 foundation document also names as part of the park’s significance the freedmen’s settlement called Cemetery, built on the battlefield after the war; the park brochure says the park’s creation in 1927 uprooted many of its residents. [1] [1]

black.html:
In 1865 soldiers of the 111th U.S. Colored Infantry began reburying the Union dead in the new national cemetery; afterward veterans such as William Holland and other freed people built homes, a school, churches and a store around it, a community named Cemetery. In the section called the Cedars, Rebecca Conard’s 2016 history finds, blacksmith Sam Grisham bought 40 acres in 1872 and in 1875 Holland bought three acres beside the Hazen monument. By 1910 about 80 people lived there in 17 households. Cemetery School, built on donated land in 1874, taught children through eighth grade until 1962. [1] [1] [1]

The park’s web page says that after Congress approved the military park in 1927, African Americans, who owned more than half the land, were forced to sell; Conard dates the forced sales in the Cedars to 1929. The displacement and erasure of their history created resentment and distrust, the page says; partnerships with the Black community are slowly rebuilding trust. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Stones River National Battlefield archive page — overview (NPS brochure text) and establishment block
Conard, Cemetery Community: A Brief History (Middle Tennessee State University, February 2016)
NPS, The Cemetery Community — Stones River National Battlefield (nps.gov, last updated July 31, 2024)

slavery.html:
In 1860 Rutherford County had 27,918 people, nearly half of them enslaved, the park’s 2004 historic resource study reports. The Nashville & Chattanooga Railroad, which ran through the battlefield, was permitted by law to own slaves, and enslaved workers together with Irish immigrant labor built its line through the county. Elmwood, the Hord house on the Nashville Pike that Union forces used as a hospital, was built in 1842 of bricks made by people Thomas Hord enslaved; after the battle Union officers impressed Hord’s slaves to help build Fortress Rosecrans. [1]

Around Murfreesboro, family farms worked by white and enslaved Black people raised hogs, horses, corn, wheat and cotton. Once Union troops held Murfreesboro, enslaved people flocked to their camps to seize their freedom, leaving hundreds of farms untended, and more than 20,000 formerly enslaved men from Tennessee went on to fight in the U.S. Colored Troops. [1]

sources.title: Styles, Stones River National Battlefield Historic Resource Study (NPS Southeast Region, February 2004)
NPSHistory.com: Stones River National Battlefield archive page — overview (NPS brochure text) and establishment block

women.html: In Murfreesboro, women formed a soldiers’ relief society to support the hospital at Union University and carried food, clothing and medicine to the front lines. [1] During the battle Elmwood, the home of Thomas and Mildred Amelia Gilmer Hord, was taken so suddenly for a hospital that the family could not move the carpets or furniture; Amelia Hord helped care for the wounded despite being far along in pregnancy. In 1911 the family was awarded part of its $60,000 claim for property seized or destroyed by Union forces. [1]

SUCR.summary:
Sunset Crater is the youngest of some 600 volcanoes in northern Arizona’s San Francisco Volcanic Field, a 1,000-foot cinder cone that the Foundation Document calls the Colorado Plateau’s most recent eruption and the only series of eruptions in the Southwest indisputably witnessed by local peoples. The monument protects 3,040 acres of lava flows and cinder fields where small islands of pine and aspen, desert shrubs and wildflowers grow and life is slowly returning. [1] The brochure dates the eruption to sometime between 1040 and 1100, and a 2018 National Register nomination to the late 1080s. In the brochure’s account, molten rock sprayed from a crack in the ground and fell as bombs and cinders, ash dusted 800 square miles of northern Arizona, and the Kana-a and Bonito lava flows destroyed all living things in their path. The red and yellow cinders on the rim, glowing like a sunset, gave the volcano its name. [1] [1]

In 1928 filmmakers who wanted to stage a landslide on the cone prompted activists to push for its protection, and President Herbert Hoover proclaimed Sunset Crater National Monument on May 26, 1930; it took its present name in 1990. After thousands of climbers scarred it, the cone was closed to climbing. [1] From 1964 to 1972 the U.S. Geological Survey used the Bonito Lava Flow and nearby Cinder Lake, where it built replicas of lunar crater fields, to test equipment and train Apollo astronauts; Apollo 17’s crew practiced here in November 1972. [1]

indigenous.html:
The eruption, the brochure says, forced the farmers living just northeast of today’s Flagstaff off land they had cultivated for 400 years; a few generations later families returned to farm at nearby Wupatki and Walnut Canyon, and the memory of the eruption lived on in the stories of Indigenous Southwest peoples. [1] The 2015 Foundation Document lists 13 traditionally associated tribes and says the volcano remains significant to contemporary American Indian tribes. [1]

Drawing partly on 80 interviews with Pai, Southern Paiute, Zuni and Western Apache representatives from a 2004 NPS study, researchers Richard Stoffle and Kathleen Van Vlack wrote in 2022 that Native Americans have come to perceive volcanoes as earth navels, places where the earth is reborn. The authors argue that the new volcano drew pilgrims and led to the ceremonial communities around Wupatki. Participants in their NPS studies agreed that the Park Service need not accept Native beliefs as true but should tell both stories side by side. [1]

TAPR.name: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
TAPR.summary: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in the Flint Hills of east-central Kansas protects a remnant of the tallgrass prairie ecosystem that once covered 170 million acres of North America — from Indiana to Kansas and from Canada to Texas. Less than 4 percent of the original tallgrass prairie remains today, making it one of the most endangered ecosystems on the continent, and the Flint Hills contain the largest remaining expanse. The preserve was established in 1996 through a public-private partnership between the National Park Service and The Nature Conservancy. The nearly 11,000-acre site includes the historic Spring Hill/Z Bar Ranch with an 1881 limestone ranch house, a massive stone barn, and a one-room schoolhouse. A bison herd was reintroduced to the preserve in 2009.

THIS.summary:
Theodore Roosevelt Island is a wooded island in the Potomac River that serves as the nation’s memorial to its 26th president; the Park Service’s 2015 foundation document calls its Memorial Plaza the only monument to Roosevelt in Washington, D.C. Trails cross upland forest, swamp and tidal marsh, and the same document says the island holds the largest naturally occurring tidal wetland in the District and plants and animals that are rare in the region. It measures 70 acres by the foundation document’s count; the 2004 park brochure gives 88.5 acres for the island together with adjacent Little Island. [1] [2]

The Roosevelt Memorial Association bought the island in October 1931, according to the 2016 Cultural Landscapes Inventory (the brochure dates the purchase to 1932), and gave it to the federal government; Congress established the memorial on May 21, 1932. Landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr., and Henry Vincent Hubbard designed it as a living memorial, a native woodland meant to mature over decades and centuries into a “climax” forest that would honor Roosevelt’s conservation record. Architect Eric Gugler designed the plaza and sculptor Paul Manship its bronze statue of Roosevelt, set among four granite tablets carrying Roosevelt’s words on citizenship; it was dedicated in October 1967. [3] [1] [2]

The forest covers an older history. The island has been called My Lord’s Island, Barbadoes, Analostan and Mason’s Island; it was a Native American fishing place, a plantation, a Union Army camp and a camp for people freed from slavery before it was a memorial. The foundation document lists the remnants of American Indian habitation, farmsteads and Civil War encampments as part of its archeological record. [3] [1]

black.html:
Early in the Civil War an employment depot for people who had escaped slavery — “contraband,” in the term of the time — was set up on the island. In the summer of 1863 it quartered and trained the 1st United States Colored Troops, an infantry regiment of free Black men and men who had escaped slavery, the District of Columbia’s Black regular Army regiment, which went on to fight mainly in Virginia and the Carolinas. [3] [1]

From May 1864 the island became a refugee camp for recently freed people and other Black people arriving in the area. They were housed in the empty barracks and told to make do with limited supplies; the inventory records that many died there from lack of basic supplies, disease and overcrowding. An 1864 inspection counted seven barracks and noted plans for a schoolroom and meeting house. The camp was disbanded in June 1865. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Theodore Roosevelt Island (NPS, 2016) — Civil War history, statement of significance and chronology
Foundation Document Overview, Theodore Roosevelt Island National Memorial (NPS, 2015)

indigenous.html: People were on the island long before any European claim. The National Register nomination quoted in the 2016 landscape inventory says pottery sherds, fire-cracked rock, projectile points and stone flakes found there suggest intensive, long-term prehistoric use, and that through the 18th century the Potomac valley was a meeting place where members of the Five Nation Iroquois traded with Algonquian-speaking peoples whose fishing and farming villages lined the river. The English captain Henry Fleet described Necostin Indians in the area in the 1620s and 1630s, and the nomination adds that the name Analostan likely derives from the Necostin (Anacostian). The park brochure says the island served as a seasonal fishing village. The record is thin: the nomination calls the past survey work small and substandard, and judges the published account of a 1967 excavation inadequate. [3] [2]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Theodore Roosevelt Island (NPS, 2016) — summary, chronology, physical history and archeology sections
NPSHistory.com: Theodore Roosevelt Island archive page overview (2004 NPS brochure)

labor_ccc.html: The park brochure credits Olmsted and the Civilian Conservation Corps with creating the island’s mature woodland. [2] From 1934 to 1937, Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr., directed young CCC men in clearing most of the non-native vegetation, including most of what remained of John Mason’s plantings, and in planting about 20,000 native hardwood trees and shrubs. In 1936 a Historic American Buildings Survey team recorded the remains of Mason’s mansion before they were removed; CCC crews did the digging. The National Register nomination, quoted in the inventory, notes that the exploration was assigned to a Park Service architect with no archeological training, who was given 12 weeks. The Olmsted firm’s general plan for the island was completed in 1945. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Theodore Roosevelt Island (NPS, 2016) — physical history and archeology sections
NPSHistory.com: Theodore Roosevelt Island archive page overview (2004 NPS brochure)

slavery.html: From about 1792 until a bank foreclosed on him in 1833, John Mason, son of George Mason of Gunston Hall, ran the island as a small plantation estate, with a neoclassical mansion, fields, livestock and terraced gardens. The National Register nomination says Mason probably relied on slave labor to build, farm and maintain the estate; its statement of significance says the estate was almost certainly run by slave labor. Slave quarters and workshops stood south of the house, some along the walled eastern shore, and cotton and maize were planted to the north. Newspapers in 1902 and 1907 described the overgrown ruins, among them buildings identified as slave quarters. The nomination counts slave sites from the Mason era among the island’s likely archeological resources. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Theodore Roosevelt Island (NPS, 2016), quoting the National Register nomination and the 2008 HALS report

THRO.name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park
THRO.summary: Theodore Roosevelt National Park in the badlands of western North Dakota memorializes the 26th president and the landscape that profoundly influenced his conservation philosophy. Roosevelt first came to the Dakota Territory in 1883 to hunt bison and subsequently established two cattle ranches — the Maltese Cross and Elkhorn — in the Little Missouri River badlands. His experiences with the harsh beauty of the landscape and his witness to the decimation of wildlife and open range shaped his lifelong commitment to conservation. As president from 1901 to 1909, Roosevelt established the United States Forest Service, created 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 bird reserves, and 150 national forests, protecting roughly 230 million acres. The park was designated a national memorial park in 1947 and redesignated a national park in 1978.

TIMU.summary:
Where the St. Johns and Nassau rivers meet the Atlantic, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve protects one of the largest remaining salt marsh estuaries on the Southeast coast: 46,000 acres of salt marsh, coastal dunes, hardwood hammocks and fresh, brackish and salt water inside the city limits of Jacksonville, with dolphins, migratory birds, manatees, wood storks and loggerhead sea turtles. More than 200 archeological sites, among them Archaic shell rings, record over 6,000 years of human habitation. Congress created the preserve in 1988 around Fort Caroline National Memorial, authorized in 1950; only 8,430 acres, 18 percent of the preserve, are federally owned. [1]

Fort Caroline recalls la Caroline, the colony of mostly Huguenot settlers that René de Laudonnière planted on the river’s south bank in 1564 — by the park brochure’s account the first French colony in what is now the United States. In September 1565 Spanish forces under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés captured it and massacred most of its defenders; the brochure calls the battles here the first time European nations fought for control of lands in what is now the United States. [1]

On Fort George Island, Kingsley Plantation keeps a 1798 plantation house and the ruins of the tabby cabins where enslaved people lived; the foundation document calls it the oldest surviving example of an antebellum Spanish Colonial plantation. The preserve also includes American Beach on Amelia Island, which the same document calls the largest and most popular beach resort established by and for African Americans in the Jim Crow era. [1]

climate.html: Most of the preserve is salt marsh. A 2024 U.S. Geological Survey fact sheet prepared with the Park Service estimates that about 81 percent of its non-water area is likely to be inundated by 2050 under an intermediate-low sea-level scenario, and about 88 percent by 2100 under an intermediate-high scenario, and it pictures Fort Caroline flooded after Hurricane Ian in September 2022. [1] The Park Service’s 2024 climate futures summary for Fort Caroline finds that the area has warmed at a rate of 6 °F per century since 1970, and that the amount of rain falling in the region’s heaviest storms has risen 37 percent since 1958. [1]

sources.title: USGS Fact Sheet 2024–3008, Projected Sea-Level Rise and High Tide Flooding at Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve, Florida (June 2024)
NPS Climate Change Response Program, Fort Caroline National Memorial Climate Futures Summary (2024)

indigenous.html: The preserve is named for the Timucua. Their ancestors lived along the St. Johns estuary for thousands of years and left the shell mounds found throughout the preserve. The people who met the French in 1562 under Chief Saturiwa were one of several Timucua-speaking groups of north and central Florida and southeastern Georgia; they fished, gathered oysters and clams, hunted, planted maize, squash and beans, and traveled in dugout canoes. They shared food with the colonists and helped build their fort, and later helped French forces recapture it in 1568. Spain then imposed tribute, forced them into missions, and European disease devastated them: from a population once in the tens of thousands, the park brochure says, only 550 were recorded in 1698, and no known Native people today call themselves Timucua. [1] The 2012 foundation document states they were extinct as a people by 1752. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve / Fort Caroline archive page — overview (NPS brochure texts) and establishment block
Foundation Document, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve, Florida (NPS, 2012)

slavery.html: Kingsley Plantation’s cabins are the largest concentration of tabby slave quarters in the United States, the foundation document says. [1] Amani T. Marshall’s 2022 Park Service study traces the hundreds of enslaved people on Fort George Island. John McQueen, granted the island in 1791, had brought more than 300 enslaved people, many of whom considered themselves free and had likely been re-enslaved by him after the Revolution; slave trader Zephaniah Kingsley rented the island from 1814 and bought it in 1817. Laborers worked by the task system and could sell crops from their own plots. But stocks have been found in the main-house basement (staff are unsure whether they were used there), and after Kingsley’s death in 1843 his nephew Charles McNeill, at the San Jose plantation, flogged Romeo, and when Romeo ran away offered a reward for him “dead or alive.” Marshall concludes that the evidence contradicts Kingsley’s claims of mild discipline, and calls the violence torture. [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve, Florida (NPS, 2012)
Amani T. Marshall, The Enslaved Communities on Fort George Island: A Special History Study for Timucuan Ecological & Historic Preserve (NPS/OAH, March 2022)

women.html: Anta Majigeen Ndiaye was thirteen, the study says, when Kingsley bought her in Havana in 1806; the special history study, following Senegalese historian Abdou Cisse, identifies her as the daughter of a member of the royal lineage of Jolof, enslaved after her father’s failed challenge for the throne. The study describes Kingsley’s sexual exploitation of her; she was pregnant with his son when she reached his Laurel Grove plantation. Freed with her three children in 1811, Anna Kingsley managed his plantations in his absence. [1] She acquired land and enslaved people of her own; after Florida became a U.S. territory in 1821, oppressive new laws led Anna, her two sons and some former slaves to move to Haiti in 1837. She returned to Jacksonville and died in 1870. [1] The study also records Nansy, who in 1792 petitioned the Spanish governor that she and her husband had freed themselves during the Revolution; no further record of her petition survives. [1]

sources.title: Amani T. Marshall, The Enslaved Communities on Fort George Island: A Special History Study for Timucuan Ecological & Historic Preserve (NPS/OAH, March 2022)
NPSHistory.com: Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve / Fort Caroline archive page — overview (NPS brochure texts) and establishment block

Foundation Document, Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site, Missouri (NPS, June 2016)

ULSG.summary:
White Haven, a two-story house now set amid the suburban development of south St. Louis County, is where Ulysses S. Grant and Julia Dent met and courted in the 1840s and where, in the 1850s, they raised a family and farmed. The Dents bought the place in 1820 as a summer home, far enough from St. Louis to escape its pollution and disease; Dent and Grant ownership lasted until 1885. The historic site preserves 9.65 acres of what the 2016 foundation document calls an 862-acre slave plantation (the 2012 brochure gives the farm as about 850 acres), with the main house, a stone summer kitchen and laundry, a chicken house, an icehouse and a stable. [1] [2]

The Park Service presents White Haven as a microcosm of a nation coming apart. Grant grew up in Ohio, where his father Jesse taught him that slavery was morally wrong; Julia’s father, “Colonel” Frederick Dent, taught his children that slavery was the proper relationship between whites and blacks, held upwards of 30 people in bondage, and supported secession. After resigning from the army in 1854 Grant farmed here, working side by side with the Dent slaves; unseasonable weather, a severe economic depression and prolonged illness set him back, and in 1859 he was forced to abandon farming. [1]

Congress established the site on October 2, 1989. Its foundation document says its significance comes not from a single event but from Grant’s interaction with slavery: White Haven, 1854–1859, is the only place he lived alongside enslaved African Americans, experiences the document calls crucial to understanding his views as the general who won the Civil War and as a president who championed civil rights. [2]

black.html: As president, Grant urged ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment in his 1869 inaugural address; it became part of the Constitution on March 30, 1870. After he reported on Ku Klux Klan violence, Congress passed the Ku Klux Act on April 20, 1871, and on October 17 Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties and sent in federal troops while Attorney General Amos Akerman prosecuted Klansmen. On March 1, 1875, he signed the Civil Rights Act, which barred racial discrimination in public accommodations, travel and juries; Supreme Court rulings stripped it of force by the late 1890s. Little’s 1993 study sees his part in passing that law as foreshadowed by his days working beside the Dent slaves at White Haven, while judging that he evidently did not fully comprehend the plight of Southern blacks. [1] [2]

sources.title: Little, Ulysses S. Grant’s White Haven: A Place Where Extraordinary People Came to Live Ordinary Lives, 1796–1885 — Historic Resource Study (NPS, 1993)
Foundation Document, Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site, Missouri (NPS, June 2016)

slavery.html:
The 1850 slave schedule, as cited in the park’s 1993 historic resource study, counted thirty people enslaved by Frederick Dent: eighteen female and twelve male, aged one to sixty, only six of them adult men. Enslaved laborers cooked and washed in the stone building behind the house, and the Park Service says some of the cooks may have lived in its attic. The men Grant farmed beside belonged to Julia, though they may not have been transferred to her outright; she had grown up with four or five enslaved playmates meant to be her own. [1] [2]

On March 29, 1859, Grant signed a deed freeing William Jones, a thirty-five-year-old man whom he had bought from Frederick Dent; historian Kimberly Little notes that Grant did not state why. When the family moved to Galena in 1860, Julia hired out her four slaves, Eliza, Julia, Dan and John, to St. Louis families. They were freed under Missouri’s new constitution in 1865. [1]

sources.title: Little, Ulysses S. Grant’s White Haven: A Place Where Extraordinary People Came to Live Ordinary Lives, 1796–1885 — Historic Resource Study (NPS, 1993)
NPS, “Summer Kitchen” place page, Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site (nps.gov)

women.html:
Julia Dent grew up in slaveholding Missouri, and White Haven remained the place she and Ulysses called home all their lives. She called herself a “splendid farmer’s wife” and raised Shanghai, Bantam and Brahma chickens. The 2012 park brochure describes her views: comfortable in a life built largely on enslaved labor, she regarded the Dent slaves as “family,” content in their servitude, beliefs that war and Reconstruction challenged. Signing the last deed when they gave it up, she wrote, well-nigh broke her heart. [2] [3]

Julia remembered “Black Mary” as an artist of cakes, biscuits and gumbo, words the park now quotes on its page for the summer kitchen where enslaved cooks worked. Mary Robinson, a Dent family slave, described Grant’s 1854 homecoming. Decades later, at a Sacramento reception, Henrietta Jones, the “Renny” who had gone to California as a nursemaid with Julia’s brother Wrenshall, came forward to greet her. [4] [2]

sources.title: Little, Ulysses S. Grant’s White Haven: A Place Where Extraordinary People Came to Live Ordinary Lives, 1796–1885 — Historic Resource Study (NPS, 1993)

VICK.name: Vicksburg National Military Park
VICK.summary: Vicksburg National Military Park in Vicksburg, Mississippi, preserves the site of the decisive Civil War campaign and 47-day siege that gave the Union control of the Mississippi River. After months of failed approaches, General Ulysses S. Grant executed a brilliant campaign in the spring of 1863, crossing the river south of Vicksburg, winning five battles in 17 days, and laying siege to the city's defenses. The Confederate garrison surrendered on July 4, 1863 — one day after the Union victory at Gettysburg — and President Abraham Lincoln declared that "The Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea." The park, established in 1899, contains over 1,340 monuments, markers, and plaques; a restored Union gunboat (the USS Cairo); and the Vicksburg National Cemetery with over 17,000 Union graves.

VICR.summary:
Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument lies underwater, in the submerged lands off St. John. Its 2001 proclamation says it contains all the elements of a Caribbean tropical marine ecosystem, among them mangroves, seagrass beds, coral reefs, octocoral hardbottom and algal plains, and describes the platform St. John rises from, which runs several miles out before plunging to the Anegada trough to the south and the Puerto Rican trench to the north. Humpback and pilot whales, four species of dolphins, brown pelicans, roseate and least terns, and hawksbill, leatherback and green sea turtles use its waters. [1]

At Hurricane Hole are mangroves the Park Service’s 2016 foundation document calls the most extensive and pristine remaining in the U.S. and British Virgin Islands. More than 30 coral species grow there, among them rare ones; spiny lobster, queen conch and Nassau grouper settle in its shallows as juveniles before moving out to deeper reefs, and vessels use it as a storm mooring in hurricane season. A new genus and species of polychaete worm was identified in its waters in 2014. [2] [1]

President Bill Clinton proclaimed the monument on January 17, 2001, from about 12,708 acres of federal submerged lands, extending the protection of Virgin Islands National Park, created in 1956 and enlarged with 5,650 acres of offshore waters in 1962. The proclamation barred anchoring and all extractive uses except permitted bait fishing in Hurricane Hole and blue runner line fishing south of St. John. Together the park and monument now protect more than 18,000 acres of underwater habitat The park brochure notes that the fastest-growing corals grow only two to three inches a year and that large brain corals are hundreds of years old. [2] [3] [1]

climate.html: Rafe Boulon, chief of resource management for the park and monument, told a 2007 EPA workshop (report published in 2014) that Jack Randall’s team began monitoring Lameshur Bay in 1958. He reported that in 2005 reefs throughout the U.S. Virgin Islands bleached severely amid record-high seawater temperatures; monitored reefs lost 41 to 79 percent of their live stony coral cover, elkhorn coral bleached for the first time on record there, and an unprecedented regional outbreak of coral disease, mostly white plague, followed. The 2016 foundation document reports an average 60 percent decline in coral cover on some reefs within the park from 2005 to 2007, primarily from disease, though elkhorn coral was increasing in some areas by 2015. It expects warmer seas to bring more bleaching and disease, along with ocean acidification and larger storms, and notes that Hurricane Hole is being studied for how its corals respond to a changing climate. [2] [1]

sources.title: U.S. EPA, Coral Reef Monitoring Needs Assessment Workshop, September 11–13, 2007, St. Croix, USVI (EPA/600/R-14/368, 2014), App. F presentation by NPS resource chief Rafe Boulon
NPS, Foundation Document, Virgin Islands National Park / Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument (December 2016)

VIIS.summary:
Just over half of the small, rugged volcanic island of St. John is protected as Virgin Islands National Park: moist forest on the interior mountains, cactus scrub on the dry south-facing slopes, white beaches at Trunk, Cinnamon and Hawksnest bays, and offshore a world of mangroves, seagrass and coral. More than 800 kinds of plants grow here, among them the teyer palm, the island’s only native palm, and the bay rum tree whose leaves once scented a famous cologne; over 50 species of tropical birds breed on the island, and hawksbill and green sea turtles feed in its waters. The reefs are slow work — the fastest corals grow two or three inches a year, and large brain corals are centuries old. [1]

Congress established the park on August 2, 1956, on land that Rockefeller interests had bought and given to the federal government. In 1962 it gained 5,650 acres of submerged lands, in 1978 128 acres on Hassel Island in St. Thomas harbor, and in 2001 a presidential proclamation created the adjoining Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument on 12,708 more acres of sea floor. The Park Service now manages almost 58 percent of St. John’s land and more than 18,000 acres underwater, and in 1976 UNESCO made the park one of the first international biosphere reserves. [1] [2]

People have lived on these islands for at least 3,000 years. The park’s cultural resources include hundreds of historic structures, and its 2016 foundation document is plain about what built the plantation landscape: a plantation economy raised under Danish rule with the forced labor of enslaved people, primarily from Africa. It names the park as a place to explore the experience of the enslaved Africans and the history of slavery in the West Indies. [2]

climate.html: In September and October 2005, after record-warm seawater, an average of 90 percent of the coral cover at the long-term monitoring sites around St. John and St. Croix bleached white. Many corals began to regain their color and were then hit by disease, chiefly white plague — what National Park Service and U.S. Geological Survey scientists called a “one-two punch.” By July 2006 coral cover at the study sites had fallen 48.7 percent, the worst coral mortality the islands had seen from any cause in 40 years; it was also the first time bleaching of elkhorn coral, listed as threatened that May, had ever been observed in the Virgin Islands. [5] The park’s 2016 foundation document records that Caribbean air temperatures rose more than one degree Fahrenheit over the past century and relative sea level is climbing about 3.9 inches per 100 years, and expects more bleaching and disease outbreaks; shoreline erosion is already damaging coastal archeological sites. [2]

sources.title: Patterson, Rogers, Schill & Miller, Coral Bleaching and Disease Deliver “One–Two Punch” to Coral Reefs in the U.S. Virgin Islands (NPS South Florida–Caribbean Network / USGS, October 2006)
Foundation Document, Virgin Islands NP / Virgin Islands Coral Reef NM (2016) — climate change sections

indigenous.html: From St. John it is possible to sight and navigate to Puerto Rico and every island in between, to St. Croix and to all the British Virgin Islands, and the northern Virgin Islands’ cultural chronology corresponds with eastern Puerto Rico’s throughout prehistory. Kenneth Wild of Virgin Islands National Park reports that excavations at Trunk Bay and Cinnamon Bay trace a ceramic sequence beginning around AD 800, and at Cinnamon Bay a ceremonial offering place — an articulated turtle plastron, a decorated vessel of closed ark shells, a carved zemi head, shell and gold inlays for statues — preserved beneath a colonial road in use since the mid-1600s. Wild reads the change in styles around AD 1200 as a pivotal point in the development of Taíno culture. [4] The Reef Bay petroglyphs, which the 2016 foundation document counts among the best-preserved rock art in the Caribbean, were in 2016 the only one of the 22 prehistoric sites recorded on St. John listed on the National Register. The Taíno who met Columbus were decimated by European disease, enslavement and overwork under Spanish colonization. [2] [1]

sources.title: Kenneth S. Wild, A Timeline of Taíno Development in the Virgin Islands (Virgin Islands National Park, 2013; paper to the 25th Congress of the International Association for Caribbean Archaeology)
Foundation Document, Virgin Islands NP / Virgin Islands Coral Reef NM (2016) — “Evidence of Pre-Columbian Taino Indians”
NPSHistory.com: Virgin Islands National Park archive page — 2019 NPS brochure, “Taino People”

slavery.html:
The Danes raised their flag at Coral Bay in 1718; by 1733 nearly all of St. John was in sugar cane and cotton, and enslaved people outnumbered Europeans 1,087 to 208. [1] [2] After drought, a hurricane and insects destroyed the food crops, many fled into the forest, and Governor Philip Gardelin answered with the 1733 Slave Code: flogging, amputation, public torture and execution. Early on November 23, 1733, Akwamu fighters with cane knives hidden in firewood seized the Danish fort at Coral Bay. Led by King Claes, King Juni and Kanta, they fought for six months, until about 400 French soldiers came from Martinique; many then took their own lives. The Park Service calls it the first time enslaved people took control of a colony. [3]

Slavery continued. When Annaberg’s owner James Murphy died in 1808 he held 1,300 acres and 662 enslaved people. After Britain abolished slavery across the strait in 1834, enslaved St. Johnians escaped across the narrow strait — in 1840 eleven fled together to Tortola — until Danish emancipation in 1848. Three rows of foundations from Annaberg’s enslaved laborers’ village survive west of the animal mill. [2]

WAPA.summary:
For the people of Guam, in the words of the park’s brochure, war came early and stayed late. Hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor — December 8, 1941, on Guam’s side of the date line — Japan bombed the U.S. territory, and on December 10 Japanese forces invaded. Under the naval police who ruled the island they renamed Omiyajima, English was forbidden, and Chamorros suspected of hiding family members wanted by the Japanese, or of aiding Americans, were harassed, beaten, tortured or executed. In 1944 men, women and children were made to work at bayonet point digging shelter caves and building defenses, and in early July 10,000 to 15,000 Chamorros were marched to jungle camps with little food or water; many did not survive. On July 21, 1944, 55,000 U.S. troops landed on the Asan and Agat beaches, and the island was declared secure on August 10, at a cost, by the brochure’s count, of over 7,000 American and about 17,500 Japanese casualties. [n]

Congress established War in the Pacific National Historical Park on August 18, 1978. Its seven units, around the villages of Asan, Piti and Agat, keep the invasion beaches, pillboxes, caves and gun emplacements — three Japanese coastal guns at Piti were hauled into place by Chamorros under forced labor — along with the remains of refugee camps where thousands of Chamorros were left homeless. A memorial wall above Asan Bay lists the Americans who died defending and retaking Guam and the people of Guam who suffered and died during 31 months of occupation. More than half the park is coral reef, and the Park Service counts it the most biologically diverse unit in the national park system. [n] [n]

climate.html: The reef fish that were part of the traditional Chamorro diet are still taken for food today, and the reefs are warming. Guam’s shallow reefs bleached every year from 2013 to 2017; heat stress and extreme low tides during the 2014–2015 El Niño ravaged branching Acropora corals on the island’s reef flats, including a site in the park’s Asan unit, and 2017 was the worst year on record for heat stress and bleaching. The Park Service’s 2017 foundation document lists climate change and coral bleaching from rising sea temperatures among the threats to the park’s reefs, and warns that frequent storms and typhoons, long-term climate change and potential sea level rise threaten park facilities and World War II structures that were hastily built and not meant to last 60 years or more. [n] [n] [n]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: War in the Pacific NHP archive page — overview and timeline (from the 2017 NPS brochure) and establishment block
McCutcheon & McKenna, Coral Bleaching, Mortality and Benthic Community Assemblages on the Reefs within the Pacific Island Network National Parks (NPS NRR-2021/2322)

indigenous.html:
The Chamorro people, believed to have come from Southeast Asia, set the houses of the affluent atop stone pillars called latte and were, the 2004 administrative history notes, the only people in Oceania known to have grown rice. Under Spanish rule, in September 1671, some 2,000 Chamorros besieged a fortified church for about forty days, and disease and fighting had left about 3,700 people by 1710, the history reports. [n]

After 1898, the history says, the United States turned more than a third of Guam into a military installation under a Navy governor, starting almost seventy years of military control; by Guam government figures, private landholdings fell by more than a quarter from 1950 to 1952 as military holdings grew. In 1977 Congress let the District Court of Guam hear claims over land taken between 1944 and 1963 without fair condemnation. The history concludes that this military control bred deep local resentment and mistrust, the setting in which the park was born. [n]

WEFA.summary:
In Branchville, Connecticut, the painter Julian Alden Weir found what he called a “quiet plain little house among the rocks.” He acquired the 153-acre farm in 1882 and for nearly 40 years made it his summer home, building a studio, twice enlarging the house, adding a pond and bringing the land to 238 acres. It inspired Weir and his friends Childe Hassam, John Twachtman and Albert Pinkham Ryder, who painted its stones, woodlands, meadows and pond; after 1890 Weir worked more and more outdoors in an Impressionist style, and in 1897 he, Twachtman and Hassam founded the Ten American Painters. [1]

Accounts of how he got it vary. In June 1882 he wrote that a gentleman had offered him, for a painting he had just bought for $560, the price plus a farm of 150 acres in Connecticut; the historian Hildegard Cummings found that he paid the owners, collector Erwin Davis and his wife Emily, a token ten dollars when the land was deeded to him on July 19, 1882. [2]

Weir’s daughter, the painter Dorothy Weir Young, took over the farm after his death; her husband, sculptor Mahonri Young, built a studio there for his This Is the Place monument, unveiled in 1947. After he died in 1957, painters Sperry and Doris Andrews bought it. With its future uncertain amid 1970s development, a grassroots effort won its designation as a national historic site on October 31, 1990; it became a national historical park on January 5, 2021. About 60 acres remain, with 15 historic structures and hundreds of recorded painting sites; the 2017 foundation document calls it the only place in the park system where much of a landscape integral to several generations of artists remains intact. [1] [3]

climate.html: The 2017 foundation document lists climate change among the threats to the landscape the painters recorded: warmer, wetter conditions that make trees and shrubs bloom earlier and change the views, and more extreme rain and heat, flooding, erosion, invasive species and northward shifts in species ranges, all of which it says threaten to alter the cultural landscape. It also warns that the loss of expertise in building dry-stacked stone walls limits the park’s ability to maintain them. [3]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Weir Farm National Historic Site (NPS, 2017), Cultural Landscape threats, p. 17

labor_ccc.html: Hired farmers and servants did much of the work. For seven years Weir had trouble keeping a reliable farmer; one, a Mr. Holsten, was let go after letting 500 heads of celery, a major cash crop, freeze. Then came Paul Remy, a native of Alsace, who ran the farm with his wife and sons for fifteen years, plowing with oxen, haying and cutting oats. The 1900 census lists the Weir household in Ridgefield with four servants, all single Irish-born women: a cook, waitress, nurse and laundress. Historians Deborah Gardner and Christine McKay write that heavy immigration in the 1880s and 1890s made such help affordable on an artist’s earnings; with no heat, running water or electricity at Branchville in the 1890s, it freed Anna Weir to model for her husband and Ella Weir to travel abroad for months at a time — a reality that, they note, with few early exceptions does not appear in Weir’s art. [2]

sources.title: Gardner and McKay, An Artists’ Retreat — Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2009), “Household and Farm Employees,” pp. 69–71

WICA.name: Wind Cave National Park
WICA.summary: Wind Cave National Park in the southern Black Hills of South Dakota protects one of the longest and most complex caves in the world, with over 160 miles of explored passageways, as well as one of the largest remaining mixed-grass prairies in the United States. Wind Cave is distinguished by its extensive boxwork formations — thin calcite fins resembling honeycomb — found in greater quantity here than in any other known cave. The cave is considered sacred by the Lakota people, who know it as "Washun Niya" (the Breathing Hole), and it figures prominently in their creation story as the place from which the Lakota people emerged into the world. Wind Cave was established as the seventh national park in 1903 by President Theodore Roosevelt, making it the first cave to be designated a national park anywhere in the world. The park's surface also supports a free-ranging bison herd descended from animals reintroduced from the Bronx Zoo in 1913.
