Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

WRST.summary:
Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the United States — the brochure counts it as six Yellowstones — a place where four mountain ranges meet and nine of the sixteen highest peaks in the country rise. Mount Wrangell still vents steam near its summit. Near the coast the Bagley Icefield, North America’s largest subpolar icefield, feeds glaciers like the Hubbard and Guyot, and the Malaspina Glacier spills out of the St. Elias Range in a mass larger than Rhode Island. Its more than 9.6 million acres of designated wilderness make up nearly a tenth of the national wilderness system, and with neighboring parks in Canada and Glacier Bay it forms a 24-million-acre World Heritage Site. [1]

This is the homeland of the Ahtna, whose territory takes in the whole Copper River Basin; some 2,500 Ahtna place names — nearly every drainage, hill and ridge named — attest to the length of their presence. Yakutat, on the coast, is a traditional Tlingit fishing village. From 1911 to 1938 the Kennecott mines near McCarthy shipped copper by rail to Cordova, and their ruins are a national historic landmark. President Carter proclaimed the area a national monument on December 1, 1978, and Congress established the 13.2-million-acre park and preserve on December 2, 1980, where local rural residents may still hunt, fish and trap for subsistence. [1] [2]

climate.html: The Tlingit named the Malaspina Glacier Sít’ Tlein, Big Glacier. At about 2,400 square kilometres it is the world’s largest piedmont glacier, and it is thinning by more than a metre a year. A 2023 radar-mapping study found that two-thirds of it is grounded below sea level, its bed cut by channels that reach more than 350 metres below sea level, and that only a narrow, eroding strip of ice-cored land separates it from the Gulf of Alaska — where lagoons have formed in front of the glacier in recent decades. If the sea breaks through, the authors warn, retreat could be rapid, and the glacier holds enough ice to raise global sea level by 1.4 millimetres. [4]

sources.title: Tober et al., Comprehensive Radar Mapping of Malaspina Glacier (Sít' Tlein), Alaska, Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface 128 (2023)

indigenous.html: The Copper River, called ’Atna’ or “beyond river” in Ahtna, runs 290 miles from the Wrangells to the Gulf of Alaska, and the Ahtna have worked and traded its copper for centuries — archeologists think for 500 to 1,000 years. In 1885 Chief Nicolai showed Lt. Henry Allen a copper vein, and later revealed a source to prospectors for a cache of supplies. Some writers demeaned him as an innocent who traded a multimillion-dollar mine for food; Pratt (1998), as summarized in the 2024 ethnographic overview, argued instead that he was canny in his dealings and that his death in 1899 or 1900 opened the floodgates to rapid outside exploitation. Simeone and Miller call the Kennecott mine one of the grandest colonial land thefts in early twentieth-century Alaska: the Ahtna received no compensation for the land or the ore, though they could ride the railroad free. Ahtna reaction to the 1978 monument, the authors write, was mixed: many supported protection for the lands their subsistence depended on, but Alaska Native people felt their voices were sidelined at points in the debates over land selections and protected areas. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

labor_ccc.html: At Kennecott, a 14-story concentrator stepped down the hillside so gravity could carry ore through the mill. In 1916 the mines produced 101,410,000 pounds of copper; William Douglass, later Kennecott’s superintendent, reckoned it achieved a third of the Anaconda mine’s production in Butte with only 500 workers to Anaconda’s 15,000. The mill town was ordered by rank, the manager’s house and staff quarters at its center; the bunkhouses had no facilities for families, so married miners usually left theirs behind. In June 1917 miners struck — the only strike at Kennecott — for a flat wage instead of one that slid with copper prices. In arbitration 45 days later the company kept its sliding scale but granted a 50-cent daily raise and a new bunkhouse, mess hall and recreation hall at the Bonanza Mine; it refused collective contracts and rehired only one member of the Miners Committee. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscape Report: Kennecott Mill Town, Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve (NPS, 2001), Part I Site History

women.html: Two Ahtna elders, Katie John and Doris Charles, pushed the federal government into managing subsistence fishing across much of Alaska. In 1983 they and the Mentasta Village Council asked the state to let them fish at Tanada Creek, which the state had closed to fishing in 1964; at Batzulnetas, their natal village, salmon had been taken for hundreds of years. Refused, they sued. In March 1994 a federal court ruled that the federal government could manage subsistence fisheries on navigable waters, and the ruling was upheld in April 1995. Thousands marched in Anchorage in their support, Rosa Parks among them. John said she fought so her grandchildren would remember the way she had learned. Their victory opened Batzulnetas and extended federal subsistence jurisdiction to more than half of Alaska’s navigable waters. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

YOSE.summary:
Yosemite covers 747,956 acres of the central Sierra Nevada: granite domes and cliffs, waterfalls, three groves of giant sequoias, alpine meadows and the headwaters of the Tuolumne and Merced rivers, which supply drinking water to millions of people in the San Francisco Bay Area. About a million years ago glaciers moved down the river valleys — ice in Yosemite Valley may have been 4,000 feet thick — and carved the U-shaped valley visitors know today. More than 94 percent of the park is designated wilderness. [2]

Oral tradition and archeological evidence, the Park Service’s 2016 foundation document says, suggest people have lived continuously in the Yosemite region for at least 8,000 years, and seven present-day tribes descend from those who first called it home. On June 30, 1864, President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, giving Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove to California to be held for public use, resort and recreation, inalienable for all time — the first scenic natural area set aside by the United States for public benefit. Congress created the surrounding national park on October 1, 1890; California returned the valley and the grove in 1905 and Congress accepted them in 1906. [2] [1]

More than four million people a year now enter the park. Its own documents describe a landscape still being remade — by rockfall and flood, by fire after a century of protecting the sequoias from it, and by a warming climate pushing the pika upslope — and a human history that includes the 1851 militia campaign against the valley’s Ahwahneechee people. [2] [1] [3]

black.html: From 1891 to 1914, before the Park Service existed, the U.S. Army guarded Yosemite and the other Sierra parks. In 1899 the 24th Infantry patrolled the backcountry, and the 9th Cavalry followed in 1903 and 1904 — both regiments of African American soldiers, the Buffalo Soldiers, formed after the Civil War. Shelton Johnson argues that the nearly 500 soldiers who served over those three years were long left out of the park’s histories; Carl Russell’s One Hundred Years in Yosemite never names either regiment. He calls them invisible men and contends that such gaps in history are made, not accidental. The Park Service’s 2016 foundation document now names the Army’s role, including the Buffalo Soldiers, in its statement of the park’s significance. [4] [2]

sources.title: Johnson, Invisible Men: Buffalo Soldiers of the Sierra Nevada (NPS Yosemite, undated), pp. 1–6
Foundation Document, Yosemite National Park (NPS, 2016), significance statement 12

climate.html: The 2019 park brochure points to the pika, a small, heat-intolerant animal of the high-country rock piles, whose habitat is shifting upward as the climate rapidly warms — and asks where pikas will go when they run out of mountain. The 2016 foundation document names climate change a key issue: drought had already killed large numbers of ponderosa pines and other trees at lower elevations, and less snowpack and earlier runoff could bring longer, drier summers, larger and more intense wildfires and more flooding as precipitation falls as rain. The park is restoring meadows, riverbanks and the Mariposa Grove and using prescribed and managed fire; the brochure notes that a century of protecting sequoias from fire had harmed the trees it meant to save. [1] [2]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Yosemite archive page — 2019 NPS brochure (“High Sierra”, “Sequoia Groves”)
Foundation Document, Yosemite National Park (NPS, 2016), Key Issues: Climate Change; Planning and Data Needs

indigenous.html:
The Ahwahneechee, a Southern Sierra Miwok tribelet, lived in and around the valley they called Ahwahnee. Gold Rush miners and settlers burned their villages and felled oak groves; Indians had no civil or legal rights. Governor John McDougal — who, Greene writes, had once spoken to the legislature of the inevitability of the extermination of the Indian race — authorized a militia: the 200-man Mariposa Battalion under trader James Savage, mustered in January 1851. Savage threatened to annihilate Chief Tenaya’s people if they resisted, then burned their dwellings and food caches to starve them onto reservations. In May another company shot two captives trying to escape; one was Tenaya’s youngest son. [3]

In June 1852 Army troops shot five Indians found with clothing suspected to be the murdered prospectors’. In 1907 the Army took Koomine, the valley’s largest village, as a camp and forced out its residents; in 1969 the Park Service moved the last family from its 1933 Indian Village and burned it. [3]

sources.title: Greene, Historic Resource Study, Vol. 1 (NPS, 1987), ch. I, sections A, C–E (pp. 1–28)

labor_ccc.html: Ten Civilian Conservation Corps camps operated in Yosemite between May 1933 and October 1940, with 6,816 enrollees assigned — unemployed, unmarried young men of 18 to 25 typically earning thirty dollars a month, twenty-five of which went home to their families. Each camp held 225 to 250 men, mostly from cities, alongside local recruits and experienced local men. They built log curbing and paths around Yosemite Village, revived the 250 apple trees settler James Lamon had planted, and replaced the posts of the Half Dome cable route, drilling 41 holes into the rock by hand while roped to the posts. The Cascades camp on Highway 140 was wiped out in the 1937 flood. [6]

sources.title: Orr, The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) in Yosemite, Yosemite (Yosemite Association), Vol. 67 No. 4, Fall 2005, pp. 2–4

women.html: Enid Michael, a third-grade teacher from Pasadena, moved to the park in May 1919 and became one of the four members of Yosemite’s first Nature Guide Service. She published 195 articles in Yosemite Nature Notes and from 1931 directed the planting of a wildflower garden behind the Yosemite Museum, funded by a $4,000 gift from Marjorie Montgomery Ward, that came to hold more than a thousand plants. Some male colleagues resented a woman in the job: in 1923 she rallied the California Federation of Women’s Clubs to press for a permanent appointment, and a handwritten note on a 1937 memo said Civilian Conservation Corps boys should work under a male naturalist, the word underlined four times. After twenty-one seasonal reappointments, her service ended on September 30, 1942. [5]

sources.title: Peñalosa, Enid Michael: Yosemite’s First Woman Ranger-Naturalist, Yosemite (Yosemite Association), Vol. 66 No. 3, Summer 2004, pp. 3–6

ZION.summary:
In Zion Canyon the North Fork of the Virgin River has cut a gorge whose sandstone walls rise 2,000 to 3,000 feet above the canyon floor. The park’s Navajo sandstone cliffs, among the highest in the world, expose remnants of the largest known sand-dune system, and springs seeping from the rock feed hanging gardens. Zion sits where the Colorado Plateau, Mojave Desert and Great Basin meet, and its elevations, from 3,600 to 8,700 feet, hold desert tortoise and honey mesquite in the low canyons and fir, aspen and elk on the plateaus; the rare Zion snail lives only in its hanging gardens. [1] [1]

People have lived here for thousands of years — hunters who tracked mammoths and camels, the farmers now known as Ancestral Puebloans, and the Southern Paiute people who followed. Mormon pioneers came in the 1860s and farmed the river terraces. On July 31, 1909, President William H. Taft set aside 15,200 acres as Mukuntuweap National Monument; it was enlarged and renamed Zion National Monument in 1918, made a national park in 1919, and joined by the Kolob Canyons in 1956. The park now covers 148,733 acres, 84 percent of it designated wilderness in 2009. [1] [1]

The park’s own brochure says Zion is beautiful but not pristine: 150 years of farming, grazing and recreation have changed it, and exotic tamarisk and cheatgrass are replacing native willow and grasses. Flash floods that once destroyed towns and droughts that burned crops, it adds, are threats that still exist today. [1]

climate.html: A 2025 Park Service science report found that by the end of its 2000–2019 study period the growing season across Zion’s vegetation was starting 5.8 days later and ending 7.6 days later, with peak growth 7.4 days later; the best multivariable indicator of plant production was three years of precipitation. A 2018 Park Service brief projected that under a high-emissions pathway suitable summer climate would cease to occur for 32 bird species by mid-century, potentially extirpating them from the park, while it would become suitable for 15 species not found there today — placing Zion in the high-turnover group of parks. [1] [1]

sources.title: Thoma, Landscape Phenology, Vegetation Condition, and Relations with Climate at Zion National Park, 2000–2019 (NPS/SR—2025/287)
NPS, Resource Brief: Birds and Climate Change, Zion National Park (2018)

indigenous.html:
Southern Paiute time here, the park’s ethnographic overview (1997, revised 2013) reports, began when the people were created and given the right to use and the obligation to protect these lands. Most, it says, believe they were, or are related by marriage to, the people archaeologists call the Virgin River Anasazi — a relationship still debated. Tony Tillahash told a 1936 researcher that Muhuntuweap, the name for lower Zion Canyon, meant the land of his maternal grandfather Muhun. [1]

The overview’s chronology records depopulation of up to 90 percent for local groups after European diseases arrived, raids for Paiute children, and new diseases causing losses of up to 75 percent between 1847 and 1862, the years Mormon colonists occupied key irrigable lands and waters. An 1865 treaty negotiated with a handful of Utah Paiutes was never ratified, leaving Paiutes without treaty rights. Congress terminated four Utah Paiute bands in 1954; the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah regained federal recognition in 1980. [1]

sources.title: Stoffle, Austin, Halmo & Phillips, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment: Zion National Park and Pipe Spring National Monument (1997, revised 2013)

labor_ccc.html: From 1933 to 1942 Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees were stationed at Zion, working under Park Service landscape architects and engineers. They built and maintained trails, quarried and dressed stone, rehabilitated irrigation ditches and built the Temple of Sinawava parking lot. On the river, after 1933 CCC crews temporarily rerouted the Virgin River and stacked quarried sandstone into heavy wire baskets, building revetments that straightened the channel and protected park facilities from flooding; such revetments were built into the 1960s. Many revetments were later expanded or altered, but much CCC stonework survives; the 2006 landscape inventory cites the retaining walls of Walter’s Wiggles on the West Rim Trail. Southern Paiute adults, the ethnographic overview notes, also joined CCC Indian camps and worked on the highways near Zion. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Cultural Landscapes Inventory: Zion Canyon, Zion National Park (2006)
Stoffle et al., Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (1997, rev. 2013), Table 1.1
